It also checks whether the multiprofile and avgpool benefit carries over to another modality. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: Without an image-only reference, any multimodal result could not be attributed to complementary fusion rather than to images being strong or weak on their own. Establishing the image baseline first also shows whether multimodal configurations are worth further budget. Swapping the RNA encoder is a narrower question that can follow.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 was the first image-only run. It kept the best RNA-only setup's profile setting and aggregator (multiprofile, avgpool) and replaced the RNA PCA (n=2000) input with a ResNet50 image encoder, with no fusion. Validation accuracy was 0.3275 (primary metric) and F1 was 0.2884, well below the matched RNA-only avgpool run (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1) and also below the RNA single-profile baseline (0.4849). This suggests that, in this configuration, the image features carry less directly usable signal than RNA PCA features. This is a single run with unknown variance, and only one image encoder, aggregator, and profile setting were tried. It therefore remains uncertain whether images are weak in general or this ResNet50 setup is suboptimal (e.g., pretraining or fine-tuning choices), and whether images could still add complementary information in multimodal fusion; an image single-profile run would be needed to check whether the multiprofile benefit carries over to images.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best model so far is RNA-only PCA, multiprofile with avgpool (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). Avgpool clearly beat the transformer in that setting. Image-only ResNet50 with the same multiprofile avgpool setup was much weaker (0.328 accuracy). The central open question for this study is whether images add complementary signal to RNA, and no multimodal run exists yet. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the best configuration fixed (PCA n=2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and only adds the ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_002 isolates whether adding images helps or hurts the RNA model. Comparing it with config_011 shows the effect of adding RNA to the image model. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: whether to use multimodal fusion at all decides which part of the remaining space is worth exploring. A clean one-factor comparison is therefore more valuable now than tuning the RNA encoder or the image encoder. Concat is the simplest fusion baseline, and weighted fusion can be tested next if the result is promising. Even a null or negative result is informative, because it would justify concentrating the remaining budget on RNA encoders such as scVI and scGPT.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 was the first multimodal run. It kept the best RNA-only configuration fixed (PCA n=2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion, so it is a one-factor comparison with llm_summary_002 (adding images) and with llm_summary_004 (adding RNA to the image-only model). Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6186 (+0.028) and F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6103 (+0.038), making this the best result so far. This is an initial indication that the image features, though weak alone (0.3275 accuracy), may add complementary signal to RNA. The gain is modest, every configuration has been run only once, and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the improvement may not be robust. It also remains untested whether the benefit holds or grows with other fusion schemes (e.g., weighted fusion), other image or RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), other aggregators, or a single-profile setting.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is the dominant signal. RNA-only PCA with multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, while image-only ResNet50 reached 0.328. Adding images to the RNA model gave only a modest gain (0.619, F1 0.610). Profile setting and aggregation have each been probed once: multiprofile beat single-profile, and avgpool beat transformer. The RNA encoder has never been varied, even though it feeds the strongest branch. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only PCA n=2000 for scGPT. That cleanly measures whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats PCA, without fusion or image effects confounding the comparison. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: RNA quality drives most of the performance, so this one-factor test is likely to move accuracy more than changing fusion or the image encoder. It also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into the many remaining multimodal configurations. If scGPT helps, the natural next step is the scGPT multimodal analogue (config_042). If not, the search can focus on PCA-based multimodal variants such as weighted fusion or ViT-L. Either outcome prunes a large part of the search space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 was a one-factor test of the RNA encoder. It kept llm_summary_002's configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion) and replaced PCA (n=2000) with scGPT. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5305 (-0.060), and F1 fell in step from 0.5727 to 0.5152, so in this setting scGPT underperformed PCA. It still exceeded the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849) and was roughly comparable to the PCA transformer-aggregator run (0.5191). This is an initial indication that PCA is the stronger RNA encoder here and the better default for multimodal runs. However, each configuration was run only once with unknown variance, and the evidence does not show whether scGPT is inherently weaker or depends on choices not examined (e.g., embedding extraction, fine-tuning, or preprocessing). It also remains untested whether the ranking holds for other aggregators, for scVI, or in multimodal fusion, where scGPT could still behave differently.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal config_018 (PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.6186 accuracy and 0.6103 F1. That is a modest gain over RNA-only PCA avgpool (0.5907). Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.3275), so it is unclear whether images are weak in general or ResNet50 is a poor image encoder here. The image encoder is the largest untested lever in the leading configuration. 2) Test: config_024 keeps everything in config_018 fixed and swaps ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This one-factor comparison isolates the image encoder's effect on the multimodal model. If ViT-L gives a clearly larger gain over RNA-only, a stronger image representation is the key. If it matches or falls below config_018, the image contribution is likely capped regardless of encoder. 3) Budget: this experiment both exploits the most promising direction (multimodal, PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) and resolves a major uncertainty. That uncertainty is likely larger than the fusion choice (concat vs weighted), which can be tested next on whichever image encoder wins.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 was a one-factor test of the image encoder in the leading multimodal configuration (PCA n=2000 RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, concat fusion), replacing ResNet50 (llm_summary_005) with ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose slightly from 0.6186 to 0.6287 (+0.010), the best so far and +0.038 over RNA-only PCA avgpool (0.5907). Validation F1, however, fell from 0.6103 to 0.5993 (-0.011), so the two metrics disagree and ViT-L did not produce the clearly larger multimodal gain that would mark the image representation as the key lever; the image contribution may be modest regardless of encoder. All results are single runs with unknown variance, so this roughly 1-point difference may not be robust. It also remains uncertain whether ViT-L is stronger than ResNet50 on its own (no image-only ViT-L run), whether its F1 drop reflects worse class balance, and whether weighted fusion would change the encoder ranking.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: multiprofile avgpool clearly beats single-profile and transformer aggregation for RNA PCA. PCA beats scGPT. Adding images with concat fusion gives a modest gain (0.5907 to 0.6186 with ResNet50, 0.6287 with ViT-L). However, ViT-L and ResNet50 disagree on F1, so the image encoder ranking is unclear. Fusion strategy is a core multimodal design choice and has never been tested. 2) This run keeps the current best configuration fixed (PCA n=2000, ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. That makes it a clean one-factor comparison with config_024. It will show whether a learned modality weighting extracts more of the weak but complementary image signal, and whether it recovers the F1 lost relative to ResNet50. 3) Under a limited budget, it resolves the largest untested multimodal design question while also exploiting the strongest configuration, so it can both raise the best accuracy and inform all later fusion choices. A follow-up with ResNet50 weighted fusion (config_019) could check whether any fusion effect holds across image encoders.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 was a one-factor test of fusion. It kept the leading multimodal configuration fixed (PCA n=2000 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L images, multiprofile, avgpool) and replaced concat fusion (llm_summary_007) with weighted fusion. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose slightly from 0.6287 to 0.6352 (+0.007), the best so far and +0.045 over RNA-only PCA avgpool (0.5907). Validation F1 rose more clearly, from 0.5993 to 0.6183 (+0.019), now also exceeding ResNet50 concat (0.6103), so weighted fusion appears to recover the F1 shortfall seen with ViT-L concat. These are single runs with unknown variance, so the small accuracy gain may not be robust, and the evidence does not show whether the learned weighting actually up-weights the image signal or whether the fusion benefit generalizes to other image encoders (e.g., ResNet50 weighted fusion is untested) or to other aggregators and RNA encoders.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only PCA avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, image-only only 0.328, and adding images gave a modest +0.045 at best (0.635 with ViT-L weighted fusion). PCA beat scGPT in the matched RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting (0.591 vs 0.530). scVI, the third RNA encoder, has never been tested, so RNA representation, the most influential choice, is only partly mapped. 2) What this tests: config_005 is a clean one-factor comparison against config_002 (PCA) and config_008 (scGPT). It keeps RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed and swaps in scVI (n=200), with no image or fusion effects to confound it. This shows whether a compact learned latent space can match or beat PCA. 3) Why now: if scVI beats PCA, it becomes the natural RNA backbone for the leading multimodal setup (e.g., config_037). If it does not, PCA is confirmed as the default, and the remaining budget can go to fusion and aggregation refinements without leaving a major encoder option unexplored.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 was a one-factor test of the RNA encoder. It kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting of llm_summary_002 (PCA n=2000) and llm_summary_006 (scGPT), with no image encoder or fusion, and swapped in scVI (n=200). Validation accuracy (primary metric) reached 0.6501, up from 0.5907 for PCA (+0.059) and 0.5305 for scGPT (+0.120), and F1 (0.6275) rose in step. This RNA-only run is the best result so far, exceeding even the leading multimodal configuration (PCA plus ViT-L with weighted fusion: 0.6352 accuracy, 0.6183 F1). This suggests that RNA representation is a stronger lever than adding images, and that scVI is a promising RNA backbone. However, the swap also changed latent dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so encoder type cannot be separated from dimension. All results are single runs with unknown variance, and it remains untested whether scVI's advantage holds or adds to image signal in multimodal fusion (e.g., scVI plus ViT-L weighted fusion), with other aggregators, or in a single-profile setting.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI (n=200) is the strongest RNA encoder so far. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool scVI reached 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1, beating PCA at 0.591. With the PCA backbone, adding ViT-L images through weighted fusion gave the best multimodal result (0.635 / 0.618), about +0.045 over PCA RNA-only. The key open question is whether images still add complementary signal once the RNA representation is stronger, or whether the earlier multimodal gain only made up for weaker PCA features. 2) This run swaps PCA for scVI in the best multimodal configuration (ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion). That makes it a one-factor comparison against config_025 (RNA encoder effect within multimodal). It is also a one-factor comparison against config_005 (adding images to the scVI RNA-only model). 3) It is the logical exploitation step with the highest expected accuracy, and it also answers an important design question: is the image contribution additive with a strong RNA encoder? Either outcome is informative. A gain supports multimodal fusion. No gain or a loss suggests RNA representation dominates and the remaining budget should go to RNA-side choices. Single runs with unknown variance mean small differences should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 swapped PCA (n=2000) for scVI (n=200) in the leading multimodal configuration (ImageNet ViT-L images, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion). This makes it a one-factor comparison with llm_summary_008 (RNA encoder within multimodal) and with llm_summary_009 (adding images to scVI RNA-only). Validation accuracy (primary metric) reached 0.7062, the best so far, up from 0.6501 for scVI RNA-only (+0.056) and 0.6352 for PCA multimodal (+0.071), and F1 rose in step to 0.6671 (+0.040 and +0.049). This suggests that the image contribution is not merely compensating for weaker PCA features: the image gain appears at least as large with scVI (+0.056) as with PCA (+0.045), so RNA and image signals may be complementary and possibly additive. These are single runs with unknown variance, so the exact gain sizes are uncertain. The scVI swap also changes latent dimensionality, so encoder type and dimension remain confounded. It is also untested whether this advantage depends on weighted fusion (scVI with concat is untested), the ViT-L encoder, avgpool aggregation, or the multiprofile setting.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest baseline. It has no aggregation or fusion components, so it measures how much signal plain transcriptomic features carry. Later runs can each change one factor against it: a learned encoder (scvi, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (config_002/003), image features, or fusion. 3. Starting with the simplest reference gives the most interpretable anchor for the one-factor comparisons that follow. It also guards against assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better. It is a cheap, informative first use of the limited budget.
experiment_summary: This first experiment (llm_summary_001) set up the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using PCA with 2000 components, with no image encoder, aggregation or fusion. It was chosen as a reference point for later comparisons that change one factor at a time. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, and its validation F1 of 0.464 was close to that, which suggests performance is fairly even across classes. This shows that plain transcriptomic PCA features carry some predictive signal, but the result is only an initial observation. No comparison runs exist yet, so we cannot tell whether learned RNA encoders (e.g., scVI or scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image features or fusion would do better. We also cannot judge how stable this number is across seeds or splits, or whether the PCA dimensionality is a sensible choice.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). It shows transcriptomic features carry some signal. We know nothing yet about the image modality, which appears in 42 of the 50 remaining configurations (all image-only and multimodal runs). 2) What this tests: config_010 is the simplest image-only counterpart to the baseline. It keeps the single-profile setting, uses a standard ResNet50 encoder, and has no aggregation or fusion. It answers one question: how much predictive signal do image features provide alone, compared with RNA PCA? 3) Why this is the best next experiment: Whether images are informative is the design choice with the largest effect on where the rest of the budget goes. If images are weak, we can focus on RNA encoders and profile aggregation. If they are comparable or stronger, multimodal fusion becomes worth testing, and the ViT-L encoder comparison becomes a priority. Other single-factor changes, such as multiprofile avgpool (config_002) or scVI (config_004), each refine only a smaller part of the space, so they are better tested afterward.
experiment_summary: This experiment (llm_summary_002) tested the simplest image-only counterpart to the RNA baseline: a single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 and a validation F1 of 0.172, well below the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1). The somewhat larger gap between accuracy and F1 hints at less even performance across classes. As an initial observation, ResNet50 image features alone appear to carry much weaker predictive signal than RNA PCA features in this single-profile setting. Because modality and encoder changed together, and only one run exists per configuration, it remains uncertain whether the weakness lies in the image modality itself or in the ResNet50 representation (e.g., versus ViT-L), whether multiprofile aggregation would help image features, whether images could still add complementary signal through fusion with RNA, and how stable these numbers are across seeds or splits.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (config_001: 0.485 acc, 0.464 F1) clearly beats image-only ResNet50 (config_010: 0.208 acc, 0.172 F1). So RNA is the stronger modality so far. Each result is a single run, though, and we know nothing yet about profile setting, aggregation, alternative encoders or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only one factor from the best baseline. It switches from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, keeping RNA-only and PCA fixed. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles adds predictive signal over a single profile. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Profile setting is a core design axis that affects most remaining configurations, both unimodal and multimodal. Testing it on the strongest and simplest modality gives a clean, interpretable answer. Avgpool is the least complex aggregation, so it answers the multiprofile question before the transformer aggregation adds more uncertainty. The result will directly guide whether later encoder and fusion comparisons should focus on single-profile or multiprofile settings.
experiment_summary: This experiment (llm_summary_003) changed only the profile setting from the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1), switching to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation and no image encoder or fusion. It reached 0.591 validation accuracy and 0.573 validation F1, the best result so far. The small gap between accuracy and F1 suggests performance stays fairly even across classes. Because this is a one-factor comparison against the baseline, it suggests that pooling multiple profiles adds predictive signal for RNA PCA features, though each configuration has only a single run, so seed or split variability could account for part of the roughly 0.11-point gain. It remains uncertain whether the benefit carries over to image features or fusion models, whether a richer aggregation such as a transformer would do better than avgpool, and whether learned RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT would interact differently with the multiprofile setting.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries far more signal than ResNet50 images (0.485 vs 0.208 accuracy). Switching to multiprofile with avgpool improved RNA PCA from 0.485 to 0.591 accuracy, with F1 rising in step (0.464 to 0.573). The RNA representation is still completely untested, even though PCA, scVI and scGPT each define a large share of the remaining unimodal and multimodal configurations. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder (PCA n2000 to scVI n200) on the current best setup, keeping multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation fixed. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional transcriptomic representation beats PCA when profiles are pooled. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: the encoder choice affects many downstream configurations, including fusion models, so resolving it now prunes the search space more than testing transformer aggregation (config_003) or adding images (config_018). It also stays close to the strongest observed direction, so it remains a reasonable exploitation step. These are single runs, so the result should be read as a guide for further tests rather than a definitive ranking.
experiment_summary: This experiment (llm_summary_004) changed only the RNA encoder relative to the previous best setup (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, PCA n2000; 0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1), replacing PCA n2000 with the lower-dimensional learned scVI n200 representation and keeping no image encoder or fusion. It reached 0.650 validation accuracy and 0.628 validation F1, the best result so far, and F1 rose along with accuracy with a similarly small gap, suggesting performance stays fairly even across classes. Because this is a one-factor comparison, it suggests scVI n200 outperforms PCA n2000 for RNA features under multiprofile avgpool pooling. Each configuration has only a single run, though, so seed or split variability could account for part of the roughly 0.06-point gain. It remains uncertain whether the advantage is due to the learned representation or its lower dimensionality, whether it holds in the single-profile setting or with transformer aggregation, how scGPT would compare, and whether scVI also gives the strongest RNA branch in fusion models with image features.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Two one-factor comparisons point the same way. Going from single-profile to multiprofile avgpool helped RNA PCA (0.485 to 0.591). Replacing PCA n2000 with scVI n200 under multiprofile avgpool helped further (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). The aggregation choice has never been tested, so we cannot tell whether avgpool is limiting the multiprofile gains. 2. What this tests: Changing only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer on the current best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI n200) isolates the effect of aggregation. It also builds on the strongest direction found so far. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Aggregation is shared by nearly all remaining multiprofile configurations, including every multiprofile fusion model. Learning whether a transformer beats avgpool will narrow many later choices at once. It does this without adding the confound of the weak image modality, and it could plausibly give a new best result.
experiment_summary: This experiment (llm_summary_005) changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer on the previous best setup (llm_summary_004: RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI n200, no image encoder or fusion; 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). It reached 0.653 validation accuracy and 0.628 validation F1, essentially the same as avgpool: accuracy rose by about 0.003 and F1 was nearly unchanged, with a similarly small gap suggesting fairly even performance across classes. As a one-factor comparison, this suggests the transformer gives no clear advantage over avgpool in this RNA-only scVI setting, and avgpool does not appear to be a major bottleneck. However, with a single run per configuration, the difference is well within plausible seed or split variability. It remains uncertain whether a transformer would help with other encoders (e.g., PCA, scGPT), with image features, or in multiprofile fusion models, and whether its extra cost is justified given that the simpler avgpool performs about as well.

selection_reason: Evidence: across single runs, multiprofile input (+0.11 accuracy over single-profile) and the scVI n200 encoder (+0.06 over PCA) both appear to help. Transformer aggregation gave no clear gain over avgpool (0.653 vs 0.650). ResNet50 image-only was weak (0.208 accuracy), but no experiment has yet tested whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA. This is the central open question of a multimodal study. Test: config_030 adds a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the current strongest simple RNA setup (config_005: multiprofile, scVI n200, avgpool, 0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Everything else stays fixed, so any difference in accuracy and F1 can be attributed to adding image features through simple fusion. Why now: avgpool is the cheaper, equally good aggregation, and concat is the simplest fusion. This gives a clean first estimate of multimodal benefit or harm, and the result will guide later choices: whether to explore weighted fusion and ViT-L features, or to focus the remaining budget on RNA encoders such as scGPT.
experiment_summary: This experiment (llm_summary_006) added a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the strongest simple RNA setup (llm_summary_004: multiprofile, scVI n200, avgpool; 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) and kept everything else fixed. It reached 0.632 validation accuracy and 0.607 validation F1, a drop of about 0.02 on both metrics, and the accuracy–F1 gap stayed similarly small. As a first estimate of multimodal benefit, simply concatenating ResNet50 image features did not help and may slightly hurt compared with RNA alone, which fits the weak image-only result (llm_summary_002: 0.208 accuracy). However, the change bundles the image modality, the ResNet50 representation and concat fusion together, and each configuration has only a single run, so the small decline may fall within seed or split variability. It also remains uncertain whether weighted or learned fusion, stronger image features such as ViT-L, or transformer aggregation would let images add complementary signal rather than dilute the RNA features.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA choices have produced the largest gains so far. Multiprofile pooling gave about +0.11 accuracy over the single-profile PCA baseline, and scVI n200 gave about +0.06 over PCA n2000. Aggregation made little difference (transformer 0.653 vs avgpool 0.650). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion slightly hurt (0.632). The third RNA encoder, scGPT, has never been tested, even though it is an available choice for every remaining fusion setting. 2) This run swaps only the RNA encoder, scVI n200 to scGPT, in the best simple setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool; config_005 at 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). It shows whether a foundation-model RNA representation beats scVI and therefore which RNA branch multimodal models should build on. 3) Best use of the budget: the RNA encoder is the most influential factor seen so far. Resolving this one-factor comparison either finds a stronger baseline or confirms scVI before spending runs on fusion and image-encoder variants. Those variants depend on having the strongest RNA branch, and current evidence suggests they add little.
experiment_summary: This experiment (llm_summary_007) changed only the RNA encoder, from scVI n200 to the scGPT foundation-model representation, within the strongest simple setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion; llm_summary_004: 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). It reached 0.530 validation accuracy and 0.515 validation F1, about 0.12 below scVI on both metrics and also below multiprofile PCA n2000 (llm_summary_003: 0.591 accuracy). The accuracy–F1 gap stayed small, which suggests performance remains fairly even across classes. Because this is a one-factor comparison and the drop is much larger than the small differences seen in other single runs, it suggests that scGPT embeddings, as used here, are a weaker RNA branch than scVI and that scVI n200 remains the preferred base for fusion and image-encoder experiments. It remains uncertain whether the shortfall reflects scGPT itself or how it was applied (e.g., embedding extraction, dimensionality, lack of fine-tuning). Single-run variability is also unresolved, as is whether scGPT would fare differently with transformer aggregation, single-profile input or fusion models.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best results so far are RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI n200 runs (0.650–0.653 accuracy). Swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation made almost no difference. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_030) slightly lowered accuracy, to 0.632, and F1, to 0.607. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208). It is still unclear whether images truly add nothing or whether naive concatenation simply dilutes the strong RNA features. 2. What this tests: config_031 changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, while keeping scVI n200, ResNet50, multiprofile input and avgpool. This isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only, the concat drop was a fusion problem and images may still add complementary signal. If it stays below RNA-only, that strengthens the case that ResNet50 image features add little. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: fusion is the main untested design axis, and this is a clean one-factor comparison against an existing run. Its result will guide whether later budget goes to stronger image encoders (ViT-L) under the better fusion method or back to refining RNA-only models. Changing the image encoder now would leave fusion and encoder effects harder to separate.
experiment_summary: This experiment (llm_summary_008) changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, relative to llm_summary_006 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool; 0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1). It reached 0.678 validation accuracy and 0.646 validation F1, the best result so far. That is about 0.046 above concat fusion and about 0.025 above the best RNA-only runs (llm_summary_004/005: 0.650–0.653 accuracy, about 0.628 F1), with a similarly small accuracy–F1 gap suggesting fairly even performance across classes. Because the comparison with llm_summary_006 isolates fusion, it suggests that the earlier multimodal drop came at least partly from naive concatenation, and that ResNet50 image features may add complementary signal under weighted fusion despite being weak on their own (llm_summary_002: 0.208 accuracy). However, each configuration has only a single run, so it is uncertain whether the smaller gain over RNA-only exceeds seed or split variability; the learned modality weights and their contribution are not reported; and it remains open whether stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or transformer aggregation would extend the gain under weighted fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Its edge over RNA-only (about 0.65) is about 0.025, which suggests weighted fusion lets images add some signal. However, ResNet50 is weak on its own (0.208 accuracy), and no ViT-L image encoder has been tested anywhere, so image representation is the largest untested design choice. Aggregation matters less: transformer and avgpool were nearly identical for RNA-only scVI. 2. What this tests: config_037 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps the best setup otherwise fixed. This shows whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal under weighted fusion. It also helps tell whether earlier weak image results came from the modality itself or from ResNet50 features. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It is a clean one-factor test of an important unexplored choice, and it builds directly on the strongest configuration. It has good odds of improving on the current best, and the result is informative either way. A gain would favor ViT-L for later aggregation tests. No gain would suggest image features add little beyond what weighted fusion already extracts.
experiment_summary: This experiment (llm_summary_009) changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, relative to the previous best setup (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 RNA, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1). It reached 0.706 validation accuracy and 0.667 validation F1, the best result so far: about 0.029 above ResNet50 and about 0.055 above the best RNA-only runs (llm_summary_004/005: about 0.650–0.653 accuracy). Its accuracy–F1 gap of about 0.04 is slightly wider than in earlier runs. Because this is a one-factor comparison, it suggests that a stronger image representation lets images add more complementary signal under weighted fusion, and that the earlier weak image results came at least partly from ResNet50 features rather than only from the image modality. However, each configuration has a single run, so the roughly 0.03-point gain may partly reflect seed or split variability. ViT-L has not been tested image-only or with concat fusion, and the learned modality weights are not reported. It also remains open whether transformer aggregation or other image encoders would improve on this configuration.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (multiprofile, scVI n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). It came from a chain of one-factor improvements: multiprofile input, scVI, weighted fusion and ViT-L. Aggregation is the one design choice not yet tested in the fusion setting. In RNA-only scVI, transformer aggregation was essentially tied with avgpool (0.653 vs 0.650). It is still uncertain whether a transformer helps when the pooled profiles carry richer ViT-L image features, which are combined with RNA through weighted fusion. 2) Test: This changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, on the best configuration. It isolates whether attention-based pooling across profiles adds value in the multimodal setting. 3) Why now: It is the most direct extension of the current best model and a clean one-factor comparison. If it improves, it likely sets a new best. If it ties again, that is stronger evidence that the simpler avgpool is sufficient, and the remaining budget can go to fusion and image-encoder questions such as ViT-L with concat fusion or ViT-L image-only.
experiment_summary: This experiment (llm_summary_010) changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer on the previous best configuration (llm_summary_009: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L images, weighted fusion; 0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). It reached 0.725 validation accuracy and 0.685 validation F1, the best result so far, about 0.019 above avgpool on accuracy and 0.018 on F1, with a similar accuracy–F1 gap of about 0.04. Because this is a one-factor comparison, it tentatively suggests that attention-based pooling across profiles may add value in this multimodal ViT-L setting, even though transformer aggregation was essentially tied with avgpool in the RNA-only scVI setting (llm_summary_005 vs 004: 0.653 vs 0.650). However, each configuration has a single run and the gain is modest, so seed or split variability could account for much of it. It also remains untested whether the transformer interacts specifically with image features or fusion (e.g., with ResNet50 or concat fusion), how ViT-L performs image-only or with concat fusion, and what the learned modality weights are.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest, cheapest reference point in the design space. Every later comparison can be measured against it: scVI or scGPT versus PCA, multiprofile versus single-profile, image-only versus RNA-only, and multimodal versus unimodal. 3) With a limited budget, a clean baseline is the best first use of an experiment. It shows how much the more complex choices add, if anything, without assuming they help. Running a complex configuration first would leave its result hard to attribute to any one design choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 ran the simplest reference configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 and a validation F1 of 0.464. The F1 is slightly below the accuracy, which may point to uneven performance across classes, but this is not confirmed. No other experiments have been run, so this is an initial baseline and not evidence for or against any design choice. It is still unknown whether alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings, image-based inputs, or multimodal fusion would improve on it. The variance across seeds or runs is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: we have only one result, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about how informative the image modality is, and that is the biggest open question for a multimodal study. Whether fusion, image encoders or multiprofile image aggregation are worth exploring depends heavily on whether images carry useful signal on their own. 2) This experiment tests the simplest image-only setup: single profile, ResNet50 encoder, no aggregation or fusion. It is directly comparable to the RNA-only baseline because the profile setting is the same and there is no aggregation. The comparison gives an initial estimate of image-only versus RNA-only performance. 3) Why now: it changes one major factor (modality) relative to the existing result. If images are weak, the search can deprioritize image-heavy configurations. If they are competitive, multimodal fusion and image encoder comparisons become promising. With a limited budget, this tells us more than a smaller tweak such as changing the RNA encoder or adding aggregation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image-only configuration: single profile, ResNet50 image encoder, no RNA encoder, aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 and a validation F1 of 0.172, well below the RNA-only PCA baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1). This is an initial sign that this image-only setup carries less discriminative signal than the RNA-only baseline. However, the comparison changes modality and encoder together and rests on single runs with unknown seed variance, so it cannot show whether the gap reflects the image modality itself or this particular ResNet50 setup. It also remains unknown how this result compares with chance, whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would improve image performance, and whether images could still add complementary value in multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: So far there are two single runs. The RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (config_001) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. The image-only ResNet50 model (config_010) did much worse, at 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. RNA is therefore the strongest starting point. Whether a multiprofile setting helps is still untested, and it is one of the main design axes. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the modality (RNA-only) and encoder (PCA, 2000 components) the same as the baseline. It changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Any change in accuracy or F1 can then be attributed to multiprofile input, without aggregation complexity as a confound. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: the answer applies to many remaining configurations, both unimodal and multimodal, so it reduces uncertainty broadly. It also builds on the best-performing modality, which may improve performance directly. Testing image encoders or fusion now would build on a weak image signal. Encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) remain good candidates for later single-variable experiments.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only PCA (2000 components) setup from the llm_summary_001 baseline but switched from single-profile to multiprofile input, aggregated with average pooling. Validation accuracy rose to 0.591 from 0.485, with F1 rising similarly to 0.573 from 0.464. This is the best result so far and suggests that multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation may help the RNA-only PCA model. The experiment changes the profile setting and adds aggregation together, so it cannot separate a multiprofile effect from the avgpool choice. Each configuration was run once with unknown seed variance, and it remains untested whether other aggregation methods, other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), or multiprofile image or multimodal settings would show similar gains.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA multiprofile with avgpool (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1), well above the single-profile baseline (0.485, 0.464). That comparison changed the profile setting and added aggregation together, so it cannot show whether the gain comes from multiprofile input generally or from avgpool specifically. Each result is also a single run with unknown seed variance. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps the modality, encoder and multiprofile setting fixed and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the aggregation choice within the strongest setup. If accuracy and F1 hold up or improve, the multiprofile gain is not tied to avgpool. A clear drop would suggest the aggregation method matters. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it is a one-variable extension of the current best direction, so it exploits that evidence while resolving a design choice that every multiprofile configuration depends on, including RNA, image and multimodal ones. Knowing which aggregation works better first should make later encoder and fusion comparisons cheaper to interpret under the limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best-so-far RNA-only PCA (2000 components) multiprofile setup from llm_summary_003 and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. It reached 0.519 validation accuracy and 0.480 F1. That is a clear drop from avgpool (0.591, 0.573) but still above the single-profile baseline (0.485, 0.464). Since aggregation was the only change, this is an initial sign that the aggregation choice matters and that avgpool outperformed this transformer aggregator here, while multiprofile input appears to help under both aggregators. However, each configuration was run once with unknown seed variance, and the transformer's hyperparameters, capacity and training adequacy are unknown, so it remains uncertain whether the gap is robust, whether a tuned transformer or other aggregators would close it, and whether the pattern carries over to other RNA encoders or to image and multimodal multiprofile settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA multiprofile with avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1). It beats the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519). Image-only ResNet50 was much weaker (0.208). The RNA encoder choice is entirely untested, even though RNA appears to be the dominant signal. 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional representation helps or hurts compared with PCA. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: The encoder choice affects every later multimodal configuration, so resolving it early guides the remaining search. Testing it within the strongest known setup gives a realistic chance of a new best. It is also more informative per experiment than adding weak image features or changing fusion before the RNA side is better understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best-so-far RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup from llm_summary_003 and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA (2000 components) to scVI (200 latent dimensions). It reached 0.650 validation accuracy and 0.628 F1, a new best, up from 0.591 and 0.573 with PCA. Because the encoder was the only change, this is an initial sign that the scVI-200 representation outperformed PCA-2000 in this setting. Encoder type and dimensionality change together, so the experiment cannot tell whether the gain comes from learned versus linear features or from the lower dimensionality. Each configuration was run once with unknown seed variance, so it remains uncertain whether the gap is robust, whether other encoders (e.g., scGPT) or other scVI sizes would do better, and whether the advantage holds under other aggregators, single-profile input, or multimodal fusion with image features.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: With RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed, swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.628. This is the best result so far, so the RNA encoder looks like an important design choice. Avgpool also beat the transformer aggregator (0.591 vs 0.519). The third RNA encoder, scGPT, is still untested. 2) Test: config_008 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. This completes a one-variable comparison of all three encoders under the strongest aggregation and profile settings, and shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats scVI. 3) Why now: The encoder has produced the largest single-factor gain so far, so finishing this comparison both exploits that lead and may find a new best. It also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal fusion tests, so the costly multimodal experiments are not built on a weaker RNA backbone. Results are single runs with unknown seed variance, so small differences should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best-so-far RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup and changed only the RNA encoder to scGPT, completing a one-variable comparison of the three RNA encoders. It reached 0.530 validation accuracy and 0.515 F1, below both scVI-200 (0.650, 0.628) and PCA-2000 (0.591, 0.573) under the same settings, which is an initial sign that this scGPT representation was the weakest of the three encoders here and that scVI-200 remains the strongest RNA backbone so far. All runs are single runs with unknown seed variance, and the scGPT setup details (embedding dimensionality, pretraining checkpoint, whether it was frozen or fine-tuned, preprocessing compatibility) are not described. It therefore remains uncertain whether the gap is robust, whether a differently configured or fine-tuned scGPT would close it, and whether the encoder ranking holds under other aggregators, single-profile input, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI-200 with multiprofile avgpool (config_005: 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). In one-variable comparisons, scVI beat PCA and scGPT, and avgpool beat transformer aggregation. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208 accuracy), but that was single-profile. It is completely untested whether image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA. 2. Test: config_030 keeps the best RNA setup exactly the same (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with the simplest fusion, concat. Comparing it directly with config_005 isolates whether adding the image modality helps, hurts or does nothing. ResNet50 is the only image encoder with a reference result, so this avoids confounding the test with an untested encoder. 3. Why now: multimodal fusion is the largest unexplored design axis and covers most of the remaining search space. Testing it on the strongest backbone exploits current evidence and resolves a major uncertainty. The outcome will guide whether to explore fusion variants and ViT-L, or to focus remaining budget on the RNA-only branch. Both results are single runs with unknown seed variance, so a small difference from config_005 should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_005 (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool) and added ResNet50 image features with concat fusion. This makes it a one-variable test of whether adding the image modality helps. It reached 0.632 validation accuracy and 0.607 F1, slightly below the RNA-only result (0.650, 0.628). This is an initial sign that naive concat fusion of ResNet50 features did not add complementary signal and may have slightly hurt, so scVI-200 RNA-only remains the best configuration so far. The gap is small and both are single runs with unknown seed variance, so the difference may not be robust. It also remains untested whether other fusion strategies, other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), image feature normalization or weighting, or other aggregators would let images contribute; multiprofile image-only performance is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is scVI-200 RNA-only with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation (config_005: 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion (config_030) gave a slightly lower result (0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1). Single-profile ResNet50 image-only was weak (0.208 accuracy). So it is unclear whether images carry no useful signal or whether naive concat lets weak, high-dimensional image features dilute the strong RNA representation. 2. What this tests: config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted and keeps everything else in config_030 fixed. This is a clean one-variable test of fusion strategy. Weighted fusion can learn to down-weight the weaker image modality, so it tests whether a better fusion lets images match or exceed the RNA-only best. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: Whether the image modality can add value is the main open question for multimodal design. Fusion is the cheapest and most directly comparable lever, since it builds on the current best RNA backbone. If weighted fusion beats 0.650, it is an immediate gain and points to further multimodal exploration, such as swapping in ViT-L. If it does not, that strengthens the case that ResNet50 features add little, and the remaining budget can go to the image encoder or to RNA-side refinements.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the multimodal setup from llm_summary_007 (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted. This makes it a one-variable test of fusion strategy. It reached 0.678 validation accuracy and 0.646 F1, a new best, above both concat fusion (0.632, 0.607) and the RNA-only scVI-200 result from llm_summary_005 (0.650, 0.628). This is an initial sign that weighted fusion outperformed concat here and that, with this fusion, adding ResNet50 image features may give a modest gain over RNA-only, so the earlier concat result may have reflected the fusion method rather than an absence of image signal. However, the gains are small (about 2.8 points over RNA-only) and all results are single runs with unknown seed variance. The learned modality weights are not reported, so it is unclear how much the image branch actually contributes versus effects of the fusion mechanism itself. It also remains untested whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), other fusion methods, or other aggregators would extend the gain, and multiprofile image-only performance is still unknown.

selection_reason: Evidence: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI-200, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.678 acc, 0.646 F1). It modestly beats RNA-only scVI (0.650) and concat fusion (0.632). So weighted fusion appears to let image features contribute. The image branch looks weak, though: single-profile ResNet50 image-only reached only 0.208, and no other image encoder has been tested. Test: config_037 keeps every setting of the current best and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain. Why now: it builds on the strongest direction so far and also resolves the largest untested design choice, the image encoder. Either outcome is useful. A gain would point to image representation quality as the bottleneck. No gain would suggest the improvement comes from the fusion mechanism or that image signal is limited, which would argue for checking multiprofile image-only performance next. Both results are single runs, so a small difference should be treated as tentative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best-so-far multimodal setup from llm_summary_008 (scVI-200 RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, making it a one-variable test of image representation quality. It reached 0.706 validation accuracy and 0.667 F1, a new best, up from 0.678 and 0.646 with ResNet50 and above the RNA-only scVI-200 result (0.650, 0.628). This is an initial sign that the stronger image encoder increased the multimodal gain under weighted fusion, consistent with image representation quality being a bottleneck. However, the improvement is modest (about 2.9 points), all results are single runs with unknown seed variance, and the learned modality weights and multiprofile image-only performance (for either encoder) are unreported, so it remains uncertain how robust the gain is, how much the image branch contributes on its own, and whether ViT-L would also help under concat fusion, other aggregators, or other image encoders.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). It beats RNA-only scVI-200 (0.650) and the ResNet50 multimodal run (0.678). However, the only image-only result is the weak single-profile ResNet50 run (0.208). The image branch's standalone strength under multiprofile avgpool has never been measured, for either encoder. So we cannot tell whether the multimodal gains come from real image signal or from the fusion mechanism. 2) What this tests: config_014 is config_037 with the RNA branch removed (ViT-L image-only, multiprofile, avgpool). It measures how much signal ViT-L images carry on their own under the best profile and aggregation settings. It also shows whether multiprofile aggregation helps images as it did for RNA, and whether ViT-L is much stronger than ResNet50 on its own. 3) Why now: Under a limited budget, this one experiment explains the source of the current best result. That tells us whether further work should go to image encoders or fusion, or whether the multimodal gain may be fragile. It is more informative than small exploitation variants such as transformer aggregation, which underperformed in the RNA-only comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 removed the RNA branch from the best-so-far multimodal configuration (llm_summary_009: scVI-200 + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), leaving a ViT-L image-only multiprofile avgpool model. This gave the first standalone measurement of the image branch under these settings: 0.332 validation accuracy and 0.315 F1. That is well below RNA-only scVI-200 (0.650, 0.628) and the multimodal best (0.706, 0.667), but above the single-profile ResNet50 image-only run (0.208, 0.172). The improvement over that ResNet50 run cannot be attributed to ViT-L or to multiprofile aggregation, because encoder and profile setting changed together. Overall this is an initial sign that the images carry real but weak standalone signal, and that the roughly 5.6-point multimodal gain over RNA-only arises from combining a weak image signal with strong RNA. It remains uncertain whether that gain reflects complementary image information or the weighted-fusion mechanism itself, because learned modality weights, chance-level accuracy, multiprofile ResNet50 image-only performance and seed variance are all unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about any design choice. We do not yet know whether modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters, or how well a minimal model does. 2. What it tests: config_001 is the simplest configuration, an RNA-only single-profile model with a PCA (2000) encoder. It sets a low-complexity reference point for validation accuracy and F1. Each design choice can later be added to it one at a time: scVI or scGPT encoders (004, 007), multiprofile aggregation (002, 003), the image modality (010), and fusion (016, 017). 3. Why it is the best next experiment: under a limited budget, a clean baseline lets later single-factor comparisons be read clearly. It also avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models will help. Starting with a complex configuration would mix several design choices together and make early results hard to attribute.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 and a validation F1 of 0.464. The F1 is close to the accuracy, which loosely suggests no severe class imbalance in predictions, but this is uncertain. Because this is the first completed experiment, it is a baseline only. It gives no evidence about whether other encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or fusion would improve performance. Run-to-run variance is also unknown, so later single-factor comparisons against this reference should be read cautiously.

selection_reason: 1) The only evidence is one RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). Nothing is known yet about the image modality, which half of all remaining configurations depend on. 2) Running config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50) tests whether imaging alone carries useful signal compared with RNA. It keeps the simple single-profile, no-aggregation, no-fusion setup, so modality is the main difference. 3) Whether images are competitive, complementary, or weak decides whether multimodal and image-encoder comparisons are worth the budget. That makes this a broader uncertainty-reducing step than an RNA encoder swap (config_004/007) or an aggregation test (config_002), which can follow next.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 and a validation F1 of 0.172, well below the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.485, F1 0.464). This is an initial observation that, in this simple single-profile setup, imaging alone carried weaker discriminative signal than RNA. However, modality and encoder change together here (ResNet50 vs PCA), so the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone. It also remains unknown whether other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion with RNA would help, whether image features add complementary information despite weak standalone performance, and how large run-to-run variance is.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there are only two runs so far. The RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464) clearly beats the image-only ResNet50 baseline (acc 0.208, F1 0.172), so RNA is the stronger anchor. Whether multiprofile aggregation helps is completely untested, and that choice affects most of the remaining search space across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor from the best configuration, moving from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. The RNA encoder (PCA) and modality stay the same, so any accuracy or F1 difference can be attributed to the profile setting. 3) Why now: answering whether multiprofile context adds signal tells us how to weight about two-thirds of the untested configurations. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it gives a clean reference before trying the transformer. It is cheaper to interpret than adding image fusion or swapping encoders, and it extends the most promising branch (RNA).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation, without image encoder or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.591 and F1 of 0.573, about 0.11 above the single-profile RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.485, F1 0.464) on both metrics. Because the encoder and modality were held fixed, this is suggestive evidence that multiprofile context with avgpool adds useful signal for RNA-only PCA models. However, the profile setting and the aggregator change together, both comparisons are single runs with unknown run-to-run variance, and it remains untested whether the gain carries over to image-only or multimodal settings, other RNA encoders, or stronger aggregators such as a transformer.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It beat the single-profile PCA baseline by about 0.11 on both metrics. Image-only ResNet50 was much weaker (0.208), so the multiprofile RNA direction is the strongest lead. The aggregator has not been varied, so we cannot yet separate the benefit of multiprofile context from the choice of avgpool. 2. Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA encoder) and swaps only avgpool for a transformer. This isolates the aggregation effect and shows whether a learned aggregator extracts more from profile context than simple averaging. 3. Why now: Aggregation is shared by every remaining multiprofile configuration, including the multimodal ones, so settling avgpool vs transformer early informs most of the search space. It also exploits the current best direction while changing a single factor. Encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) and fusion can follow once the better aggregator is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and transformer aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It changed only the aggregator relative to llm_summary_003, which used avgpool. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519 and an F1 of 0.480. That is below the avgpool variant (acc 0.591, F1 0.573) by about 0.07 accuracy and 0.09 F1, though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.485, F1 0.464). Because only the aggregator was swapped, this is a direct but single-run observation that, in this setup, the transformer aggregator underperformed simple averaging, so avgpool remains the current best choice. It is uncertain whether the gap reflects run-to-run variance, transformer hyperparameters or training (e.g., capacity, optimization, data size), or a real limitation, and whether the ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image-only, or multimodal multiprofile settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only PCA multiprofile with avgpool is the current best (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It beat single-profile PCA by about 0.11 and the transformer aggregator by about 0.07. Image-only ResNet50 single-profile was weak (acc 0.208), but we do not yet know whether image features add complementary signal when combined with RNA. Modality is the largest untested design axis. 2) This experiment adds ResNet50 image features to the best setup using simple concat fusion, keeping the PCA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool fixed. Comparing it with config_002 isolates the effect of adding the image modality. 3) It both exploits the strongest known configuration and resolves the key open question of whether multimodality helps. Concat is the simplest fusion and makes a clean baseline before testing weighted fusion, ViT-L image features or other RNA encoders. A single run with unknown variance should still be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 added ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion to the previous best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_003: multiprofile, PCA n2000, avgpool), keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregator fixed. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.619 and an F1 of 0.610, which is about 0.028 accuracy and 0.038 F1 above llm_summary_003 (acc 0.591, F1 0.573), making it the new best configuration. Because only the image modality (with its necessary concat fusion) was added, this is direct initial evidence that ResNet50 image features carry some complementary signal when combined with RNA, even though image-only single-profile performance was weak (llm_summary_002: acc 0.208). The gain is modest and comes from a single run with unknown run-to-run variance, so it may partly be noise; it also remains untested whether other fusion strategies (e.g., weighted fusion), stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), other RNA encoders, or other aggregators would increase or change the multimodal benefit.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal so far (RNA-only 0.485 vs image-only 0.208). Multiprofile avgpool helped clearly (0.591), and adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave a modest gain to the current best (config_018: acc 0.619, F1 0.610). The RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis: every RNA-containing run so far used PCA n2000, and scGPT and scVI have not been tried at all. 2) Test: swap PCA n2000 for scGPT while keeping everything else in config_018 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat). This is a single-factor comparison that shows whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA in the strongest known setup. 3) Why now: RNA dominates performance, so the choice of RNA representation likely matters more than the image encoder or fusion variant. Running the test on the current best setup also exploits the promising direction and could set a new best. If it underperforms, that is still informative and can be followed by scVI or by an RNA-only scGPT check.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the current best setup fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; llm_summary_005: acc 0.619, F1 0.610) and replaced only the PCA n2000 RNA encoder with scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.512 and F1 of 0.477, about 0.107 accuracy and 0.133 F1 below llm_summary_005, and also below the RNA-only multiprofile PCA model (llm_summary_003: acc 0.591), though slightly above the single-profile RNA-only PCA baseline (acc 0.485). Because only the RNA encoder changed, this is a direct single-run observation that scGPT embeddings, as used here, underperformed PCA in this setup, so PCA n2000 remains the best tested RNA encoder. It is uncertain whether this reflects run-to-run variance, how the scGPT embeddings were extracted or adapted (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned, dimensionality, gene vocabulary overlap), or a poor interaction with concat fusion or avgpool. An RNA-only scGPT run or an scVI comparison would help separate encoder quality from multimodal interaction effects.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; acc 0.619, F1 0.610). Adding ResNet50 image features to the RNA-only multiprofile PCA model gave a modest gain of about 0.03 accuracy and 0.04 F1. ResNet50 alone was weak (acc 0.208). PCA beat scGPT as the RNA encoder, and avgpool beat the transformer aggregator, though each comparison is a single run. The image encoder has never been varied, so it is unclear whether the small multimodal benefit is limited by weak ResNet50 features. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. It directly measures whether a stronger image representation increases the complementary image signal. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean one-factor comparison against the current best on the largest untested representation choice. It also has a plausible chance of improving the best result. Weighted fusion (config_019) and scVI (config_030) remain good follow-ups, but this question comes first because the image encoder choice likely sets how much fusion can gain.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the current best setup fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, avgpool, concat; llm_summary_005: acc 0.619, F1 0.610) and swapped only the ResNet50 image encoder for ImageNet ViT-L. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.629 and F1 of 0.599, about 0.010 higher in accuracy but 0.011 lower in F1 than the ResNet50 version, making it the nominal best on the primary metric; both multimodal variants remain above the RNA-only multiprofile PCA model (llm_summary_003: acc 0.591, F1 0.573). Because only the image encoder changed, this is a direct single-run comparison, but the evidence is mixed: the small accuracy gain and F1 drop are well within plausible run-to-run variance and point in opposite directions, so it does not clearly show that a stronger image representation increases the complementary image signal, and the lower F1 may hint at less balanced per-class performance. It remains uncertain whether ViT-L truly beats ResNet50 (repeated seeds would help), whether ViT-L alone carries more standalone signal (no image-only ViT-L run), and whether concat fusion is limiting the image contribution, which untested weighted fusion or scVI-based variants could clarify.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Several design choices now have single-run evidence. Multiprofile beat single-profile, avgpool beat transformer, and PCA beat scGPT. Adding images helped modestly. ResNet50 and ViT-L are roughly tied: ViT-L had slightly higher accuracy (0.629 vs 0.619) but lower F1 (0.599 vs 0.610). Fusion strategy has never been varied, so concat may be limiting how much the image features contribute. 2. What this tests: config_025 keeps the nominal best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ViT-L, avgpool) and swaps only concat for weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion. It also shows whether weighting can recover the F1 drop seen with ViT-L. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: fusion is the main design axis with no evidence yet, and this is a clean single-factor change on the strongest setup, so it is both exploratory and likely to perform well. scVI is the other untested axis and can be checked next against whichever fusion wins.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the nominal best setup fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool; llm_summary_007: acc 0.629, F1 0.599) and swapped only concat fusion for weighted fusion, the first test of the fusion axis. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.635 and an F1 of 0.618, about +0.007 accuracy and +0.019 F1 over the concat version. It also edges out the ResNet50+concat run on both metrics (llm_summary_005: acc 0.619, F1 0.610), making it the new best configuration on both metrics. Because only fusion changed, this is a direct but single-run observation that weighted fusion performed at least as well as concat with ViT-L and recovered the F1 drop seen in llm_summary_007, which loosely suggests concat may have limited the image contribution or class balance; however, the accuracy gain is small and within plausible run-to-run variance. It remains uncertain whether the benefit is real across seeds, whether weighted fusion would also help with ResNet50 (so the encoder–fusion interaction is unresolved), what the learned weights imply about modality contributions, and how scVI or other untested fusion and aggregation variants would compare.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best configuration so far is config_025 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.635, F1 0.618). PCA clearly beat scGPT when both were tested in the same setup (about 0.11 accuracy). scVI is the only RNA representation never tested, in any setting. The image-encoder and fusion differences seen so far are small and could be noise, so the RNA encoder is the largest open question. 2. What this tests: config_037 changes only the RNA encoder of config_025, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200. This directly shows whether a compact latent representation of RNA can match or beat PCA within the current best multimodal pipeline. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: RNA has been the dominant source of signal, so the choice of RNA representation likely matters more than further small fusion or image-encoder tweaks. A one-factor swap from the best configuration keeps the comparison clean. It also has a real chance of producing a new best, while settling whether PCA should stay fixed for the rest of the search.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the previous best configuration fixed (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.635, F1 0.618) and swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scVI n200, the first test of scVI in any setting. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.706 and an F1 of 0.667, about +0.071 accuracy and +0.049 F1 over the PCA version, making it the new best configuration on both metrics. Because only the RNA encoder changed, this is direct single-run evidence that scVI n200 outperformed PCA n2000 in this pipeline, and the gap is much larger than the earlier image-encoder and fusion differences (about 0.01). Together with the scGPT result (llm_summary_006), it reinforces that the RNA representation is a high-leverage axis. Several points remain uncertain. Run-to-run variance is unknown. Encoder type and dimensionality (200 vs 2000) change together, so the gain cannot be attributed to the compact latent space specifically. It is untested whether scVI's advantage holds in RNA-only or single-profile settings or with ResNet50, concat fusion or other aggregators. The F1 gap relative to accuracy widened slightly (about 0.039 vs 0.017 before), which may hint at less balanced per-class performance.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Swapping PCA n2000 for scVI n200 gave the largest single-factor gain so far (+0.071 accuracy, reaching 0.706 in config_037). In contrast, image-related changes were small: adding ResNet50 gave about +0.03, and the image-encoder and fusion swaps gave about +0.01. We do not know whether scVI's gain also holds without images, or whether image features still add complementary signal once the RNA representation is stronger. 2. What this tests: config_005 is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI n200 with avgpool. Compared with config_037, it removes only the image modality, which shows how much ViT-L plus weighted fusion contributes on top of scVI. Compared with config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA, avgpool), it changes only the RNA encoder, which shows whether scVI's advantage is intrinsic to the RNA representation or comes from a multimodal interaction. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: One run answers two questions at once. If RNA-only scVI comes close to 0.706, the image branch adds little and the remaining budget should go to RNA and aggregation choices. If it falls clearly short, multimodal fusion is confirmed as worthwhile, and later runs can refine fusion and aggregation with scVI. This makes it more useful than a marginal exploitation step such as a transformer-aggregator variant, which is already weakly disfavoured by the PCA results.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with scVI n200 and avgpool, and no image encoder or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.650 and F1 of 0.628, which gives two single-factor comparisons. Relative to the PCA n2000 RNA-only version (llm_summary_003: acc 0.591, F1 0.573), it gained about +0.059 accuracy and +0.055 F1. This is direct initial evidence that scVI's advantage over PCA is largely intrinsic to the RNA representation, similar in size to the +0.071 gain seen in the multimodal setting. Relative to the best multimodal scVI model (llm_summary_009: acc 0.706, F1 0.667), removing the image branch (ViT-L plus weighted fusion) cost about 0.056 accuracy and 0.040 F1, suggesting images still add complementary signal on top of a stronger RNA encoder, at least as large as the roughly +0.045 seen with PCA (llm_summary_008 vs llm_summary_003). Uncertainties remain: all comparisons are single runs with unknown run-to-run variance; removing images also removes weighted fusion, so the encoder and fusion contributions are not separated; scVI's latent dimensionality (200 vs 2000) is confounded with encoder type; and scVI remains untested in single-profile settings, with ResNet50, with concat fusion, or with other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against one change at a time: swapping the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), switching to multiprofile with avgpool or transformer, using image-only, or adding an image modality with concat or weighted fusion. 3) Measuring this simple baseline first is the most budget-efficient start. It anchors every later comparison and avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models will win. The following experiments can then probe one design factor at a time.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849 (supporting F1 of 0.4639). This is an initial reference point, not evidence for or against any design choice, because no other configurations have been run yet. It remains unknown whether alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only models, or multimodal fusion (concat, weighted) would improve on this baseline, and the run-to-run variance of this result has not been characterized.
