selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the only result so far is an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about how informative the image modality is on its own, and that is the biggest open question in the design space, because about 42 of the remaining configurations are image-only or multimodal. 2) This run tests a simple image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion. It changes only the modality relative to the baseline, so the result gives a clean RNA-vs-image comparison. It also tells us whether images carry enough signal to make the multimodal configurations worth pursuing. 3) Under a limited budget, finding out early whether images are weaker, comparable, or stronger than RNA will decide whether to spend later runs on RNA encoder variants or on image encoders and fusion. That makes it a better next step than a within-RNA tweak such as scVI or multiprofile, which would leave the modality question unresolved.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079 (supporting F1 of 0.1718), well below the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). This initial observation suggests that, in this setup, the image representation carries less discriminative signal on its own than the PCA RNA representation. However, switching modality also switched the encoder, so the comparison cannot separate a weakness of the image modality from the specific ResNet50 setup. Each configuration has only one run with uncharacterized variance, and it remains unknown whether other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion with RNA (concat, weighted) would add complementary information on top of the RNA baseline, so a weak image-only result does not by itself rule out multimodal gains.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: the RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. The ResNet50 image-only single-profile model was much weaker at 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. Each result comes from one run, so variance is unknown. A weak image-only result also does not show whether image features add complementary information to RNA. 2) This experiment adds the ResNet50 image branch to the existing PCA single-profile baseline using simple concat fusion. Encoder and profile setting stay the same, so the only change from config_001 is adding the image modality. Comparing the two directly tests whether multimodal fusion helps, does nothing, or hurts when the second modality is weak. 3) Whether multimodality is worth pursuing determines how much of the remaining budget, which is mostly multimodal configurations, deserves attention. Answering it now with a one-factor change is efficient. Concat is the simplest fusion and gives a clean reference for later tests of weighted fusion, multiprofile aggregation and alternative encoders.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 added a ResNet50 image branch to the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) single-profile baseline using simple concat fusion, with no aggregation. Relative to config_001 (llm_summary_001), the only change was adding the image modality. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5266 (supporting F1 of 0.5104), above both the RNA-only baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1) and the image-only ResNet50 model from llm_summary_002 (0.2079 accuracy, 0.1718 F1). Because this was a one-factor comparison, it is an initial indication that the image features may add complementary signal to RNA despite being weak alone. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized variance, so the ~4-point accuracy gain is not yet confirmed as robust, and it remains unknown whether weighted fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or alternative RNA/image encoders would improve on this concat reference.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: So far there is one run each, with no variance estimate. RNA (PCA n=2000) carries most of the signal at 0.485 accuracy. ResNet50 image-only is weak at 0.208. Combining them with concat fusion gave the best result so far, 0.527 accuracy and 0.510 F1, which tentatively suggests the image features add complementary signal. Multiprofile aggregation is untested and is one of the largest open design axes. 2) What this tests: config_018 keeps the best configuration (config_016: PCA, ResNet50, concat) fixed and changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles helps the current best pipeline. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it gives a clean first look before trying transformer aggregation. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: it builds directly on the most promising result while resolving a major untested design choice with a single-factor change. Either outcome is useful. A gain points toward exploring aggregation further, including transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. No gain shifts priority to the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) or the fusion type.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best prior configuration (multimodal, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, concat fusion from llm_summary_003) fixed and changed only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6186 (supporting F1 of 0.6103), about 9 points above the single-profile concat model (0.5266 accuracy, 0.5104 F1) and the best result so far. Because this was a single-factor change, it is an initial indication that multiprofile avgpool aggregation helps this pipeline, and the gain is the largest observed so far. However, each configuration has only one run with uncharacterized variance. Avgpool has also only been tested in this multimodal concat setting, so it remains unknown whether the benefit carries over to RNA-only or image-only models, whether transformer aggregation or weighted fusion would add further gains, and whether alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) would change the picture.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile avgpool aggregation gave the largest gain so far (0.527 to 0.619 accuracy, F1 0.510 to 0.610) in the multimodal PCA + ResNet50 concat pipeline (config_018). This suggests aggregation over profiles is a high-leverage design axis. However, only avgpool has been tested, and each result comes from a single run. 2. What this tests: config_020 keeps config_018 fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This shows whether a learned, attention-based aggregation captures more from multiple profiles than simple averaging, or whether avgpool is already enough. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It builds on the strongest signal so far with a clean one-factor comparison against the current best. Its result will guide which aggregation to carry into later tests of fusion type (weighted) and encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L). Weighted fusion and alternative encoders remain important open questions for later experiments.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best prior configuration fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, concat fusion from llm_summary_004) and changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5793 (supporting F1 of 0.5631). That is about 4 points below the avgpool counterpart (0.6186 accuracy, 0.6103 F1), though still above the single-profile concat model (0.5266 accuracy, 0.5104 F1). Because this was a one-factor comparison, it is an initial indication that learned attention-based aggregation did not beat simple averaging in this setup, and that the multiprofile benefit held under both aggregators, so avgpool remains the current best choice. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized variance, and transformer aggregation was tested with only one setup, whose hyperparameters were not reported. It therefore remains unknown whether the gap is robust or reflects tuning and sensitivity to data size, and whether the ranking would hold with weighted fusion or alternative encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; 0.6186 accuracy, 0.6103 F1). Single-factor changes have already shown signals for adding images (+4 points over RNA-only), for multiprofile avgpool (+9 points over single-profile), and for avgpool over transformer (+4 points). Fusion strategy is the one core design axis that has never been varied: every multimodal run used concat. 2. What this tests: config_019 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. The result is a clean answer on whether learned modality weighting helps. That matters here because the image branch is weak alone (0.21 accuracy) but still adds signal, so weighting could reduce noise from the image branch or could underuse it. F1 will help interpret a small accuracy difference. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: It resolves an untested design dimension with a one-factor comparison while also exploiting the strongest region of the search space, so it could produce a new best. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) and RNA-only multiprofile controls remain valuable follow-ups. Settling fusion first gives a firmer reference pipeline against which to compare those encoder changes.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best prior configuration from llm_summary_004 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation) and changed only the fusion strategy, from concat to weighted. This is the first time fusion has been varied. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6390 (supporting F1 of 0.6197), about 2 points above the concat counterpart (0.6186 accuracy, 0.6103 F1) and the new best result so far. Because this was a one-factor comparison, it is an initial indication that learned modality weighting may help modestly in this pipeline. However, the gain is small, the F1 improvement is even smaller (about 1 point), and each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized variance, so the difference may fall within run-to-run noise. The learned modality weights were not reported, so it is unknown whether weighting downweighted or better used the weak image branch. It also remains untested whether the weighted-fusion advantage holds with transformer aggregation, single-profile inputs, or alternative encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L), and RNA-only multiprofile controls are still missing.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.639 accuracy). Multiprofile avgpool gave the largest single gain, about 9 points over single-profile. However, it has only been tested in multimodal models. Adding the weak image branch (0.208 accuracy alone) helped by about 4 points, but only in the single-profile setting. So we do not know whether the multiprofile gain comes mainly from aggregating RNA profiles, or whether the image branch still adds anything once profiles are aggregated. 2) What this tests: config_002 is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n=2000, avgpool. It is a one-factor control in two directions. Against config_001 it isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation on RNA alone. Against config_018 and config_019 it isolates what the image modality adds under multiprofile. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: Its result decides where to spend later runs. If RNA-only multiprofile comes close to 0.62-0.64, the image branch and fusion choices matter little, and RNA encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) become the priority. If it falls well short, image and fusion work, such as a ViT-L swap, is justified. This is worth more than another small fusion or encoder tweak made without this control.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 was a one-factor control: an RNA-only, multiprofile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, and no image branch or fusion. It reached 0.5907 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.5727), about 10.6 points above the RNA-only single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). This is an initial indication that most of the multiprofile avgpool benefit arises from aggregating RNA profiles alone, not only in multimodal models. Adding the ResNet50 image branch under multiprofile avgpool still gave higher accuracy: about 2.8 points with concat fusion (llm_summary_004, 0.6186) and about 4.8 points with weighted fusion (llm_summary_006, 0.6390, the current best). This suggests the image modality adds a modest but non-negligible increment once profiles are aggregated, similar in size to its roughly 4-point gain in the single-profile setting. However, every configuration has a single run with uncharacterized variance, so these 3–5 point image contributions may partly reflect noise, and the learned fusion weights remain unreported. It is still untested whether stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) would shrink or widen the image contribution, or whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) would enlarge it, so both RNA-encoder and image/fusion directions remain plausible next steps.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Single-run results suggest RNA is the dominant signal source. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, while image-only was 0.208. Multiprofile avgpool gave the largest gain (about 10 points). Weighted fusion is the current best (config_019: 0.639 accuracy, 0.620 F1), though its edge over concat is small. Every result so far used the PCA n2000 RNA encoder, so the RNA representation is the largest untested design axis on the dominant modality. 2. What this tests: config_043 keeps the best pipeline fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA, and whether it changes how much the image branch adds. 3. Why this is the best next run: the RNA encoder probably has more leverage than swapping the image encoder, since images add only about 3-5 points. Testing it inside the best-known context is both informative and a plausible new best. Whether the result is a gain or a loss, it tells us whether to keep PCA or pursue scGPT (and scVI next) across later aggregation and fusion choices. An RNA-only scGPT control (config_008) can follow if the effect needs to be separated from fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the current best pipeline fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion from llm_summary_006) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n=2000 to scGPT. It reached 0.5251 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.4979), about 11 points below the PCA counterpart (0.6390 accuracy, 0.6197 F1). It also fell below the RNA-only PCA multiprofile control (0.5907) and roughly matched the single-profile PCA concat model (0.5266). Because this was a one-factor comparison, it is an initial indication that scGPT embeddings, as used here, are a weaker RNA representation than PCA in this pipeline, so PCA remains the preferred encoder for now. The gap is large relative to the 2–5 point differences seen elsewhere, but each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized variance. scGPT was also tested with only one setup, with unreported details such as frozen versus fine-tuned weights, gene vocabulary overlap, and preprocessing, so a setup mismatch cannot be ruled out. It also remains unknown whether the drop stems from the RNA embedding itself or its interaction with weighted fusion: an RNA-only scGPT multiprofile control is needed to separate these, the fusion weights are unreported, and scVI is still untested.

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA n=2000, ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Profile setting, aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder have each been varied at least once. The scGPT swap lowered accuracy by about 11 points, so PCA remains the preferred RNA encoder. The image encoder has never been varied. ResNet50 is weak on its own (0.208) and adds only about 3 to 5 points when fused, so we cannot tell whether image signal is inherently limited or limited by this encoder.

2. What this tests: config_025 keeps the best pipeline fixed and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This one-factor comparison asks whether a stronger image representation enlarges the multimodal gain over the RNA-only multiprofile control (0.591).

3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Image encoder is the only design dimension with no evidence at all, so this run reduces the most uncertainty. It is also a plausible route to a new best. The scVI swap (config_031) is a strong alternative, but RNA encoders already have one comparison, so it is a better candidate for a later run.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the current best pipeline from llm_summary_006 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, the first time the image encoder has been varied. It reached 0.6352 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.6183), essentially matching the ResNet50 counterpart (0.6390 accuracy, 0.6197 F1; about 0.4 points lower) and staying about 4.5 points above the RNA-only PCA multiprofile control (0.5907). This one-factor comparison is an initial indication that a larger ImageNet-pretrained image encoder did not enlarge the multimodal gain in this pipeline, so the roughly 3–5 point image contribution may reflect limited image signal or a fusion/aggregation bottleneck rather than ResNet50 specifically, and llm_summary_006 remains the nominal best. However, the difference is well within plausible run-to-run noise given single runs, and several things remain unknown: ViT-L setup details (frozen vs. fine-tuned, input resolution, feature layer), image-only ViT-L performance, the learned fusion weights, and whether domain-specific image encoders or concat fusion would behave differently.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA encoder has had the largest effect so far. Swapping PCA for scGPT cost about 11 points, while swapping the image encoder (ResNet50 to ViT-L) changed almost nothing. Multiprofile avgpool and the RNA representation appear to drive most of the performance. scVI (n=200) is the only RNA encoder never tested, so its effect is the largest open uncertainty. 2. What this tests: config_031 keeps the current best pipeline fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.6390 accuracy) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA n=2000 to scVI n=200. This shows whether a compact, count-aware latent beats or matches PCA, and whether the large scGPT drop was specific to scGPT or applies to learned embeddings in general. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: It is a clean one-factor comparison on the most influential dimension and has a realistic chance of a new best result. Fusion, aggregation and image-encoder questions now show only small differences, so further tests there would likely fall within noise. If scVI does well, an RNA-only scVI control (config_005) can follow; if it does poorly, PCA is confirmed as the RNA choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the current best pipeline from llm_summary_006 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n=2000 to scVI n=200. This was the first test of scVI. It reached 0.6776 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.6464), about 3.9 points above the PCA counterpart (0.6390 accuracy, 0.6197 F1), making it the new best result. It was also about 15 points above the scGPT variant (llm_summary_008, 0.5251). Because this was a one-factor comparison, it is an initial indication that a compact, count-aware scVI latent is a stronger RNA representation than PCA in this pipeline. It also suggests that the large scGPT drop was specific to scGPT as used here rather than a general weakness of learned RNA embeddings. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized variance, and scVI setup details (training data, epochs, likelihood, batch handling) are unreported. An RNA-only scVI multiprofile control is still needed to tell whether scVI improves RNA signal on its own or changes how weighted fusion uses the image branch. It also remains untested whether the gain holds under concat fusion, transformer aggregation, or ViT-L, and whether other latent sizes would do better.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference point for every later comparison. Image-only, scVI/scGPT encoders, multiprofile aggregation and fusion can each be judged by changing one factor from this baseline. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Starting with the simplest, cheapest model avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better. It also makes later single-factor comparisons interpretable. Without this baseline, a good result from a complex model could not be credited to any specific design choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as the reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. Because no other experiments have been run, this is only an initial baseline. It says nothing yet about whether image data, alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI/scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or fusion would help or hurt, and the run-to-run variance of this number is unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: We have one run, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). We do not know its variance, and no other factor has been tested. The biggest open question is whether the image modality carries useful signal on its own. The answer decides whether the large multimodal part of the search space (most remaining configs) is worth budget. 2) Test: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50) matches the baseline on profile setting and the absence of aggregation and fusion, so the only change is the modality. It gives a direct RNA-vs-image comparison and sets the image reference point needed to read later fusion results. 3) Why now: Knowing whether image alone is weak, comparable, or strong guides most later choices: whether to prioritize multimodal fusion, which modality to optimize first, and whether image-encoder comparisons (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) deserve budget. Testing RNA encoders (scVI/scGPT) or multiprofile aggregation first would refine only one branch. This experiment reduces uncertainty across the whole search space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as a direct modality comparison against the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001), and it reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079 (F1 0.1718), well below that baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). This is an initial observation that this image-only configuration carries less usable signal than the RNA-only baseline under the current setup. However, the comparison changes both the modality and the encoder (ResNet50 vs. PCA), each result comes from a single run with unknown variance, and the chance level is not stated, so it remains unclear whether image data is generally weak, whether a different image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) would perform better, and whether image features could still add complementary value when fused with RNA.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1) clearly beats the ResNet50 image-only run (0.208 accuracy). So RNA is the strongest base to build on. Whether multiprofile aggregation helps is still completely unknown, and that choice is shared by most of the remaining search space. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. Everything else matches the baseline (RNA-only, PCA encoder). This isolates the effect of using multiple profiles with the simplest aggregator. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: The result tells us whether to favour multiprofile configurations across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings, so it prunes or prioritises a large part of the space. It does this without mixing in encoder or fusion changes. Comparing avgpool against transformer aggregation, and testing alternative RNA encoders or fusion, can follow once we know whether the multiprofile setting is worth pursuing.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and simple avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It changed only the profile setting relative to the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5907 (F1 0.5727), compared with 0.4849 accuracy (F1 0.4639) for the baseline, a gain of roughly 0.11 on both metrics. Because only the profile setting differed, this is initial evidence that using multiple profiles with avgpool aggregation improves RNA-only performance under the current setup. However, each result comes from a single run with unknown variance. It also remains untested whether the benefit carries over to image-only or multimodal settings, whether a learned aggregator (e.g., a transformer) would outperform avgpool, and how the gain interacts with alternative RNA encoders or fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The clearest signal so far is that going from single-profile to multiprofile (avgpool) raised RNA-only PCA accuracy by about 0.11 (0.485 to 0.591), with a matching F1 gain (0.464 to 0.573). Whether a learned aggregator beats simple averaging is still unknown, and so far only one aggregator has been tried. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from the current best (config_002: RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It extends the strongest direction found so far. The answer will guide every later multiprofile experiment, including the RNA-encoder and multimodal ones, since aggregation is needed in all of them. If the transformer helps, it becomes the default; if it does not, the cheaper avgpool can be kept and the budget moved to the RNA-encoder (scVI/scGPT) and fusion questions.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and transformer aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It changed only the aggregation relative to the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003, avgpool), and it reached a validation accuracy of 0.5191 (F1 0.4797), compared with 0.5907 (F1 0.5727) for avgpool, a drop of roughly 0.07 in accuracy and 0.09 in F1, while remaining modestly above the single-profile baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). Because aggregation was the only change, this is initial evidence that, in this setup, the transformer aggregator underperforms simple avgpool, which suggests keeping avgpool as the default. However, each result comes from a single run with unknown variance, and the transformer's hyperparameters, capacity, and training budget may not have been tuned, so it remains unclear whether a better-configured learned aggregator could match or beat avgpool, or whether this ranking holds with other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI/scGPT), image-only, or multimodal fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is the strongest modality so far. The RNA-only PCA baseline reached 0.485 accuracy, while image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.208. Multiprofile with avgpool gave a clear gain (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1), and transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool. All of these runs used the PCA RNA encoder, so RNA encoder choice is the largest untested factor for the dominant modality. 2) This run changes only the encoder, from PCA to scVI, within the current best setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). It directly tests whether a learned, lower-dimensional representation improves on PCA. 3) Under a limited budget, this one-factor comparison against the best configuration both exploits the promising multiprofile/avgpool direction and resolves an important representation question. The answer will guide which RNA encoder to carry into the later scGPT comparison and into multimodal fusion experiments, instead of committing to PCA by default.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with avgpool aggregation and no image encoder or fusion, and it swapped the RNA encoder from PCA (2000 components) to scVI (200 dimensions). This was a one-factor change relative to the previous best configuration (llm_summary_003). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6501 (F1 0.6275), compared with 0.5907 (F1 0.5727) for the PCA version, a gain of roughly 0.06 accuracy and 0.05 F1, making it the best configuration so far. Because only the encoder differed, this is initial evidence that the scVI representation outperforms PCA in this setting, and it supports carrying scVI forward into later scGPT comparisons and multimodal fusion experiments. However, each result comes from a single run with unknown variance. The change also bundles a learned model with a large dimensionality reduction (200 vs. 2000), so the evidence cannot separate which of these drives the gain. It also remains untested whether the scVI advantage holds with single-profile input, transformer aggregation, or fusion with image features.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Under RNA-only multiprofile avgpool, scVI (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1) beat PCA (0.591, 0.573). Multiprofile with avgpool beat single-profile, and avgpool beat the transformer aggregator. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is still untested, so we do not know which RNA representation is strongest. 2) Test: config_008 changes only the encoder from scVI to scGPT and keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). It tells us whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats scVI or whether scVI's lead holds. 3) Why now: RNA carries far more signal than images so far (image-only ResNet50 scored 0.208), so the RNA encoder is likely the main driver of performance. Settling the encoder choice first gives later fusion experiments the strongest RNA backbone. This avoids spending the limited budget on multimodal combinations built on a possibly weaker encoder. The cost is that the open question of whether adding images helps is deferred by one experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with avgpool aggregation and no image encoder or fusion, changing only the RNA encoder from scVI (200 dimensions; llm_summary_005, the best so far at 0.6501 accuracy, 0.6275 F1) to the pretrained scGPT embedding. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5305 (F1 0.5152), roughly 0.12 below scVI on both metrics and also below the PCA version (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1), though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849). Because only the encoder differed, this is initial evidence that, in this setup, scGPT embeddings underperform both scVI and PCA, which supports keeping scVI as the RNA backbone for later fusion experiments. However, each result comes from a single run with unknown variance, and it is unclear how the scGPT embeddings were extracted or adapted (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned, embedding dimensionality, gene vocabulary overlap), so a better-configured scGPT might close the gap, and the ranking is untested under single-profile, transformer aggregation, or multimodal fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA-only results point consistently toward multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation and the scVI encoder. config_005 is the best so far at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Fusion with image features, the central multimodal question, has not been tested at all. The only image result (ResNet50 single-profile, 0.208) is weak, but that does not rule out image features adding complementary signal. 2) Test: config_030 keeps everything from config_005 fixed (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Comparing it directly with config_005 isolates whether adding the image modality helps, hurts or is neutral on the strongest RNA backbone. 3) Why now: This exploits the best-known setup while answering the most important open design question. Concat is the simplest fusion baseline, and ResNet50 is the only image encoder with an observed result, so any change can be attributed cleanly. The outcome will show whether later experiments should go into fusion variants (weighted fusion, ViT-L) or into refining RNA-only models.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 was the first multimodal run. It kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_005 fixed (scVI 200-dim encoder, multiprofile input, avgpool aggregation) and added ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy was 0.6315 (F1 0.6068), about 0.02 below the RNA-only scVI configuration (0.6501 accuracy, 0.6275 F1) but still above all other prior runs. Because adding the image modality was the only change, this is initial evidence that naive concat fusion with ResNet50 features does not help, and may slightly hurt, the strongest RNA backbone, so RNA-only scVI remains the best configuration so far. However, the gap is small and each result comes from a single run with unknown variance, so the difference may be within noise. It also remains untested whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L, given ResNet50's weak image-only result of 0.208), weighted or learned fusion, feature normalization or rebalancing between the 200-dim RNA and image embeddings, or different training settings would let image features add complementary signal.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI, multiprofile, avgpool (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 image features with naive concat fusion (config_030) gave a slightly lower 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. ResNet50 image-only was weak (0.208), so the open question is whether the drop comes from concat letting a weak modality dilute the strong scVI signal, or from the image features carrying no complementary information. 2. Test: config_031 keeps every setting of config_030 fixed (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. Weighted fusion can learn to down-weight the weaker modality. If it recovers or beats the RNA-only accuracy, fusion design is the bottleneck. If it still trails, the ResNet50 features likely add little. That result would point the next experiment toward the image encoder (ViT-L) rather than fusion. 3. Budget rationale: This is a clean one-factor comparison against an existing run. It isolates fusion, one of the main design axes not yet tested. It also stays close to the best-performing region of the search space, so it balances learning about the design with a realistic chance of a new best result. The answer also decides which fusion type to carry into later ViT-L multimodal runs.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the first multimodal setup from llm_summary_007 fixed (scVI 200-dim RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, multiprofile input, avgpool aggregation) and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6776 (F1 0.6464), the best result so far. That is about 0.046 accuracy above concat fusion (0.6315 accuracy, 0.6068 F1) and about 0.027 above the previous best, RNA-only scVI (0.6501 accuracy, 0.6275 F1). Because fusion was the only change relative to llm_summary_007, this is initial evidence that weighted fusion outperforms concat here and that concat was a bottleneck, which supports carrying weighted fusion into later multimodal runs such as ViT-L. The comparison with RNA-only scVI changes two things at once (adding images and using weighted fusion), and each result comes from a single run with unknown variance, so the modest margin over RNA-only may be within noise. The learned modality weights were not reported, and whether a stronger image encoder (ViT-L), feature normalization, or other fusion schemes would add further gains remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal scVI + ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool and weighted fusion (config_031: 0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1). Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.046. The image encoder remains the main untested design choice in the fusion setting. ResNet50 was weak on its own (0.208 image-only), so the image branch is a plausible bottleneck. 2) Test: Keep config_031 fixed and swap only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds complementary signal under the fusion scheme that already works best. 3) Why now: This is a one-factor extension of the current best configuration. It is the most likely candidate for a new best while still answering a clean design question. If ViT-L does not help, that points to RNA (scVI) as the dominant signal and suggests limiting further image-encoder exploration. Image-only ViT-L runs could clarify the encoder's standalone signal, but testing ViT-L directly in the best pipeline uses the limited budget better.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best configuration so far fixed (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI 200-dim RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7062 (F1 0.6671), the new best result. That is about 0.029 accuracy and 0.021 F1 above the ResNet50 version (0.6776, 0.6464) and about 0.056 accuracy above RNA-only scVI (0.6501). Because the image encoder was the only change, this is initial evidence that ViT-L image features add more complementary signal than ResNet50 under weighted fusion, which suggests the image branch was a bottleneck and that image-encoder choice is worth continued attention. However, each result comes from a single run with unknown variance, so the modest margin may be partly noise. ViT-L has not been tested image-only, so its standalone signal is unknown. The learned modality weights were not reported, and it remains untested whether the ViT-L gain holds under concat fusion, with other RNA encoders, or with transformer aggregation.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Encoder and fusion choices now each have some one-factor support. Aggregation has only one comparison: RNA-only with PCA, where the transformer underperformed avgpool (0.519 vs 0.591). That single run may not generalize. In the multimodal setting, a learned aggregator could weigh profiles differently when richer image features are present. 2) What this tests: Changing only aggregation from avgpool to transformer in the current best setup checks whether the avgpool advantage holds with scVI, ViT-L and weighted fusion. 3) Why this is the best next run: Aggregation is the least-tested design choice, and this comparison isolates it. If the transformer wins, the result is a new best, so it may improve performance. If it loses, it strengthens the evidence that avgpool should be the default, which reduces uncertainty for the remaining budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration so far fixed (llm_summary_009: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI 200-dim RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, weighted fusion) and changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer, to check whether avgpool's earlier advantage in the RNA-only PCA setting (0.591 vs 0.519 accuracy) generalizes. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7250 (F1 0.6847), the new best result, about 0.019 accuracy and 0.018 F1 above the avgpool version (0.7062, 0.6671). Because aggregation was the only change, this is initial evidence that the transformer aggregator helps in this multimodal setup, even though it hurt in the RNA-only PCA setting. Aggregation rankings may therefore depend on context (encoder, modality, or fusion), so avgpool should not be assumed as the universal default. However, each result comes from a single run with unknown variance and the margin is small, so it may be partly noise. It also remains untested which factor (scVI vs PCA, the image modality, or weighted fusion) underlies the reversal, whether transformer aggregation would help in RNA-only scVI or concat-fusion settings, and whether tuning the transformer's capacity or training budget would change the picture.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest baseline. It anchors later comparisons: swapping the encoder (scVI, scGPT), adding multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), adding the image modality, or adding fusion each changes one factor relative to it. 3) Under a limited budget, a cheap and interpretable reference point is worth more than an early guess at a complex multimodal configuration. Without a baseline, we could not tell whether added complexity actually improves accuracy or F1.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first reference point in this study: an RNA-only, single-profile configuration using a PCA encoder with 2000 components, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 (primary metric), with a supporting validation F1 of 0.464. The close agreement between accuracy and F1 is an initial sign that performance is not heavily driven by a few classes, though no per-class evidence was provided. Because no other experiments have been completed, this result is a baseline only. It is unknown whether alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or fusion would improve on it, and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, so small future differences relative to this baseline should be interpreted cautiously.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Its accuracy and F1 are close, but run-to-run variance is unknown. The effects of the RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, image modality and fusion are all untested. 2) This experiment changes one factor: it switches from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, keeping the PCA RNA-only setup. That isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps. Avgpool is the simplest aggregation, so it tests the multiprofile idea before adding the cost of a transformer. 3) The profile setting cuts across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations, so its answer is relevant to most of the remaining search space. A one-variable change from the baseline gives a clean comparison. Encoder (scVI, config_004) and image-only comparisons are natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup (no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose from 0.485 to 0.591, and supporting F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573, so the gain shows up consistently in both metrics. Within this RNA-only PCA setting, this is initial evidence that multiprofile input with avgpool beats single-profile input. However, multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, so the evidence cannot separate the effect of using multiple profiles from the choice of aggregation (e.g., avgpool versus a transformer). Each configuration was run only once and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, and it is unknown whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI), image-only, or fused multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: With RNA-only PCA-2000, switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose consistently. Because multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation were introduced together, the aggregation choice remains untested. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything fixed (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile) and changes only aggregation from avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether a learned set aggregator adds value beyond mean pooling. 3) Why now: It is a one-variable, controlled extension of the strongest result so far, so it exploits the multiprofile direction while settling a design choice. Aggregation recurs in many downstream image-only and multimodal configurations, so the answer will help prune a large part of the remaining search space. Testing it before branching into encoders or modalities avoids confounded comparisons later.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 held the RNA-only PCA-2000 multiprofile setup fixed (no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool (llm_summary_002) to a transformer. Validation accuracy (primary metric) fell from 0.591 to 0.519 and supporting F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480, so the drop appears in both metrics. Because only aggregation changed, this is initial evidence that in this RNA-only PCA multiprofile setting, transformer aggregation as configured underperforms simple mean pooling, though it still beats the single-profile baseline (0.485). Each configuration was run only once, run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, and transformer hyperparameters and training details were not varied, so it remains uncertain whether the gap reflects the aggregator itself or its tuning, and whether the result carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only, or fused multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: All three completed runs are RNA-only with the PCA-2000 encoder. Within that setting, multiprofile avgpool gave the best result (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It beat both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519), with both metrics agreeing. The image modality is completely untested, which is the largest gap in the search, because half of the remaining space is image-only or multimodal. 2) What this tests: config_011 runs image-only ResNet50 with the same multiprofile avgpool setup that worked best for RNA. Keeping profile and aggregation fixed makes it a clean modality comparison against config_002. It shows whether imaging alone carries useful signal, how it compares with RNA, and gives a first check on whether the multiprofile avgpool benefit holds outside RNA. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: whether image features are informative is the main factor in whether the many fusion configurations are worth exploring. Testing a different RNA encoder (e.g., scVI) would refine a branch we already partly understand. This run instead reduces uncertainty about a whole unexplored dimension, using the strongest known profile and aggregation choice so it is less likely to underperform for avoidable reasons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 gave the first test of the image modality: image-only ResNet50 with the multiprofile avgpool setup that performed best for RNA (no RNA encoder or fusion), making it a direct comparison with llm_summary_002 (RNA-only PCA-2000, multiprofile avgpool). Validation accuracy (primary metric) was 0.328 with supporting F1 0.288, far below llm_summary_002 (0.591 / 0.573) and below every RNA-only run, including the single-profile baseline (0.485). This is initial evidence that, as configured, image-only features are much less informative than RNA-only PCA features. However, the modality and the encoder changed together, so this run cannot separate a weakness of imaging data from a limitation of this ResNet50 setup (for example, its pretraining, freezing or fine-tuning, or preprocessing). Several questions remain open: no chance level or class count was provided, so it is unclear how far above chance this result is; the slightly larger accuracy–F1 gap may hint at more uneven per-class performance, but no per-class evidence was given; there is no single-profile or transformer image run, so whether the multiprofile avgpool benefit carries over to images is untested; each configuration was run once; and whether image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA is still unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 multiprofile avgpool (config_002, 0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1). Multiprofile avgpool beat both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). Image-only ResNet50 multiprofile avgpool (config_011) reached only 0.328 / 0.288. A weak image-only result does not rule out complementary signal, and whether fusion helps is the main untested design question. 2) This run adds the ResNet50 image branch to the best RNA setup with concat fusion, keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation fixed. That makes it a controlled comparison with config_002 (adding images to RNA) and with config_011 (adding RNA to images). It shows whether combining modalities improves on RNA alone, gives no benefit, or hurts by adding noise. 3) Fusion is the highest-uncertainty factor with the largest implications. It decides whether the remaining budget should go to the many multimodal configurations or to RNA encoder choices such as scVI and scGPT. It also builds on the strongest configuration found so far. Concat is the simpler fusion baseline, so weighted fusion can be tested next if this run looks promising.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested multimodal fusion for the first time. It added the ResNet50 image branch, with concat fusion, to the best RNA setup so far (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) while keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation fixed, making it a controlled comparison with llm_summary_002 (RNA-only) and llm_summary_004 (image-only). Validation accuracy (primary metric) reached 0.619, the best result so far, compared with 0.591 for RNA-only and 0.328 for image-only. Supporting F1 rose more, from 0.573 to 0.610, and the accuracy–F1 gap narrowed. This is initial evidence that image features add some complementary signal despite their weak standalone performance, and that concat fusion did not hurt by adding noise. However, the accuracy gain is modest (~0.028) and comes from single runs with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, so it may not be robust. It is also untested whether weighted or other fusion methods, other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), or different image-encoder setups would give larger or smaller benefits.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant source of signal. RNA-only PCA multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, versus 0.328 for image-only, and adding the image branch gave only a modest gain to 0.619. Multiprofile avgpool has been the best profile and aggregation setting in every controlled comparison so far. However, only one RNA encoder (PCA-2000) has been tested, and the RNA encoder choice governs most of the remaining search space (the scVI and scGPT variants). 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the best RNA-only setup (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. This makes it a clean, single-variable comparison with config_002 that isolates the effect of RNA representation. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: because RNA drives performance, the encoder choice is likely the highest-impact open design decision. Its answer will guide whether later multimodal runs should use PCA or scVI. That is more informative than fine-tuning fusion type (concat vs. weighted) on a modest multimodal gain whose run-to-run variance is unknown.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best RNA-only setup (multiprofile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. This makes it a single-variable comparison with llm_summary_002. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose from 0.591 to 0.650, and supporting F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.628. That is the best result so far, above even the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat run (0.619 / 0.610). This is initial evidence that, in this RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting, scVI-200 gives a more useful RNA representation than PCA-2000. However, scVI and PCA also differ in dimensionality (200 vs. 2000), so this run cannot separate the encoder type from latent size or training details. Each configuration was run once with uncharacterized variance, and it remains untested whether the scVI advantage holds in multimodal fusion, with transformer aggregation, or against scGPT and other scVI variants.

selection_reason: Evidence: the best result so far is scVI-200 RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool (config_005, 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1). Separately, adding a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the PCA-2000 multiprofile avgpool setup gave a modest gain (0.591 to 0.619 acc, with a larger F1 gain). That gain is small and comes from single runs. The open question is whether the image modality's complementary signal persists once the RNA representation is stronger, or whether scVI already captures what images added to PCA. Test: config_030 changes only one factor from config_005 by adding ResNet50 with concat fusion, keeping scVI-200, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. It also mirrors the config_002 to config_018 comparison, so the two image-addition effects can be compared directly across encoders. Why now: it is a controlled extension of the best configuration. It also tests a central design question, whether multimodal fusion actually helps, and it has the highest expected immediate performance. Comparing scGPT, ViT-L or weighted fusion can follow once we know whether fusion helps on a strong RNA backbone.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 added the ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best configuration so far (scVI-200 RNA, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_006), keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation fixed. This made it a single-variable test of image addition that mirrors the PCA-2000 comparison (llm_summary_002 to llm_summary_005). Validation accuracy (primary metric) fell slightly, from 0.650 to 0.632, and supporting F1 fell from 0.628 to 0.607. This contrasts with the modest gain from adding images to PCA-2000 (0.591 to 0.619 accuracy). It is an initial observation that the complementary image signal seen with PCA may not persist, and that concat fusion may slightly hurt, once a stronger scVI RNA representation is used. However, both image-addition effects are small (about 0.02 to 0.03), come from single runs with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and could be within noise. It also remains untested whether a different fusion method (e.g., weighted), other image-encoder setups (e.g., ViT-L, fine-tuning), or other RNA encoders would change whether images help, so scVI-200 RNA-only remains the best configuration observed.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest lever found so far. Swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 (F1 0.573 to 0.628), the best result yet. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave small, inconsistent effects (+0.028 with PCA, -0.019 with scVI), likely within noise. Multiprofile avgpool has consistently beaten single-profile and transformer aggregation. The third RNA encoder, scGPT, is still completely untested. 2. Test: config_008 changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT, keeping the best-known RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup fixed. This makes it a clean single-variable comparison with config_005 (scVI) and config_002 (PCA). It shows whether a foundation-model representation beats scVI and completes the encoder comparison. 3. Why now: Representation has produced the largest gains, and the scGPT branch accounts for many remaining configurations, including multimodal ones. Resolving its standalone value prunes or prioritizes a large part of the search. Further fusion or image-encoder tweaks have so far yielded only marginal differences.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best-known RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup (no image encoder or fusion) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder to scGPT, giving a single-variable comparison with scVI-200 (llm_summary_006: 0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1) and PCA-2000 (llm_summary_002: 0.591 / 0.573). scGPT reached a validation accuracy of 0.530 (primary metric), with supporting F1 of 0.515. That is well below both scVI and PCA, though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485), and the drop of about 0.06 to 0.12 is larger than the image-addition effects (about 0.02 to 0.03) previously judged possibly within noise. This is initial evidence that scGPT embeddings, as configured here, are the weakest of the three RNA representations in this setting, which weakens the case for prioritizing scGPT-based branches, including multimodal ones. However, this is a single run with uncharacterized variance, and it remains uncertain whether the gap reflects the scGPT representation itself or its extraction and setup (for example, embedding dimensionality, pretrained checkpoint, gene vocabulary overlap, or lack of fine-tuning), and whether scGPT would behave differently with fusion or other aggregation.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scVI-200 RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool is the best result so far (0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion helped the weaker PCA encoder (0.591 to 0.619) but slightly hurt scVI (0.650 to 0.632). Both effects are small single runs, so they may be noise. Weighted fusion has never been tested, so it is unclear whether the scVI drop comes from the image signal itself or from naive concatenation letting a weak branch add noise. 2. What this tests: config_031 matches config_030 (scVI-200, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. That isolates the fusion choice. A weighted scheme could learn to down-weight the weak image branch. If it matches or beats 0.650, images may still carry complementary signal with a strong RNA encoder. If it again falls below RNA-only, that strengthens the case that ResNet50 images add little once scVI is used. 3. Why this is the best next run: it resolves a completely untested design axis (fusion type) in the highest-performing region of the search space. It is both exploitative, as a plausible new best, and informative, since it decides whether further multimodal runs (such as ViT-L variants) should use weighted or concat fusion. Running it now avoids spending budget on many fusion-confounded comparisons later.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 matched llm_summary_007 (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 images, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. This makes it a single-variable test of fusion type in the best-performing region of the search space. Validation accuracy (primary metric) reached 0.678, with supporting F1 of 0.646. That is the best result so far, above both scVI concat fusion (0.632 / 0.607) and scVI RNA-only (0.650 / 0.628), so the gain appears consistently in both metrics. This is initial evidence that weighted fusion outperforms concat in this scVI multimodal setting, and that ResNet50 images may still add complementary signal to a strong RNA encoder when fused this way. However, the gains are modest: about 0.046 accuracy over concat and about 0.027 over RNA-only. They come from single runs with uncharacterized variance, so the RNA-only margin in particular is similar in size to effects previously judged possibly within noise. It also remains untested whether learned weights actually down-weight the image branch, whether weighted fusion helps with PCA-2000 or other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), and whether it interacts with aggregation choice.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 images, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Earlier runs gave initial evidence that scVI beats PCA and scGPT, that avgpool beats the transformer, and that weighted fusion beats concat. The image encoder is the one major design choice still completely untested, since every image run has used ResNet50. ResNet50 was weak on its own (0.328), and its benefit within fusion was small and inconsistent: +0.028 with PCA concat, -0.018 with scVI concat and +0.027 with scVI weighted. 2) What this tests: config_037 keeps everything from config_031 fixed and changes only ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This is a clean single-variable test of whether a stronger image representation increases the complementary image signal in the best-performing region. A clear gain would point to the image encoder as a bottleneck. No change or a drop would suggest that images add little beyond scVI whichever encoder is used, and that config_031's margin over RNA-only may be fragile. 3) Why this is the best next run: It resolves the largest remaining uncertainty, the image encoder, while staying in the most promising region of the search space, so it has both high information value and a strong chance of a new best result. Alternatives such as config_019 (whether weighted fusion also helps with PCA) or transformer variants address questions that matter less for finding the best model or that already lean negative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 held the previous best configuration fixed (llm_summary_009: scVI-200 RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, giving the first single-variable test of image encoder choice. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose to 0.706 and supporting F1 rose to 0.667, the best result so far. That is about +0.029 accuracy over the ResNet50 version and about +0.056 over scVI RNA-only (0.650 / 0.628), so this is initial evidence that ViT-L gives a more useful complementary image signal than ResNet50 in this fused setting and that the image encoder may have been a bottleneck. However, the gain over ResNet50 is similar in size to effects previously judged possibly within noise, comes from single runs with uncharacterized variance, and cannot separate architecture from model size or pretraining differences; it also remains untested how ViT-L performs image-only, whether its benefit holds with concat fusion or PCA-2000 RNA, and how the learned fusion weights shift between modalities.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest baseline. It has no aggregation or fusion components, so its accuracy and F1 give a clean reference point. Later runs can then each change one factor against it: a learned RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), an image-only model, or a multimodal model. 3) Under a limited budget, a simple, well-understood baseline is the most informative first step. It lets each later gain be attributed to a specific design choice, and it avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will help.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.485 and validation F1 0.464. The similar F1 suggests performance is not driven by a few classes alone, but this is an initial observation. Because no other experiments exist yet, it is unknown whether learned RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image features, or multimodal fusion would improve on this, so later runs should change one factor at a time against this reference. Run-to-run variance and the chance-level baseline for this task are also unknown, so it is unclear how strong this result is or how large a difference would be meaningful.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). Nothing is yet known about the image modality, and image encoders appear in 36 of the 50 remaining configurations. 2) What this tests: An image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion is the simplest image reference. It is directly comparable to the RNA baseline and shows whether images carry signal on their own, and roughly how much compared with RNA. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: This result decides whether the large image and multimodal part of the search space is worth exploring, and it gives the second unimodal reference needed to judge later fusion gains. Finer questions within RNA (scVI or scGPT vs PCA, multiprofile aggregation) affect fewer configurations and can follow next.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image reference: an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.208 and F1 0.172, well below the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464), and the lower F1 suggests performance may be less even across classes. This is an initial observation that this image setup underperforms the RNA baseline, but it does not show that the image modality is inherently weaker, because the two runs differ in both modality and encoder type (a pretrained CNN versus PCA). Chance level, run-to-run variance, and the effect of other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation are unknown, so it remains unclear whether the image signal is meaningfully above chance and whether images could still add complementary information under multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: So far there are only two single-profile runs. RNA-only PCA (config_001) reached accuracy 0.485 and F1 0.464. Image-only ResNet50 (config_010) reached accuracy 0.208 and F1 0.172. So RNA with PCA is the strongest reference so far. We still know nothing about whether multiprofile aggregation helps, and that choice affects most of the remaining search space. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only one factor from the best baseline. It switches single-profile to multiprofile and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool), keeping the same RNA-only PCA encoder. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles improves accuracy and F1 over single-profile. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: The profile setting applies across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations, so its answer narrows many future choices at once. Starting from the strongest known baseline gives a clean comparison with a reasonable chance of immediate gains. Avgpool comes before the transformer so that any benefit can be attributed to multiprofile aggregation itself rather than aggregator complexity. Encoder and fusion comparisons can follow once we know which profile setting to build on.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with the same PCA encoder (pca_n2000) as the RNA baseline, using simple average-pooling aggregation and no image encoder or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.591 and F1 0.573, up from the single-profile RNA PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Because profile setting is the only design factor that differs from that baseline, this is the first controlled evidence that multiprofile aggregation improves RNA-only PCA performance, and the similar gains in accuracy and F1 suggest the benefit is broad across classes. This is still a single run with unknown run-to-run variance, so the size of the gain is uncertain. It is also unknown whether more complex aggregators (e.g., a transformer) would add more, and whether the benefit carries over to image-only, other RNA encoders, or multimodal fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The clearest result so far is that multiprofile aggregation improves RNA-only PCA. Accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 and F1 from 0.464 to 0.573 when only the profile setting changed. Each result is a single run with unknown variance. It is also unknown whether the aggregation method itself matters, or whether simple average pooling already captures most of the multiprofile benefit. 2. What this tests: config_003 matches the current best run (config_002: RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) except that it swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation. Aggregation is therefore the only factor that changes. This isolates whether a learned set-level aggregator adds value over mean pooling. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It builds on the strongest evidence so far while answering a design question that affects every remaining multiprofile configuration, including the multimodal ones. Knowing whether to prefer transformer or avgpool lets later encoder and fusion comparisons use the right aggregator, which saves budget. It is also a low-risk extension that could raise the best accuracy. Encoder (scVI or scGPT) and image-fusion comparisons can follow against whichever aggregator wins.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with the PCA encoder (pca_n2000) and transformer aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It differs from the current best run (llm_summary_003, avgpool) only in the aggregation method. It reached validation accuracy 0.519 and F1 0.480, below llm_summary_003 (accuracy 0.591, F1 0.573) and only modestly above the single-profile RNA PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Because aggregation is the only changed factor, this is controlled initial evidence that, in this setup, the transformer aggregator did not outperform simple average pooling and may underperform it, so avgpool is the stronger default for now. Each result is a single run with unknown variance, and the transformer's training settings and capacity are unknown, so it is unclear whether the gap is robust or reflects optimization difficulty. Whether this aggregator ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image-only, or multimodal fusion settings is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA with avgpool (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). Multiprofile beat single-profile, and avgpool beat the transformer aggregator in controlled comparisons. The RNA encoder choice is untested: every run so far used PCA. That choice also sets up most of the remaining multimodal configurations, and RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far (image-only ResNet50 reached acc 0.208). 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the encoder from PCA to scVI. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation helps or hurts compared with PCA. 3. Why this is the best next run: It is a controlled, one-factor change on the strongest pipeline, so it is informative whichever way it turns out. If scVI wins, it becomes the default RNA encoder for later fusion runs. If it loses, PCA is reinforced and the next runs can test scGPT or adding images on a solid RNA baseline. That is more efficient than jumping to multimodal fusion before the stronger modality's representation is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with avgpool aggregation and no image encoder or fusion, changing only the RNA encoder from PCA (pca_n2000) to scVI (scvi_n200) relative to the previous best run (llm_summary_003). It reached validation accuracy 0.650 and F1 0.628, the best so far and above llm_summary_003 (accuracy 0.591, F1 0.573). Because only the encoder setting differs, this is controlled initial evidence that scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 in this pipeline, with similar gains in accuracy and F1 suggesting a broad benefit across classes; scvi_n200 is a reasonable provisional default RNA encoder for later runs, including fusion. However, the encoder swap changes both the method (learned vs. linear) and the dimensionality (200 vs. 2000), so it cannot say which drove the gain, and with single runs of unknown variance the size and robustness of the ~0.06 accuracy gap are uncertain; whether scVI's advantage holds against other encoders such as scGPT, with other aggregators, or under multimodal fusion remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile in a controlled comparison (0.591 vs 0.485). scvi_n200 beat pca_n2000 under that setting (0.650 vs 0.591), so config_005 is the current best. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208). Fusion has never been tested, so it is unknown whether images add complementary signal to RNA or only add noise. 2) What this tests: config_030 keeps the best RNA pipeline (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds the ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_005 isolates whether adding images through basic fusion helps, hurts or does nothing. 3) Why now: Fusion is the central untested design axis, and this run probes it in the strongest context found so far. Concat is the simplest fusion method, so the result is easy to interpret, and a weighted-fusion follow-up can come next if the result looks promising. The scGPT encoder comparison (config_008) is also informative but only refines a choice we already have evidence on, whereas fusion is completely unexplored.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested the first multimodal fusion run. It kept the best RNA pipeline (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion, so adding images via concat is the only change relative to the current best, llm_summary_005 (RNA-only: accuracy 0.650, F1 0.628). It reached validation accuracy 0.632 and F1 0.607, slightly below llm_summary_005 on both metrics, so this is controlled initial evidence that adding ResNet50 image features through naive concatenation did not improve on RNA-only in this setup and may slightly hurt; llm_summary_005 remains the best configuration. The ~0.02 accuracy gap comes from single runs with unknown variance and may not be meaningful, and it is unclear whether the lack of benefit reflects weak image features (image-only ResNet50 scored only 0.208), the fusion method (e.g., an unweighted concat letting a noisy branch dilute the RNA signal), or optimization effects, so weighted or gated fusion, other image encoders, and multiprofile image-only references remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is RNA-only scvi_n200 with multiprofile avgpool (acc 0.650, F1 0.628). Adding ResNet50 images through concat fusion (config_030) scored slightly lower (acc 0.632, F1 0.607). We cannot yet tell whether this reflects weak image features (image-only ResNet50 scored 0.208) or unweighted concat letting a noisy image branch dilute the RNA signal. 2) What this tests: config_031 is identical to config_030 except that it uses weighted fusion instead of concat. This isolates the fusion method. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only, fusion design was the bottleneck and multimodal is still promising. If it also falls short, the problem more likely lies with the ResNet50 image features, which would point next to the ViT encoder or to more RNA-encoder work such as scGPT. 3) Why now: it is a single-factor change on the strongest pipeline. It answers a central question for this study, whether images can add value with a better fusion method, before budget is spent on the many other multimodal configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the llm_summary_006 multimodal pipeline (scvi_n200 RNA, ResNet50 images, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, which isolates fusion design. It reached validation accuracy 0.678 and F1 0.646. That is the best result so far, above both the concat run (llm_summary_006: accuracy 0.632, F1 0.607) and the RNA-only best (llm_summary_005: accuracy 0.650, F1 0.628), with consistent gains on both metrics. This is controlled initial evidence that weighted fusion outperforms concat in this setup and that ResNet50 image features can add value over RNA-only when fused this way. The concat shortfall therefore looks more like a fusion bottleneck than purely weak image features, and multimodal remains promising. However, these are single runs with unknown variance, so the ~0.03 gain over RNA-only and the ~0.05 gain over concat may not be robust. It is also unknown what weights the fusion learned or how much it relies on the image branch, and whether the benefit holds with other image encoders (e.g., ViT), RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT), aggregators, or gated or attention-based fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200, ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.678, F1 0.646). It beat the RNA-only run (0.650) and concat fusion (0.632), so weighted fusion can extract value from images. But ResNet50 alone was weak (image-only accuracy 0.208), and the image encoder choice has never been varied. That makes it the largest untested lever in the most promising pipeline. 2) What this tests: config_037 keeps everything in config_031 fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain, and whether the image branch is the bottleneck. 3) Why it is the best use of budget: It exploits the strongest direction (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) while answering a clean, single-factor question about a design choice that affects every multimodal configuration. Its result will guide later choices, such as image-only ViT references or scGPT swaps. If ViT does not help, that suggests image features add only modest complementary signal regardless of encoder.
