It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6501 (supporting F1 0.6275), compared with 0.5907 (F1 0.5727) for the PCA version, making it the best result so far. This single-factor comparison is initial evidence that scVI (200) outperforms PCA (2000) as the RNA representation in this setting. However, both are single runs with unknown variance, so the size and reliability of the roughly 0.06 gain are uncertain. It is also unknown whether the scVI advantage holds in the single-profile setting, with transformer aggregation, against scGPT, or in multimodal fusion, where the image signal (so far weak with ResNet50) remains untested as a complement.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile for RNA-only PCA (0.591 vs 0.485 accuracy). Switching the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI then gave the best result so far (0.650 accuracy, F1 0.628). Aggregation is the one core design axis that has not been tested at all: transformer aggregation has never been run. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208), so multimodal gains remain speculative. 2) What this tests: config_006 changes only the aggregator (avgpool to transformer) on the current best configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI). This isolates whether learned attention over profiles improves on simple averaging. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: it exploits the strongest direction found so far while answering an important open design question. The result will also guide the aggregator choice for later scGPT and multimodal runs, so it avoids spending budget on many-factor multimodal configurations before the unimodal design is better understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with an scVI (200) RNA encoder and transformer aggregation. It differs from the previous best, llm_summary_004 (avgpool), only in the aggregator. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6530 (supporting F1 0.6283), nearly identical to avgpool's 0.6501 (F1 0.6275). This single-factor comparison gives no clear evidence that learned attention over profiles improves on simple averaging in this configuration. The difference of about 0.003 is likely within run-to-run variance, which is unknown because each result is a single run. Untested questions include whether the aggregator matters with other encoders (PCA, scGPT), whether multimodal fusion adds value given the weak ResNet50 image-only result, and whether the extra cost of transformer aggregation is justified.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Two single-factor comparisons favour multiprofile over single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485) and scVI over PCA (0.650 vs 0.591). Transformer and avgpool aggregation were essentially tied (0.653 vs 0.650). The ResNet50 image-only model was weak (0.208), but no experiment has tested whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA. 2) This run adds the ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best RNA setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool). It differs from config_005 only in adding the image modality. Comparing the two isolates the value of multimodal fusion, with no encoder or aggregator confounds. I use avgpool because it matched the transformer at lower complexity. I use ResNet50 because it is the only image encoder with a known unimodal result. 3) Multimodal value is the largest untested design question in the study, and it determines how much budget to spend on the many fusion configurations. A gain would justify exploring fusion further, for example weighted fusion or ViT-L. No gain or a loss would let the budget focus on RNA-side choices such as scGPT. Either way the result is informative and cleanly interpretable.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 added a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best avgpool RNA setup (scVI 200, multiprofile, avgpool). The proper single-factor reference is llm_summary_004, the RNA-only version with avgpool, not llm_summary_005 as the selection rationale states, since 005 used transformer aggregation. Validation accuracy was 0.6315 (supporting F1 0.6068), below llm_summary_004's 0.6501 (F1 0.6275) and the best overall result of 0.6530 (llm_summary_005). This is initial evidence that adding ResNet50 images through simple concatenation does not help, and may slightly hurt, in this configuration. The roughly 0.019 drop comes from single runs with unknown variance, so it may not be reliable. It also cannot separate the image modality from the specific choices of ResNet50 (already weak alone at 0.2079) and concat fusion. Other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), and other RNA encoders all remain untested, so whether images can add complementary signal is still open.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant signal so far. RNA-only models reached about 0.65 accuracy, while image-only ResNet50 reached about 0.21. Multiprofile avgpool helped PCA (0.485 to 0.591), and scVI beat PCA under multiprofile avgpool (0.650 vs 0.591, F1 0.628 vs 0.573). Transformer and avgpool aggregation were nearly tied (0.653 vs 0.650). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion slightly lowered accuracy (0.632). The third RNA encoder, scGPT, has never been tested, so the RNA representation question is only partly answered. 2. What this tests: config_008 changes only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT relative to config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). It shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats scVI on the strongest modality. It uses avgpool, the cheaper aggregator with comparable performance, as the reference. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: the RNA encoder has produced the largest single-factor gain observed so far (about 0.06), so it is the design choice most likely to move performance. The result also decides which RNA backbone later multimodal experiments should build on. Fusion and image-encoder questions (weighted fusion, ViT-L) remain important, but they are better tested once the best RNA representation is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool model with a scGPT RNA encoder. Its proper single-factor reference is llm_summary_004 (scVI 200, same setting), not 'config_005' as the selection rationale labels it. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5305 (supporting F1 0.5152), well below scVI's 0.6501 (F1 0.6275) and also below PCA 2000's 0.5907 (F1 0.5727, llm_summary_003) under the same multiprofile avgpool setup. This is initial evidence that scGPT embeddings, as used here, are the weakest of the three RNA encoders tested and that scVI remains the best RNA backbone for later multimodal work. However, each result is a single run with unknown variance, and the gap cannot be separated from implementation details such as embedding extraction, dimensionality, or the absence of fine-tuning. It is also untested whether scGPT behaves differently with transformer aggregation, in the single-profile setting, or in multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-side choices are fairly well mapped. scVI 200 beats PCA and scGPT, multiprofile beats single-profile, and transformer and avgpool aggregation are roughly tied (0.653 vs 0.650). The main open question is whether images can add complementary signal. Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion lowered accuracy slightly (0.632 vs 0.650 for the RNA-only avgpool version), but ResNet50 was also very weak on its own (0.208). So that result may reflect a poor image representation rather than the image modality itself. 2. What this tests: config_036 differs from config_030 only in the image encoder, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L and keeping scVI 200, multiprofile, avgpool and concat. This isolates whether a stronger image representation turns the image branch from neutral or harmful into helpful. config_005 serves as the RNA-only reference. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: the image encoder is the most plausible bottleneck and affects every remaining multimodal configuration. This experiment answers that question directly in the setting most relevant to beating the current best. Avgpool keeps it comparable and cheap, since transformer aggregation showed no clear gain. Testing fusion type (weighted, config_031) is a sensible follow-up once we know whether a better image encoder changes the picture.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model with scVI (200) RNA, an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. It differs from llm_summary_006 only in the image encoder (ViT-L instead of ResNet50), and its RNA-only reference is llm_summary_004 (the rationale's config IDs do not match these labels). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7150 (supporting F1 0.6872), the best result so far. That is above llm_summary_006 (0.6315, F1 0.6068), the RNA-only avgpool model llm_summary_004 (0.6501, F1 0.6275) and the previous best llm_summary_005 (0.6530, transformer). The single-factor comparison with 006 is initial evidence that image-encoder quality matters and that, with ViT-L, the image branch can add complementary signal beyond RNA alone, consistent with ResNet50 having been the bottleneck. However, all results are single runs with unknown variance, and no ViT-L image-only baseline exists to gauge its standalone strength. It also remains untested whether the gain holds or grows with weighted fusion, transformer aggregation, other RNA encoders or the single-profile setting.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_036 (multimodal, scVI 200 + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, concat), at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. Earlier single-factor comparisons gave initial evidence that multiprofile helps, that scVI is the strongest RNA encoder tested, and that the image encoder matters (ViT-L beat ResNet50). Transformer aggregation was roughly equal to avgpool in the RNA-only setting. Fusion is the one major design choice never varied: every multimodal run has used concat. 2) What this tests: config_037 changes only concat to weighted fusion relative to config_036. It isolates whether the fusion method affects how well the image signal complements RNA. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest configuration while answering a question that has no evidence at all. Transformer aggregation (config_038) already looked unlikely to matter much. A ViT-L image-only baseline (config_014) would be informative but has lower expected performance, so it can follow later. All results are single runs, so a small difference in either direction should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model with scVI (200) RNA, ImageNet ViT-L images and avgpool aggregation, changing only the fusion method from concat to weighted relative to the best run so far, llm_summary_008 (the rationale's config_036/037 IDs do not match these labels). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7062 (supporting F1 0.6671), slightly below concat's 0.7150 (F1 0.6872) but still well above the RNA-only scVI avgpool reference llm_summary_004 (0.6501, F1 0.6275). This single-factor comparison is initial evidence that weighted fusion gives no improvement over concat in this configuration, and that the ViT-L image benefit persists under either fusion method. However, the roughly 0.009 accuracy gap (about 0.020 in F1) comes from single runs with unknown variance and may not be meaningful, and it remains untested whether fusion choice matters with other image encoders, transformer aggregation or the single-profile setting; a ViT-L image-only baseline is also still missing.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI 200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.7150 accuracy (F1 0.6872). Weighted fusion (config_037) did not improve on concat. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L was the largest single gain. Aggregation has only been compared in the RNA-only scVI setting. There, transformer and avgpool were essentially tied (0.6530 vs 0.6501), so it is still unknown whether learned attention over profiles matters once image features are included. 2) Test: config_038 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to config_036. This isolates whether attention-based profile aggregation helps in the multimodal setting, for example by weighting informative image profiles. A clear gain would show the two choices interact. A tie or drop would confirm avgpool as the simpler, adequate choice across model settings. 3) Why now: It is a single-factor extension of the strongest configuration, so it may improve the best result while also answering an open design question. A ViT-L image-only baseline (config_014) would help explain where the gain comes from. However, the multimodal-over-RNA gain already shows images add signal, so under a limited budget, testing the remaining untested factor on the best backbone is the more useful next step.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model with scVI (200) RNA, ImageNet ViT-L images and concat fusion, changing only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer relative to the previous best, llm_summary_008 (the rationale's config_036/038 IDs do not match these labels). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7207, nominally the best so far, compared with 0.7150 for llm_summary_008. However, its supporting F1 of 0.6815 was slightly lower than avgpool's 0.6872, so the two metrics point in opposite directions by similarly small margins (about 0.006 each). This single-factor comparison therefore gives no clear evidence that attention-based aggregation helps once image features are included, which mirrors the near-tie seen in the RNA-only scVI setting (llm_summary_004 vs 005); avgpool remains a simpler, roughly equivalent choice. All results are single runs with unknown variance, so the small accuracy gain may not be reliable, and a ViT-L image-only baseline, the single-profile setting, and transformer aggregation combined with weighted fusion or other encoders all remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so we have no reference point for how well any representation, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice performs. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest, least confounded configuration. It sets a baseline for validation accuracy and F1. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it: scVI or scGPT encoders (config_004/007), multiprofile aggregation (config_002/003), adding images (config_016/017), or image-only (config_010). 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Starting with a complex multimodal, multiprofile model would mix several design choices together and could not show which ones help. A simple baseline makes every later comparison interpretable and guards against assuming that more complex models are better.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest, least confounded configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. With no prior experiments to compare against, this is a baseline only and says nothing about whether other encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or image modalities would help or hurt. It is unknown whether this result reflects a limit of PCA features, the single-profile setting, or the task's inherent difficulty, and the run-to-run variance is also unknown, so future runs should change one factor at a time against this reference.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: We have one result, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality, which is the largest unexplored axis. Every multimodal configuration (35 of the 50 remaining) depends on whether images carry useful signal. 2) What this tests: config_010 is image-only, single-profile, ResNet50, with no aggregation or fusion. This is the simplest image baseline and is directly comparable to config_001 under the same single-profile setting, so the comparison isolates modality (RNA vs. image). 3) Why now: Knowing whether image features alone match, exceed, or fall short of RNA PCA is the most decision-relevant information for a limited budget. It tells us whether to prioritize multimodal fusion or focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. It also gives the reference point needed to judge later fusion gains. Encoder or aggregation variants within RNA are refinements best tested after this coarse question is answered.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image baseline: an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.1718, well below the RNA-only single-profile PCA (pca_n2000) baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). Both runs used the single-profile setting, but the comparison changes modality and encoder type together. So it suggests that ResNet50 image features alone are much weaker than RNA PCA features here, but it does not show whether the image modality itself carries little signal or whether this encoder or representation is the limit. Several questions remain open: run-to-run variance is unknown with one run each, other image encoders are untested, and it is unclear whether image features could still add complementary signal when fused with RNA or under multiprofile aggregation.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA-only single-profile PCA (config_001, accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464) clearly beat image-only single-profile ResNet50 (config_010, accuracy 0.208, F1 0.172). So RNA is the strongest base so far. The profile setting and aggregation are completely untested, and they apply across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the best baseline fixed (RNA-only, pca_n2000) and changes only single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregator, avgpool. This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles improves accuracy. 3. Why now: a single-factor comparison against the strongest reference answers a question that shapes most of the remaining search space (roughly two-thirds of the configurations are multiprofile). Testing RNA encoders or image fusion first is less urgent. The weak image result also suggests fusion gains, if any, may be small. If avgpool helps, the transformer aggregator is the logical next step. If it hurts, multiprofile variants can be deprioritized.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the strongest baseline fixed (RNA-only, pca_n2000 encoder, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the profile setting from single-profile to multiprofile, using avgpool aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5907 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.5727, up from 0.4849 accuracy and 0.4639 F1 in the single-profile reference (llm_summary_001). Because the profile setting and aggregation were introduced together, this suggests that multiprofile input with avgpool helps RNA PCA features, but it cannot separate the effect of having multiple profiles from the choice of avgpool. Several questions remain open: with one run per configuration, run-to-run variance is unknown; other aggregators such as the transformer are untested; and it is unclear whether the gain carries over to image-only or multimodal settings, which makes multiprofile variants a promising but unconfirmed direction.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Switching RNA-only pca_n2000 from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, with F1 rising from 0.464 to 0.573. This is the strongest signal so far. Image-only ResNet50 was much weaker at 0.208. Because the profile setting and the aggregator changed together, we cannot tell whether the gain comes from having multiple profiles or from avgpool specifically. Transformer aggregation is still untested. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything from the best run (RNA-only, pca_n2000, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation. 3) Why now: it builds directly on the most promising direction while answering a design question that affects every later multiprofile experiment. Those include the RNA encoder swaps and the multimodal fusion runs, which must each choose an aggregator. It is a cleaner, single-factor comparison than jumping to new encoders or fusion, and it could also produce a new best result.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best configuration from llm_summary_003 fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000 encoder, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5191 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.4797. That is below avgpool multiprofile (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1) and slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). This single-factor comparison suggests that, in this setup, avgpool is the better aggregator for multiprofile RNA PCA features. It also suggests that much of the earlier multiprofile gain may depend on the aggregator choice, though the transformer run alone cannot fully separate the multiprofile effect from aggregation. Several questions remain open: with one run per configuration, run-to-run variance is unknown; the transformer's hyperparameters or training settings may have been under-tuned; and it is untested whether this aggregator ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image-only, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool with pca_n2000 (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). It clearly beat the single-profile run (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519). Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208). The RNA encoder is a major design choice that is still completely untested, since every RNA run used PCA. 2) What this tests: config_005 keeps the best setting fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. This isolates whether a learned, compact scVI representation beats PCA features. 3) Why this is the best next run: It is a clean one-factor comparison against the current best, so it is informative whichever way it turns out, and it has a real chance of improving accuracy. Its result will guide which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal fusion runs. Testing fusion now would be premature, because the weak image results suggest the RNA representation drives performance.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration from llm_summary_003 fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6501 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.6275, the best so far and up from 0.5907 accuracy and 0.5727 F1 with PCA. Because only the encoder changed, this suggests that the compact scVI representation outperforms PCA features in this setting. scvi_n200 is now the leading candidate RNA encoder for later runs. Several questions remain open: with one run per configuration, run-to-run variance is unknown, so the roughly 6-point gain is not yet confirmed as robust; the comparison mixes encoder type with dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so it cannot say whether learned features or compactness drives the gain; other encoders (e.g., scGPT, other scVI sizes) are untested; and it is unknown whether the advantage holds for single-profile, transformer aggregation, or multimodal fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Within the best setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool), scvi_n200 (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1) beat pca_n2000 (0.591 / 0.573). This makes the RNA encoder look like a high-leverage choice. scGPT, the third available encoder, is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the leading setting fixed and changes only the encoder to scGPT. This is a clean single-factor comparison that completes the encoder ranking under the setting that has worked best. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Every remaining multimodal configuration depends on choosing an RNA encoder. Knowing whether scGPT matches or beats scVI should come before spending budget on fusion and image experiments. It could also give a new best score. Since single runs have unknown variance, a clear gap either way is informative, while a close result would suggest the encoder matters less than profile setting and aggregation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the leading setting fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder to scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5305 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.5152. That is clearly below scvi_n200 (0.6501 / 0.6275) and pca_n2000 (0.5907 / 0.5727) in the same setting, though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849 / 0.4639). This single-factor comparison suggests that, as used here, scGPT embeddings are the weakest of the three RNA encoders, which gives the ranking scVI > PCA > scGPT and keeps scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder for fusion and image experiments. Several questions remain open: with one run per configuration, run-to-run variance is unknown; the scGPT result may reflect how the embeddings were extracted, their dimensionality, or a lack of fine-tuning rather than a limit of the model itself; and it is untested whether this encoder ranking holds under single-profile, transformer aggregation, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best configuration so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200 with avgpool (config_005, 0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Multiprofile avgpool beat both single-profile and transformer aggregation. scVI beat PCA and scGPT. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208), but it was tested only in the single-profile setting. So it is still unknown whether image features add complementary signal when combined with strong RNA features. That is the main untested design choice. 2. What this tests: config_030 keeps every setting from config_005 fixed (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only the ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). Comparing it with config_005 isolates the value of adding the image modality on top of the best RNA setup. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly answers whether multimodality is worth pursuing, and it might also improve on the current best. If it helps, later runs can test weighted fusion or ViT-L. If it does not, the remaining budget can go to RNA-side refinements instead of the many multimodal configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best RNA-only configuration from llm_summary_005 fixed (multiprofile, scvi_n200 encoder, avgpool aggregation) and changed only one thing: it added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6315 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.6068. Both are slightly below the RNA-only reference (0.6501 / 0.6275). This single-factor comparison suggests that adding ResNet50 image features through concat did not help in this setup and may have slightly hurt, which fits the weak image-only result from llm_summary_002 (0.2079 accuracy). Several questions remain open. With one run per configuration, run-to-run variance is unknown, so the roughly 2-point drop may be within noise. The result cannot tell whether the image modality lacks complementary signal or whether the specific choices (ResNet50 features, unweighted concat fusion that may let weak image features dilute the RNA signal) are the limit. Other encoders such as ViT-L and other fusion methods such as weighted fusion remain untested, so multimodality is not ruled out, but its expected payoff now looks lower than that of RNA-side refinements.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200 with avgpool (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 through concat fusion (config_030) dropped slightly to 0.632 / 0.607. That run cannot tell whether the image modality lacks complementary signal or whether unweighted concat lets weak image features dilute the strong RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 keeps every other choice of config_030 fixed (multiprofile, scvi_n200, ResNet50, avgpool) and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates the fusion effect. If weighted fusion matches or beats the RNA-only reference, dilution was the problem and multimodal fusion stays viable. If it still falls short, ResNet50 features likely add little, and later runs should test a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or focus on RNA-side refinements. 3. Why now: it is a clean single-factor comparison that settles a key open question about fusion. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best model. That makes it a better use of the limited budget than changing the image encoder and fusion together.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept every setting of llm_summary_007 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation) and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6776 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.6464, the best so far. That is above both concat fusion (0.6315 / 0.6068) and the RNA-only reference from llm_summary_005 (0.6501 / 0.6275). Because only fusion changed relative to llm_summary_007, this suggests that weighted fusion handles the ResNet50 branch better than concat, which fits the hypothesis that unweighted concat let weak image features dilute the RNA signal. It also suggests that image features may add some complementary signal when weighted appropriately, which keeps multimodal fusion viable. Several questions remain open: with one run per configuration, run-to-run variance is unknown, so the roughly 2.8-point gain over RNA-only and 4.6-point gain over concat are not yet confirmed as robust; the learned fusion weights were not examined, so it is unclear how much the image branch actually contributes versus being largely down-weighted; and it is untested whether stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), other fusion methods, or other aggregators would extend the gain.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Weighted fusion beat concat (0.632) and the RNA-only reference (0.650), so image features may add complementary signal when weighted. However, ResNet50 is weak on its own (0.208 image-only), and image encoders other than ResNet50 are untested. The image encoder is now the largest open question in the leading configuration. 2. Test: config_037 keeps everything in config_031 fixed and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds to the multimodal gain or whether the gain comes mainly from weighted fusion protecting the RNA signal. 3. Why now: It is a clean one-factor extension of the strongest configuration, so it can plausibly improve accuracy (exploitation). It is also informative either way. A gain would point to image representation quality as a key lever. No gain would suggest the image contribution is limited, which would shift the remaining budget toward RNA-side or aggregation refinements. With single runs, a small difference should be read cautiously, using F1 as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept every setting of the leading configuration from llm_summary_008 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to imagenet_vit_l. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7062 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.6671, the best so far. That is up from 0.6776 / 0.6464 with ResNet50 and above the RNA-only scVI reference (0.6501 / 0.6275). Because only the image encoder changed, this suggests that a stronger image representation adds to the multimodal gain under weighted fusion, rather than the gain coming only from weighted fusion protecting the RNA signal, and it makes image representation quality a promising lever. Several questions remain open: with single runs, run-to-run variance is unknown, so the roughly 2.9-point gain is not confirmed as robust; ViT-L image-only performance and the learned fusion weights were not examined, so the image branch's standalone strength and actual contribution are unclear; and it is untested whether ViT-L would also help under concat fusion, other aggregators, or other image encoders.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_037 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. With ResNet50, weighted fusion beat concat by about 4.6 points (0.678 vs 0.632), and concat even fell below RNA-only. That pattern fits the idea that weighted fusion mainly protects the RNA signal from weak image features. It is still unknown whether that fusion advantage holds once the image branch is stronger, as with ViT-L. 2) What this tests: config_036 keeps config_037 fixed and changes only the fusion, from weighted to concat. If concat with ViT-L matches or beats weighted fusion, the earlier fusion gain was specific to weak image features and image quality is the main lever. If concat still lags, weighted fusion is a robust design choice. 3) Why this is the best next run: it is a clean single-factor test of a design choice that interacts with image representation, and it could plausibly reach top performance. The alternatives look less informative. Transformer aggregation already underperformed avgpool for RNA, and multiprofile already showed a large gain.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept llm_summary_009 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool) and changed only the fusion from weighted to concat. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7150 and a supporting F1 of 0.6872, the best so far and slightly above weighted fusion with ViT-L (0.7062 / 0.6671). It is also well above concat with ResNet50 from llm_summary_007 (0.6315 / 0.6068), a comparison that changes only the image encoder. These single-factor comparisons suggest that the weighted-over-concat advantage seen with ResNet50 (about 4.6 points) does not carry over to a stronger image encoder, so image representation quality looks like the main lever and the fusion choice matters less once image features are strong. However, with single runs and unknown variance, the roughly 0.9-point accuracy gap between concat and weighted may be noise, so the two are best treated as roughly equivalent. ViT-L image-only performance, the learned fusion weights, and other aggregators or image encoders remain untested, so it is still unclear how much the image branch contributes on its own and whether the proposed dilution mechanism explains the ResNet50 result.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2. What this tests: The simplest configuration, RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (2000 components), with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference point that later experiments can be compared against one factor at a time. For example, swapping the encoder to scVI or scGPT isolates the representation effect, and switching to multiprofile with avgpool isolates the profile-setting effect. Adding an image encoder isolates the gain from multimodality. 3. Why it is the best use of the first experiment: Starting with a complex multimodal or multiprofile model would mix several design choices together, and any result would be hard to attribute to a specific one. A simple, cheap baseline lets every later experiment be read as a controlled comparison. It also checks whether extra complexity is actually needed.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) established a baseline using the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 (supporting validation F1 of 0.464), which serves as an initial reference point rather than evidence that any particular design choice helps or hurts. With no other completed experiments to compare against, it is still unknown whether alternative RNA representations (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings with aggregation, or adding image features would improve performance. The number of classes and chance level are not given here, so how strong this baseline is in absolute terms is also uncertain. Single-factor comparisons against this baseline are needed to attribute any future gains.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We do not yet know which design axis matters most: RNA representation, profile setting, aggregation, or modality. 2) What this tests: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile. It keeps RNA-only and the PCA encoder, and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be credited to using multiple profiles rather than to a new encoder or a more complex aggregator. 3) Why now: Profile setting is a structural choice that affects a large share of the remaining configurations, including many multimodal ones, so learning its effect early is very useful. Avgpool is the cleanest first test of that question. Only after it shows whether multiprofile helps is it worth testing the transformer aggregator. Encoder swaps (config_004 or config_007) and an image-only baseline (config_010) are good follow-ups under the same one-factor-at-a-time approach.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile configuration with the same PCA encoder (2000 components) as the baseline, aggregating profiles with avgpool and using no image encoder or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.591, up from 0.485 for the single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001), and validation F1 rose in step from 0.464 to 0.573. This suggests that moving to multiprofile input with simple average pooling is associated with a meaningful gain, but the comparison changes two things at once (profile setting and adding avgpool aggregation), so the gain cannot be credited to either factor alone. Each setting was run only once, so the size of run-to-run variance is unknown, and it remains untested whether other aggregators (e.g., a transformer), other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), or image features would interact with or add to this multiprofile improvement.

selection_reason: Evidence: in the RNA-only PCA setting, moving from single-profile (0.485 acc) to multiprofile with avgpool (0.591 acc, F1 0.573) gave the only gain observed so far. Each setting was run once, so run-to-run variance is unknown. Within multiprofile, the choice of aggregator has not been tested. Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the aggregation effect. Why now: aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, including RNA-only, image-only and multimodal ones. Settling avgpool versus transformer early will narrow a large part of the remaining search space. It also builds on the strongest current result rather than changing encoder or modality, which would be harder to interpret. Encoder (scVI/scGPT) and image comparisons can follow against a fixed, better-understood multiprofile baseline.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile configuration with the PCA encoder (2000 components), no image encoder, and no fusion, as in llm_summary_002, changing only the aggregator from avgpool to a transformer. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519 (supporting F1 0.480), well below avgpool's 0.591 (F1 0.573) and only slightly above the single-profile baseline's 0.485 (F1 0.464). Because aggregation is the only factor that differs from llm_summary_002, this is the cleanest comparison in the study so far, and it suggests avgpool is the stronger aggregator in this RNA-only PCA setting. However, each configuration was run once, so run-to-run variance is unknown. Transformer hyperparameters, training budget, and number of profiles were not reported, so the transformer may have been under-tuned or under-trained, and it is untested whether this ranking holds for other encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), image-only, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile PCA with avgpool (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). Avgpool clearly beat the transformer aggregator (0.519) in the one controlled comparison. The image modality is entirely untested, yet most of the remaining space (configs 010-051) depends on whether image features carry useful signal. 2) Test: An image-only ResNet50 model using the same multiprofile + avgpool setting that worked for RNA. This isolates the value of the image modality while holding profile setting and aggregation at their current best values. It also checks whether the multiprofile/avgpool advantage carries over to another modality. 3) Why now: This one run reduces the largest remaining uncertainty. If image-only performance is near or above RNA-only, multimodal fusion experiments (e.g., config_018/019) become a strong next step. If it is weak, the budget can shift toward RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT). ResNet50 is the simpler image encoder, so it gives a reasonable first read before trying ViT-L.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 gave the first read on the image modality: an image-only, multiprofile model with a ResNet50 encoder, avgpool aggregation, and no RNA encoder or fusion, matching the profile and aggregation settings of the best run so far (llm_summary_002). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 (supporting F1 0.288), far below the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool run (0.591 / 0.573) and below even the single-profile RNA PCA baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This is an initial observation that ResNet50 image features alone carry less class signal than PCA RNA features under this setup. However, the comparison changes both the modality and the encoder, so it cannot separate weak image signal from a weak choice of image encoder. Several questions remain open: whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or another aggregator would close the gap, whether image features still add complementary information when fused with RNA, how large run-to-run variance is given single runs, and what the chance level is, since the number of classes is not reported.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far. PCA RNA reached 0.591 accuracy (F1 0.573) in the multiprofile avgpool setting, versus 0.328 for ResNet50 image-only. Avgpool beat the transformer in the one clean single-factor comparison (0.591 vs 0.519). However, only one RNA encoder (PCA) has been tested, so RNA representation is still a completely unexplored design axis. That axis feeds into every RNA-only and multimodal configuration that remains. 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA (2000 components) to scVI (200 latent dimensions). Any accuracy or F1 difference can therefore be credited to the representation. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: it exploits the most promising direction while still answering an important open question about representation. If scVI beats PCA, all later multimodal comparisons should be built on scVI. If it does not, PCA is supported as the RNA backbone. Testing image fusion or the ViT-L image encoder first would be less efficient, because the RNA representation those comparisons rest on is not yet settled.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool configuration identical to the best prior run (llm_summary_002) except that the RNA encoder was changed from PCA (2000 components) to scVI (200 latent dimensions). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.650 (supporting F1 0.628), compared with 0.591 (F1 0.573) for PCA, making it the best result so far. Because the encoder was the only factor changed, this single-factor comparison suggests scVI is the stronger RNA representation in this setting and a reasonable RNA backbone for later multimodal runs. However, each configuration was run once, so run-to-run variance is unknown and the roughly 0.06 gain is not confirmed as robust. The change also altered representation type and dimensionality together (2000 vs 200), and it remains untested whether scVI's advantage holds with other aggregators, with image fusion, or against other RNA encoders such as scGPT or other scVI latent sizes.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.328, while RNA-only multiprofile runs reached 0.519 to 0.650. Within RNA, multiprofile with avgpool beat the transformer aggregator (0.591 vs 0.519 with PCA). Switching the encoder from PCA to scVI then gave the best result yet (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). The third RNA encoder, scGPT, has not been tested in any setting, so we don't know whether scVI is actually the best RNA backbone. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best-performing setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. This is a clean single-factor comparison against both scVI (config_005) and PCA (config_002), and it completes the RNA encoder comparison under the strongest known settings. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: the RNA backbone will be carried into many later multimodal runs. Settling that choice first, using the modality that carries the most signal, avoids spending the limited budget on fusion runs built on a possibly weaker encoder. It is also a strong exploitation candidate, since it could set a new best accuracy.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool configuration identical to llm_summary_005 (scVI) and llm_summary_002 (PCA) except that the RNA encoder was switched to scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.530 (supporting F1 0.515), well below scVI's 0.650 (F1 0.628) and PCA's 0.591 (F1 0.573). Because the encoder is the only factor changed, this single-factor comparison suggests scGPT is the weakest of the three RNA encoders in this setting and supports keeping scVI as the RNA backbone for later multimodal runs. Each configuration was run only once, so run-to-run variance is unknown. scGPT's embedding dimensionality, whether it was frozen or fine-tuned, and its preprocessing were not reported, so it may have been under-adapted. It is also untested whether this ranking holds with other aggregators or with image fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Among RNA-only runs, multiprofile scVI with avgpool is the strongest at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. It beat PCA (0.591) and scGPT (0.530), and avgpool beat the transformer aggregator with PCA (0.591 vs 0.519). Image-only ResNet50 multiprofile avgpool was weak (0.328). The biggest open question is whether image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA, or only add noise. No multimodal run exists yet. 2) Test: This configuration keeps the best RNA setting (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds the already-characterized ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion, concat. It is a near single-factor comparison against config_005 (adding the image modality) and config_011 (adding RNA). 3) Why now: It directly tests the study's central design choice, multimodal versus unimodal, starting from the strongest backbone. It exploits current evidence while staying informative whatever the outcome. A gain would justify further fusion and image-encoder exploration, such as weighted fusion or ViT-L. No gain would suggest concentrating the remaining budget on RNA-only refinements.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 was the first multimodal run. It kept the best RNA-only setting (scVI n200, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_005), added the ResNet50 image branch from llm_summary_004, and joined the two by concat fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.632 (supporting F1 0.607), slightly below RNA-only scVI's 0.650 (F1 0.628) but far above image-only ResNet50's 0.328 (F1 0.288). Adding the image modality is the only change from llm_summary_005, so this initial observation suggests that ResNet50 features fused by simple concat do not add complementary signal here and may add mild noise. However, each configuration was run once and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the roughly 0.02 drop may not be meaningful. It remains untested whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), a different fusion method (e.g., weighted or gated fusion), or modality balancing or normalization of the concatenated features would let images contribute.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: scVI n200 with multiprofile avgpool is the best run so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_030) dropped slightly to 0.632 / 0.607. The image-only ResNet50 run was weak (0.328). It is unclear whether images add nothing, or whether simple concat lets the weak image branch add noise. 2. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, keeping scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool the same as config_030. This isolates the fusion effect. If weighted fusion learns to down-weight the weaker image features, it may match or beat RNA-only. If it still trails, that is stronger evidence that ResNet50 images offer little complementary signal here. 3. Value: fusion is untested and affects every later multimodal run, so resolving it first guides the remaining budget, including whether a ViT-L image encoder is worth trying. It is a clean comparison and also a plausible chance to set a new best result.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model with scVI (n200) RNA features, ResNet50 image features and avgpool aggregation. It differed from llm_summary_007 only in using weighted fusion instead of concat. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.678 (supporting F1 0.646), the best result so far. That is above concat fusion's 0.632 (F1 0.607) and above the best RNA-only scVI run's 0.650 (F1 0.628, llm_summary_005). Because fusion was the only factor changed from llm_summary_007, this suggests weighted fusion handles the weak image branch better than concat, and that ResNet50 images may offer modest complementary signal when fused this way. However, the gain over RNA-only (about 0.03) comes from single runs with unknown run-to-run variance, so it is not confirmed as robust. The learned modality weights were not reported, so it is unclear whether the model down-weighted the image features or drew real complementary signal from them. It also remains untested whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or other fusion schemes (e.g., gated or attention-based) would add further gains on top of weighted fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best run so far is config_031 (scVI n200, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. It beats RNA-only scVI (0.650) and concat fusion (0.632). This suggests weighted fusion lets the image branch add some signal. Still, ResNet50 image-only results were weak (0.328), and the image encoder is the main design choice not yet tested. It is unclear whether the weak image results reflect limited signal in the images or a weak encoder. 2. What this tests: config_037 keeps everything from config_031 and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This single-factor comparison isolates the image encoder's effect inside the best-performing setup. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: A stronger image encoder is the most plausible way to raise the multimodal result. The comparison is informative either way. A gain would show that image representation quality limits performance. No gain would suggest image signal is limited, so further image-side experiments would be less valuable. Running image-only ViT-L (config_014) first would tell us less about whether the model can improve, because its fused setting is already known to work. Because each setting was run once, a small difference should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the best prior configuration (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 RNA, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.706 (supporting F1 0.667), the best result so far. That is above ResNet50 weighted fusion's 0.678 (F1 0.646) and RNA-only scVI's 0.650 (F1 0.628). Because the encoder was the only factor changed, this single-factor comparison suggests image representation quality was limiting the multimodal model, so the image branch can add more complementary signal with a stronger encoder. However, the roughly 0.03 gain comes from single runs with unknown run-to-run variance. Several points remain open: no image-only ViT-L run exists to measure the encoder's standalone signal, learned modality weights were not reported, encoder details (frozen vs. fine-tuned, embedding size) are unknown, and it is untested whether ViT-L's advantage holds with concat or other fusion schemes, or whether other image encoders would help further.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best run is config_037 (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Its gain came from swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L. With ResNet50, weighted fusion beat concat (0.678 vs 0.632), and concat even fell below RNA-only scVI (0.650). That suggests concat struggled with a weak image branch. It is unknown whether that fusion ranking holds once the image features are stronger. 2) Test: config_036 changes only one factor from the best run, using concat instead of weighted fusion. If concat now matches or beats weighted fusion, fusion design matters mainly when one modality is weak, and image encoder quality is the key lever. If weighted fusion still clearly wins, its advantage is robust across encoders. 3) Why now: this single-factor exploitation of the best region resolves the main uncertainty about the fusion choice, using F1 as supporting evidence. It also has a realistic chance of matching or exceeding the current best. Aggregation (transformer) and image-only ViT-L remain useful follow-ups. However, the transformer already underperformed in the clean RNA-only comparison, so testing fusion is the higher-value next step.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 kept the best prior configuration (llm_summary_009: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L images, avgpool) and changed only the fusion method, from weighted to concat. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.715 (supporting F1 0.687), slightly above weighted fusion's 0.706 (F1 0.667), making it the best result so far. With ResNet50, concat had trailed weighted fusion clearly (0.632 vs 0.678) and even fell below RNA-only scVI (0.650). This single-factor comparison therefore suggests that weighted fusion's advantage does not carry over once the image branch is stronger, and that fusion choice mattered mainly when the image modality was weak, with image encoder quality the larger lever. However, the roughly 0.01 accuracy gap (about 0.02 in F1) comes from single runs with unknown run-to-run variance, so concat and weighted fusion should be treated as roughly tied with ViT-L rather than concat being confirmed as better. Several points remain open: no image-only ViT-L run exists, learned modality weights and encoder details (frozen vs. fine-tuned, embedding size) are unreported, and other fusion schemes (gated, attention) and other aggregators with this stronger backbone are untested.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration. It sets a reference point for accuracy and F1 that every later change can be compared against one design choice at a time: swapping the encoder (scVI, scGPT), moving to multiprofile with avgpool or transformer, or adding the image modality and fusion. 3) Anchoring the search on a simple, cheap baseline is the most efficient first step under a limited budget. Starting with a complex multimodal or multiprofile model would mix several design choices together, so its result could not be attributed to any one of them. It would also assume that more complexity helps, which has not yet been shown.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single-profile, a PCA encoder with 2000 components, and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as a cheap reference point so that later runs can change one design choice at a time. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 with a supporting validation F1 of 0.464. This is only an initial baseline, and the similar F1 suggests performance is not driven by a single dominant class, although per-class behavior is unknown. No comparisons exist yet, so the effects of alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), and adding the image modality with fusion are all untested. Run-to-run variance is also uncharacterized.

selection_reason: 1) The only evidence is the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (config_001: accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Every other design axis is untested, and run-to-run variance is unknown. 2) Config_002 changes exactly one factor, single-profile to multiprofile, using avgpool, the simplest aggregator, while keeping the modality and RNA encoder fixed. This isolates whether combining multiple profiles helps at all, without the extra capacity of a transformer aggregator confounding the result. 3) Profile setting affects most of the remaining search space (aggregation choices and most multimodal configurations). A clean, cheap test of it will tell us whether multiprofile variants deserve further budget. Encoder and image-only baselines can follow as the next single-factor comparisons.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only setup with the PCA (2000-component) encoder from llm_summary_001 and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile. Multiprofile requires an aggregator, so it used avgpool, the simplest one. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (+0.106), and validation F1 rose in step from 0.464 to 0.573, which is consistent with multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation helping in the RNA-only PCA setting. This is still a single run per configuration with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, so the size and reliability of the gain are unconfirmed. It is also unknown whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), to a transformer aggregator, or to image and fused multimodal settings, all of which remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: In the RNA-only PCA setting, moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose in step (0.464 to 0.573). This is promising but rests on single runs, and the aggregation method is untested. 2. Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000) and swaps only avgpool for a transformer aggregator. This isolates whether a learned aggregator beats simple pooling in the best direction found so far. 3. Why now: Aggregation will carry through to every later multiprofile run, including the image-only and multimodal ones. A clean one-variable comparison now exploits the multiprofile gain and narrows a large part of the remaining space. Encoder and modality comparisons are still open and are logical next steps.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 kept llm_summary_002's setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 encoder) and changed only the aggregator, replacing avgpool with a transformer. Validation accuracy dropped from 0.591 to 0.519 (-0.072), and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480. Both metrics favor avgpool in this RNA-only PCA setting, though the transformer still beat the single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1). Because each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and the transformer's hyperparameters and training budget were not explored, the result does not show that transformer aggregation is inherently worse. Whether this ranking holds for other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), the image-only setting, or fused multimodal settings remains untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Within RNA-only PCA-2000, multiprofile with avgpool (config_002: 0.591 acc, 0.573 F1) clearly beat single-profile (0.485 acc) and transformer aggregation (0.519 acc). Accuracy and F1 agree in each comparison. Each result is a single run, so run-to-run variance is unknown. The image modality is completely untested, even though most of the remaining search space (image-only and all multimodal configurations) depends on it. 2. What this tests: config_011 keeps the best-performing profile and aggregation setting (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps the RNA encoder for the image modality (ResNet50, image-only). This shows how informative image features are on their own under the same aggregation, relative to config_002. 3. Why now: The image-only result is the main guide for the large multimodal branch. Strong image performance would justify fusion experiments. Weak image performance would point the budget toward RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) instead. Using the setting that worked best so far makes the comparison with config_002 as clean as possible.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 is the first test of the image modality. It kept llm_summary_002's best-so-far profile and aggregation setting (multiprofile, avgpool) and replaced the RNA PCA-2000 encoder with an image-only ResNet50. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 and a supporting F1 of 0.288, well below RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1) and even the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.485 acc). Because this comparison changes the modality and the encoder together, and ResNet50 is the only image encoder tried, it shows that this image setup is weak on its own, not that image data is inherently uninformative. It also does not establish whether image features add complementary signal in fused multimodal settings. Each result is a single run with uncharacterized variance, and several factors remain unknown or untested: the ResNet50 training details, other image encoders, transformer aggregation for images, and the slightly larger accuracy-F1 gap, which may hint at uneven per-class performance.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile avgpool with PCA-2000 (config_002: 0.591 acc, 0.573 F1). Multiprofile beat single-profile, and avgpool beat the transformer in that setting. Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool was much weaker (0.328 acc). It is still unknown whether image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA, which is a central design question for this study. Each result is a single run, so these rankings are provisional. 2) Test: config_018 keeps config_002's RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation fixed. It adds the ResNet50 image branch from config_011, which used the same multiprofile avgpool setting, and fuses the two with concat, the simplest fusion option. This directly tests whether adding the image modality helps, hurts or is neutral relative to the best RNA-only model. 3) Why now: both component branches have already been measured under identical profile and aggregation settings, so the comparison isolates the effect of adding image data via fusion. The result also decides where the remaining budget should go. If fusion gives no gain over RNA-only, effort should shift to RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT). If fusion helps, comparing fusion methods and image encoders becomes worthwhile.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept llm_summary_002's best RNA-only setup fixed (multiprofile, PCA-2000 encoder, avgpool aggregation) and added llm_summary_004's ResNet50 image branch, fusing the two with concat, the simplest fusion option. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619 (+0.028) and F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.610 (+0.038), making this the best result so far, even though image-only ResNet50 was weak on its own (0.328 acc). This initially suggests the image features carry some complementary signal when fused with RNA, and the narrower accuracy-F1 gap may hint at more balanced per-class performance, though per-class results are unknown. The gain is modest and comes from single runs with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, so it may not be reliable. Other fusion methods, other image or RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), and transformer aggregation in the fused setting all remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA is the dominant signal so far. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, while image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.328. Fusing the two with concat added a modest +0.028 (0.619). Multiprofile with avgpool has consistently beaten single-profile and transformer aggregation. Yet every RNA result uses PCA-2000, so the RNA encoder, arguably the most consequential design choice, is completely untested. 2. Test: swap PCA-2000 for the scGPT foundation-model encoder while keeping config_002's RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup fixed. This changes one variable and shows whether a learned RNA representation improves on PCA in accuracy and F1. Leaving out the image branch avoids confounding with fusion. 3. Why now: because RNA carries most of the predictive signal, the choice of RNA encoder likely bounds the performance of every downstream multimodal configuration. Settling it now guides which encoder to carry into fusion experiments. This should yield more information than smaller tweaks to fusion or image encoder around the current best, whose gains so far are modest and unreplicated.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 kept llm_summary_002's RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, swapping PCA-2000 for the scGPT foundation-model encoder. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.530 (-0.061) and F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.515, so in this setting scGPT underperformed PCA-2000, though it still beat the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485 acc). Because this is a single run with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and scGPT usage details (frozen vs. fine-tuned embeddings, preprocessing, gene-vocabulary overlap, training budget) are unknown, the result does not show that learned RNA representations are inherently worse than PCA. Other encoders such as scVI, and scGPT in the fused multimodal setting or with transformer aggregation, remain untested, so PCA-2000 is the better-supported RNA encoder for now.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool and concat fusion (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). It improved modestly over RNA-only PCA avgpool (0.591), even though image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.328). PCA beat scGPT, and avgpool beat the transformer, so those choices are reasonably supported for now. The image encoder is the weakest component and the least explored: only ResNet50 has been tried. 2) Test: Keep the best configuration fixed and swap only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal in the fused setting. 3) Why now: The image branch is the most likely bottleneck, so this one-variable change has high potential to improve on the best result. It is also informative either way. A gain would point future runs toward ViT-L, for example with weighted fusion. No gain would suggest the image contribution is limited regardless of encoder. That would shift the remaining budget toward fusion (weighted) or RNA encoder (scVI) tests.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration from llm_summary_005 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and changed only the image encoder, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.619 to 0.629 (+0.010), making this the best result so far on the primary metric. Validation F1 fell from 0.610 to 0.599 (-0.011), so the evidence is mixed rather than a clear improvement, and the wider accuracy-F1 gap may hint at less balanced per-class performance, though per-class results are unknown. Both differences are small, come from single runs with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and may be within noise. ViT-L has also not been tested image-only, so it remains unclear whether it adds more complementary signal than ResNet50 or whether the image contribution is limited regardless of encoder. Weighted fusion, other RNA encoders such as scVI, and transformer aggregation in the fused setting remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Fusing RNA with images using multiprofile avgpool gives the best results so far. ViT-L with concat (config_024) reached 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1, and ResNet50 with concat reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Every multimodal run has used concat, so the fusion method is still a completely untested design choice. The RNA encoder and aggregator comparisons already point toward PCA-2000 and avgpool. 2. What this tests: config_025 keeps the top-accuracy configuration (config_024) fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion. Any difference is therefore attributable to fusion alone. Weighted fusion could also down-weight the image branch, which was weak on its own, and might narrow ViT-L's wider accuracy-F1 gap. 3. Why this is the best next use of the budget: It removes the largest open uncertainty in the most promising region, so it is informative whether fusion helps or not. It also has a good chance of matching or beating the current best, so it balances exploration of an untested dimension with exploitation of the leading setup. Testing scVI could follow, but scGPT underperformed PCA, which makes another RNA encoder a less promising use of the next run.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept llm_summary_007's configuration fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, giving the first test of a non-concat fusion. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.629 to 0.635 (+0.007), the best so far on the primary metric. Validation F1 rose more, from 0.599 to 0.618 (+0.019), narrowing ViT-L's accuracy-F1 gap and edging past ResNet50 concat (0.610 F1). This is an initial observation that weighted fusion may help in this setup. However, the gains are small and come from single runs with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and the learned modality weights are unreported, so it is unknown whether the image branch was actually down-weighted. Weighted fusion with ResNet50, other fusion variants, scVI, and transformer aggregation in the fused setting remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.635 accuracy, 0.618 F1). Multiprofile with avgpool has consistently helped, and adding the image branch gave small gains. The RNA encoder is the strongest driver of performance, since RNA-only PCA at 0.591 far exceeds image-only at 0.328. Yet scVI, one of only three RNA encoder options, is completely untested. scGPT underperformed PCA, but that does not tell us whether a compact probabilistic embedding like scVI-200 would do better or worse. 2) This experiment changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, inside the current best configuration. It tests whether the RNA representation can be improved in the setting that matters most, and the result is directly comparable to config_025. 3) Budget value: this is a single-factor change on the most important untested axis. It is likely to be competitive, so it may yield a new best. Even if it underperforms, it clarifies whether PCA's advantage holds against scVI as well as scGPT. That makes it more useful than further fusion or aggregation tweaks, which have so far shown only small or negative effects.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept llm_summary_008's best configuration fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, which is the first test of scVI. Validation accuracy rose from 0.635 to 0.706 (+0.071) and F1 rose from 0.618 to 0.667 (+0.049). This is by far the best result so far and suggests that scVI-200 is a stronger RNA representation than PCA-2000 in this fused setting, consistent with the RNA encoder being the main performance driver. The widened accuracy-F1 gap (about 0.039) may hint at less balanced per-class performance, though per-class results are unknown. The result is a single run with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and several questions remain untested: whether scVI's advantage holds in the RNA-only setting, which would separate encoder quality from interaction with the image branch and weighted fusion; whether it holds with transformer aggregation, ResNet50, or concat fusion; and how the learned modality weights shifted.

selection_reason: Evidence: switching the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200 gave the best result so far (config_037: 0.706 acc, 0.667 F1, up from 0.635/0.618). However, that test was only run in the fused setting (ViT-L image encoder with weighted fusion). Earlier, adding the image branch to PCA gave only modest gains (about +0.03-0.04). So it is unclear whether scVI is simply a better RNA representation or whether its gain depends on the image branch and fusion. Test: config_005 is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200 with avgpool. It differs from config_002 (PCA RNA-only, 0.591) only in the encoder, and from config_037 only in dropping the image branch and fusion. This single run therefore gives a clean encoder effect without images. It also shows how much the image modality adds on top of a strong RNA encoder. Why now: this decides where the remaining budget should go. If scVI RNA-only comes close to 0.706, the image branch and fusion choices matter little, and effort should go to RNA and aggregation choices. If it falls well short, the multimodal fusion settings deserve further exploitation, such as testing transformer aggregation or concat fusion with scVI.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 isolated the RNA encoder in the RNA-only setting by running RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool with scVI-200. It differs from llm_summary_002 (PCA-2000, 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1) only in the encoder, and from llm_summary_009 (fused scVI with ViT-L and weighted fusion, 0.706 / 0.667) only in dropping the image branch and fusion. It reached 0.650 validation accuracy and 0.628 F1, a gain of about +0.059 accuracy and +0.055 F1 over PCA RNA-only. This suggests scVI-200 is a stronger RNA representation on its own, not only when combined with images, and it even exceeds every PCA-based fused configuration (best 0.635). It still falls about 0.056 accuracy and 0.040 F1 short of the fused scVI run, a gap similar to or slightly larger than the image-plus-weighted-fusion gain seen with PCA (about +0.044 accuracy), so the image branch and fusion appear to add complementary signal rather than being negligible. All comparisons are single runs with uncharacterized variance, and the fused-versus-RNA-only gap confounds the image branch with weighted fusion. Untested directions that would clarify where the remaining gains lie include scVI with concat fusion, transformer aggregation, other image encoders, other scVI dimensionalities, and the learned modality weights.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest and cheapest configuration. It sets a reference baseline. Each later change can then be tested against it one factor at a time: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation, image-only models, and multimodal fusion. Each comparison would isolate the effect of that single choice. 3. With a limited budget, starting from the simplest baseline is the best first step. It avoids assuming that more complex models will do better, and it makes every following experiment easier to interpret.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest, cheapest configuration as a reference baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. F1 sits close to accuracy, which suggests performance is not dominated by a few classes, but this is tentative. With no prior experiments for comparison, this is only an initial baseline, so it is still unknown whether other choices would do better: other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only models, or multimodal fusion. The result also comes from a single run with no variance estimate, so later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons should treat small differences from this baseline with caution.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA (pca_n2000) baseline (val acc 0.485, F1 0.464). We do not yet know whether any design axis matters. Profile setting and aggregation apply to almost every remaining configuration, so they are among the most consequential open questions. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the modality (RNA-only) and encoder (pca_n2000) fixed. It changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether combining multiple profiles helps, without confounding it with a new encoder or modality. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It is a clean one-factor comparison against the baseline. The answer applies broadly: if multiprofile helps, most multiprofile RNA, image and multimodal configurations become more attractive. If it does not, we can deprioritize them. Avgpool is the natural first step before testing the more complex transformer aggregation. A single run is limited evidence, so we will not overinterpret a small difference.
