experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only pca_n2000 setup from the baseline (llm_summary_001) and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (about +0.106), and supporting validation F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573, with F1 still close to accuracy. Because this is a one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that multiprofile input with avgpool helps RNA-only PCA models, which makes multiprofile variants of other configurations more promising. Several things remain uncertain: each result is a single run with no variance estimate; multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, so the effect of combining profiles cannot be separated from the choice of pooling (e.g., versus transformer aggregation); and it is unknown whether the gain transfers to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: moving the RNA-only pca_n2000 model from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, with F1 rising alongside it (0.464 to 0.573). The gain came from introducing multiprofile and avgpool together, so it is unclear whether combining profiles drives the gain or whether the aggregation choice also matters. 2) This experiment keeps everything from config_002 fixed and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. That isolates the aggregation effect within the best setting found so far. 3) Aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, including the image-only and multimodal ones. Settling avgpool versus transformer now with a clean one-factor comparison narrows the space for later encoder and fusion comparisons. It is also a reasonable exploitation step, extending the strongest direction seen so far. A single run cannot rule out noise, so a small difference should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only multiprofile pca_n2000 setup from llm_summary_002 fixed and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, giving a one-factor test of aggregation. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 (about -0.072), and supporting validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480. This is initial evidence that avgpool works better than transformer aggregation in this setting. The transformer result still beats the single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy), which tentatively suggests that combining profiles helps regardless of how they are aggregated. Each result comes from a single run with no variance estimate, and the transformer's hyperparameters and training budget may not be tuned. It is also unknown whether avgpool's advantage holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models, or multimodal fusion, so avgpool is a reasonable default for now but not a settled choice.

selection_reason: Evidence: all three runs so far are RNA-only PCA models. Multiprofile with avgpool is clearly best (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). It beats single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). The largest open question is the image modality, which has not been tested at all. This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only a resnet50 image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). That makes it a near one-factor test of whether adding imaging improves on the strongest RNA-only model. It is the best use of the budget because it addresses the most consequential unknown, the value of multimodality, while building on the best-supported direction. A gain would point the search toward multimodal variants such as weighted fusion, ViT-L, and other RNA encoders. No gain or a drop would be informative too: it would suggest focusing on RNA encoders or running an image-only check next. Either way it extends the current best configuration toward possibly higher accuracy.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 fixed (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and added a resnet50 image branch with concat fusion, making it a near one-factor test of adding imaging. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619 (about +0.028), and supporting validation F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.610, a slightly larger gain that also narrows the gap between F1 and accuracy. This is initial evidence that adding image features helps the strongest RNA-only model, which makes multimodal variants (e.g., other fusion methods, image encoders such as ViT-L, other RNA encoders) worth exploring. The gain is modest and comes from a single run with no variance estimate, so it may fall within run-to-run noise. Image-only performance is still untested, so the image modality's standalone contribution is unknown, and it is unclear whether the gain depends on resnet50, concat fusion, or the PCA RNA encoder.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile with avgpool clearly beat single-profile for RNA-only PCA (0.591 vs 0.485 accuracy). Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool (0.519). Adding resnet50 with concat fusion gave a modest further gain (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1), which may be within noise. The RNA encoder is still completely unexplored: every run so far used pca_n2000, and a large share of the remaining configurations depend on whether scVI or scGPT is better. 2. What this tests: config_005 swaps only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, within the best RNA-only setup (multiprofile, avgpool). This is a clean one-factor comparison against config_002 that isolates the effect of RNA representation. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: RNA representation is the largest unresolved design axis, and the result decides which encoder to carry into the multimodal runs. Testing it RNA-only avoids confounding it with image or fusion choices. A clear gain or loss will efficiently prune or prioritize many downstream configurations, which is more valuable under the budget than fine-tuning fusion on the current PCA-based model.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 fixed (multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, giving a clean one-factor test of RNA representation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 (about +0.059), and supporting validation F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.628. This RNA-only scVI model also exceeds the PCA-based multimodal resnet50+concat run (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1), which is initial evidence that scVI is the stronger RNA encoder and should be the default carried into multimodal runs. Uncertainties remain: each result is a single run with no variance estimate; scVI also used far fewer dimensions (200 vs 2000), so the effect of the encoder method cannot be separated from the effect of dimensionality; scGPT is still untested; and it is unknown whether scVI's advantage persists, or how large the image modality's added gain is, once scVI is combined with image encoders and fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile with avgpool beat single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485) and beat transformer aggregation (0.519). scVI beat PCA as the RNA encoder (0.650 vs 0.591). Adding resnet50 with concat fusion gave a modest gain on top of PCA (0.619 vs 0.591; F1 0.610 vs 0.573). The open question is whether that imaging gain still holds once the RNA encoder is stronger, or whether scVI already captures most of the signal. 2) Test: config_030 keeps the best setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds the resnet50 concat image branch. It differs by one factor from config_005 (adding imaging) and by one factor from config_018 (PCA to scVI in the multimodal setting). This cleanly measures whether the image gain and the encoder gain add together. 3) Why now: it uses the strongest current evidence and is the most likely next best performer. Whatever the result, it settles whether further budget should go to multimodal fusion variants (weighted fusion, ViT-L) or to RNA-side choices such as scGPT.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 combined the strongest RNA-only setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_005) with the resnet50 image branch and concat fusion, making it a one-factor test of adding imaging to scVI and a one-factor test of PCA→scVI within the multimodal setting (vs llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy was 0.632, below the scVI RNA-only model (0.650, about -0.019) and slightly above the PCA multimodal model (0.619, about +0.013). Supporting F1 (0.607) was below both scVI RNA-only (0.628) and PCA multimodal (0.610). This is initial evidence that the image gain seen with PCA and the scVI encoder gain do not add together: once the RNA encoder is stronger, resnet50+concat imaging gave no benefit and may slightly hurt, so scVI RNA-only remains the best configuration so far. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with no variance estimate, so differences of about 0.01–0.02 may be noise; it is unclear whether the lack of gain reflects overlap between scVI and image information or a limitation of naive concat fusion (e.g., an untested imbalance between the 200-dim scVI features and the higher-dimensional resnet50 features), which weighted fusion or other image encoders (ViT-L) could address; and image-only performance and RNA-side alternatives such as scGPT are still untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA representation has been the strongest lever so far among single-factor changes. Switching from PCA to scVI raised accuracy by about +0.059. Adding resnet50+concat imaging gave only +0.028 with PCA and about -0.019 with scVI. scVI RNA-only (config_005: 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) is the current best, but scGPT, the third RNA encoder, has never been tested. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the winning setup fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from scVI to scGPT. This is a clean one-factor comparison that shows whether a foundation-model embedding beats scVI. It also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal and fusion experiments. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: An entire level of the most influential design factor is still unexplored. This run could produce a new best configuration and would also guide every later multimodal choice. Testing weighted fusion (config_031) is a reasonable follow-up, but the effects of imaging so far are small and within plausible noise. Fixing the strongest RNA encoder first makes later fusion comparisons more meaningful.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_005 fixed (multiprofile, avgpool, no imaging) and changed only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT, giving a clean one-factor test of the third, previously untested RNA encoder. Validation accuracy was 0.530, well below scVI (0.650, about -0.120) and also below PCA under the same setup (0.591, about -0.060), and supporting F1 (0.515) followed the same pattern while staying close to accuracy. This is initial evidence that scGPT embeddings, as used here, are the weakest of the three RNA encoders in this setting, so scVI remains the default RNA encoder for later multimodal and fusion experiments and scVI RNA-only remains the best configuration so far. The gap is much larger than the ~0.01–0.02 differences seen earlier, but it still comes from a single run with no variance estimate, and it is unclear whether it reflects scGPT itself or untested choices such as embedding dimensionality, preprocessing or gene-vocabulary mismatch, frozen versus fine-tuned use, or interaction with avgpool aggregation.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the best result so far is scVI RNA-only (multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Adding resnet50 with concat fusion to scVI gave lower results (0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1), even though imaging helped the weaker PCA encoder. The open question is whether this reflects redundancy between scVI and image features, or a limitation of naive concat fusion, such as imbalance between 200-dim scVI features and higher-dimensional resnet50 features. 2. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, holding scVI, resnet50, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This is a clean one-factor test of fusion in the strongest setup. If weighted fusion lifts multimodal above 0.650, fusion is the bottleneck and the multimodal direction is worth pursuing. If it does not, that strengthens the case that images add little once scVI is used. 3. Why now: it addresses the most decision-relevant uncertainty, whether multimodal fusion is worth more budget. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best. It is preferable to switching to ViT-L or running image-only first, because it isolates a single factor in the top configuration.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the scVI multimodal setup from llm_summary_006 fixed (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted, giving a clean one-factor test of fusion in the strongest configuration. Validation accuracy reached 0.678, above concat fusion (0.632, about +0.046) and above the previous best, scVI RNA-only (0.650, about +0.028). Supporting F1 (0.646) showed the same pattern (vs 0.607 and 0.628). This is initial evidence that the earlier lack of image benefit with scVI reflected a limitation of concat fusion rather than simple redundancy between scVI and image features, which makes scVI+resnet50+weighted fusion the new best configuration and multimodal fusion a direction worth more budget. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with no variance estimate, so the roughly +0.03 margin over RNA-only may be partly noise. It is untested why weighted fusion helps (e.g., balancing the 200-dim scVI features against higher-dimensional resnet50 features, or other properties of the weighting), whether the gain holds with other image encoders such as ViT-L or with the PCA encoder, and how the image modality performs on its own.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best configuration so far is scVI + resnet50 + multiprofile avgpool + weighted fusion (config_031: 0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1). Earlier one-factor runs favored scVI over PCA and scGPT, avgpool over transformer, and weighted over concat fusion. The image encoder is the one major design choice not yet varied: every image-containing run used resnet50, so we don't know whether ViT-L would help or hurt. 2. What this tests: config_037 keeps everything in config_031 fixed and swaps only resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This isolates the effect of the image representation in the strongest setting. It also shows whether the weighted-fusion gain holds for a different image encoder. 3. Why it's the best next run: it exploits the most promising direction while resolving an untested, high-impact design choice through a clean one-factor comparison. Testing image-only models (e.g., config_011) would clarify the standalone value of imaging, but it is less likely to improve the best result. Given that all results are single runs, a small difference either way should be read cautiously, with F1 as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best configuration from llm_summary_008 fixed (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swapped only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This is a clean one-factor test of image representation and the first run to vary the image encoder. Validation accuracy rose from 0.678 to 0.706 (about +0.029), and supporting F1 rose from 0.646 to 0.667, making this the new best configuration. It is initial evidence that ViT-L image features beat resnet50 in this setting and that the weighted-fusion multimodal setup still works with a different image encoder. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with no variance estimate, so a gain of about +0.03 may be partly noise. It is unclear whether the gain comes from the ViT architecture, model scale, or feature dimensionality. Image-only performance is still untested, as are ViT-L with concat fusion, the PCA encoder, or transformer aggregation, so it is unknown how much of the improvement depends on weighted fusion and scVI.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). The image modality has never been tested on its own. Its contribution has only been inferred from multimodal gains of roughly 0.03 over the scVI RNA-only model (0.650), and those gains come from single runs and depended on the fusion method. 2) What this tests: config_014 is image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool. It is a one-factor ablation of config_037 that removes the RNA branch. Paired with the existing scVI RNA-only result (config_005, 0.650), it shows how strong ViT-L image features are on their own, whether the multimodal gain reflects complementary information or mostly one modality dominating, and whether multiprofile avgpool also helps image features. 3) Why this is the best next run: it addresses the most often flagged gap in the design space, standalone modality value. That answer guides where to spend the remaining budget, such as further fusion and image-encoder work versus RNA-side work. Alternatives like transformer aggregation (worse in prior tests) or concat fusion with ViT-L (concat already underperformed) are less likely to change decisions.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested the image modality on its own for the first time. It is a one-factor ablation of the best configuration, llm_summary_009 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.706 accuracy), with the RNA branch removed, leaving image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool. Validation accuracy was 0.332 (supporting F1 0.315, close to accuracy), far below the full multimodal model (about -0.37), the scVI RNA-only model (0.650), and even the single-profile PCA RNA-only baseline (0.485). This is initial evidence that RNA is the dominant modality and that ViT-L image features are weak predictors alone, so the roughly +0.03–0.06 multimodal gains under weighted fusion appear to come from images adding complementary information to RNA rather than from images driving performance. Uncertainties remain: this is a single run with no variance estimate, and chance level is not stated. No single-profile image-only run exists, so it is unknown whether multiprofile avgpool helps image features. Image-only resnet50 is untested, so encoders cannot be compared standalone. It is also unclear whether the image-only setup (e.g., classifier head, training budget) was adequately tuned.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: no experiments have been completed, so we know nothing yet about how modality, RNA or image representation, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion affect accuracy. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space, with no aggregation or fusion. It gives a reference point. Later runs can then change one factor at a time against it: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile avgpool or transformer aggregation, image-only models, and multimodal fusion. 3. Why now: a cheap, interpretable baseline is the most efficient first use of the budget. It shows how hard the task is and lets each later experiment isolate the gain from a single design choice. This avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA-2000 RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as a cheap, interpretable reference point. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 (validation F1 0.464), which serves as an initial baseline for task difficulty. The similar F1 suggests no extreme class-level imbalance in performance, though this is tentative. Because no other configurations have been run, it remains unknown whether alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-based models, or multimodal fusion would improve on this, and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized. Future one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against this baseline are needed to attribute any gains to specific design choices.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: Only one run exists, the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). We know nothing yet about the image modality, which is the biggest unknown in the search space. Image encoders, and whether multimodal fusion is worthwhile, all depend on whether images carry useful signal for this task. 2. What it tests: config_010 is the image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model. It keeps the profile setting the same as the baseline and also has no aggregation or fusion, so the only change is the modality (RNA vs. image). This gives a clean read on how well images alone predict the labels relative to RNA alone. 3. Why it is the best next step: Comparing modalities is a high-value, low-complexity experiment. A strong image result would justify spending budget on image-encoder comparisons and multimodal fusion. A weak result would push the search toward RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and multiprofile aggregation. In both cases, the outcome narrows the large multimodal portion of the search space more than a single RNA-encoder or aggregation change would at this stage.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was selected to get a first read on whether the image modality carries useful signal, compared with the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (llm_summary_001: val acc 0.485, F1 0.464). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1 0.172), well below the RNA baseline, which is initial evidence that ResNet50 image features alone are much weaker predictors than PCA-reduced RNA in this setup. This comparison changes both the modality and the encoder, and each configuration has only one run with uncharacterized variance, so it does not show that images lack signal in general, and the chance level is not stated here. Several questions remain open: whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would help the image branch, and whether images add complementary information when fused with RNA.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline (config_001) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. The image-only ResNet50 single-profile model (config_010) was much weaker at 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. Each is a single run, so variance is unknown. The biggest open question is whether the weak image branch still adds complementary signal when combined with RNA. Multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space (36 of 49), so this answer affects most later choices. 2) This experiment adds the ResNet50 image branch to the baseline with simple concat fusion and changes nothing else: same PCA-2000 encoder, single-profile setting, no aggregation. Both parts have already been measured alone, so any gain or loss over 0.485 can be attributed to fusion itself. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because the result decides how much budget the multimodal region deserves. A clear gain would justify exploring encoders, aggregation and weighted fusion within multimodal models. No gain or a loss would argue for focusing on RNA-only factors next, such as scVI or scGPT encoders and multiprofile aggregation. Concat is the simplest fusion option, so it gives a clean first test before trying weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that adds the ResNet50 image branch to the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline via simple concat fusion, with no aggregation and no other changes, to check whether the weak image modality (image-only: val acc 0.208, F1 0.172) adds complementary signal to RNA. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.527 (F1 0.510), about 0.04 above the RNA-only baseline (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1), with F1 improving by a similar margin. Because only the image branch plus concat fusion was added, this is initial evidence that combining ResNet50 image features with PCA RNA may help despite the image branch's weak standalone performance, which tentatively supports giving the multimodal region more budget. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized variance, so the modest gain may not be robust; it is also unclear whether the gain reflects genuine image information or simply added model capacity, and whether other encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or weighted fusion would change the picture.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is multimodal single-profile PCA-2000 + ResNet50 with concat fusion (config_016: acc 0.527, F1 0.510). It beats RNA-only by about 0.04, but each setting has only one run. Profile setting (single vs. multi) is a major design axis that has not been tested at all, while RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion type are also open. 2) What this tests: config_018 keeps the modality, both encoders and concat fusion the same as config_016. It changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), since multiprofile requires some aggregation. This gives a near one-factor read on whether pooling multiple profiles helps the current best model. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: It exploits the most promising region found so far while answering a structural question that affects about half the remaining search space. If multiprofile helps, later runs can compare transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and other encoders within that setting. If it does not help, many multiprofile configurations can be deprioritized. Testing it on the strongest configuration first makes the result most relevant to the final model.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the current best multimodal setup (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, concat fusion; llm_summary_003: val acc 0.527, F1 0.510) and changed only the profile setting from single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), which multiprofile requires. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.619 (F1 0.610), about 0.09 above the single-profile counterpart and the best result so far, with F1 improving by a similar margin (about 0.10). This near one-factor comparison is initial evidence that multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation helps this configuration, which tentatively supports prioritizing the multiprofile region. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized variance, the effect of multiprofile cannot be separated from the choice of avgpool, and it remains untested whether multiprofile also helps RNA-only or image-only models, or how alternative aggregation (e.g., transformer), weighted fusion, or other encoders would perform in this setting.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving the multimodal PCA-2000 + ResNet50 + concat model from single-profile to multiprofile raised validation accuracy from 0.527 to 0.619, with F1 rising by a similar margin. This is the largest gain so far. However, it was tested only with avgpool, so the multiprofile benefit cannot yet be separated from the aggregation choice. 2. What this tests: config_020 keeps the best configuration (config_018) fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates how aggregation affects the most promising region, which is a learned set-level combination versus a simple mean. 3. Why now: This single-factor change extends the strongest direction found so far, and could produce a new best result. Its outcome also tells us which aggregation to use in later tests of fusion type (weighted) and encoders (ViT-L, scVI, scGPT). Running the RNA-only multiprofile control (config_002) next would then help show whether the image branch contributes beyond added capacity.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, concat fusion; llm_summary_004: val acc 0.619, F1 0.610) and changed only the aggregation from avgpool to a learned transformer, to test whether set-level learned aggregation beats a simple mean. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.579 (F1 0.563), about 0.04 below the avgpool counterpart, with F1 dropping by a similar margin (about 0.05), but still above the single-profile multimodal model (0.527 accuracy). This single-factor comparison is initial evidence that avgpool works better than transformer aggregation in this setup, so avgpool tentatively remains the default aggregation for later fusion and encoder tests. However, each configuration has only one run with uncharacterized variance, and the transformer's training settings (e.g., tuning, data per set, overfitting) are not described, so the gap may not be robust and may not generalize to other encoders, weighted fusion, or RNA-only multiprofile models, which remain untested.

selection_reason: Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat), with validation accuracy 0.619 and F1 0.610. That is about 0.09 above its single-profile counterpart, and avgpool beat transformer aggregation. In the single-profile setting, adding images gave only a modest gain of about 0.04 over RNA-only (0.527 vs 0.485), and the image branch alone was weak (0.208). So it is unclear whether the multiprofile gain comes from aggregating RNA profiles or from multimodal fusion. This experiment changes only the model setting of config_018, removing the image branch while keeping PCA-2000, multiprofile and avgpool. If RNA-only multiprofile matches config_018, the image branch adds little and the budget should go to RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT and RNA aggregation. If it falls clearly below, the multimodal gain is confirmed in the strongest setting, which justifies spending more on image encoders like ViT-L and on weighted fusion. Many configurations still differ by encoder, fusion and modality, so this cheap ablation is the best next use of budget: it decides which branch of the search space deserves the remaining runs.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 ablated the image branch from the best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat; val acc 0.619, F1 0.610), keeping RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 and avgpool, to test whether the multiprofile gain comes from aggregating RNA profiles or from multimodal fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.591 (F1 0.573). That is about 0.11 above the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.485, F1 0.464), a comparison that changes both profile setting and aggregation. It is also only about 0.03 below the multimodal counterpart (F1 gap about 0.04), similar to the modest image gain seen in the single-profile setting (about 0.04). This is initial evidence that most of the multiprofile improvement is available from RNA aggregation alone, while the image branch adds a small, apparently consistent increment, so the result falls between the pre-stated 'matches' and 'clearly below' outcomes. Each configuration has only one run with uncharacterized variance, so the roughly 0.03 multimodal advantage may not be robust and could reflect added capacity rather than image information. It therefore does not yet decide whether the remaining budget should go to RNA encoders and RNA aggregation (e.g., scVI, scGPT) or to stronger image encoders and weighted fusion (e.g., ViT-L).

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat), at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. The RNA-only ablation (config_002, 0.591) shows that most of the signal and most of the multiprofile gain come from RNA, while the image branch adds only about 0.03. Avgpool tentatively beat transformer aggregation. The RNA encoder is still completely unexplored: every run has used PCA-2000. Given how much RNA dominates, this is likely the most important untested design choice. 2) What this tests: config_042 keeps the best setup fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. This is a clean one-factor comparison against config_018 that shows whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA in the strongest setting. 3) Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA modality carries most of the predictive signal, so its representation should have more leverage than weighted fusion or a stronger image encoder, which mainly act on the weaker branch. The experiment combines exploitation (building on the best configuration) with exploration of a high-uncertainty axis. Its outcome will guide whether later budget goes to scGPT- or scVI-based variants or stays with PCA.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat; llm_summary_004: val acc 0.619, F1 0.610) and swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to pretrained scGPT. It was a one-factor test of whether a foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA, chosen because RNA carries most of the signal. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.512 (F1 0.477). That is about 0.11 below the PCA-2000 counterpart, with F1 about 0.13 lower, and it falls below even the single-profile PCA multimodal model (0.527) and the RNA-only multiprofile PCA model (0.591). This is initial evidence that scGPT embeddings, as used here, are a weaker RNA representation than PCA-2000 in this setup, which tentatively argues against prioritizing scGPT-based variants. However, this is a single run with uncharacterized variance, and the scGPT details (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned, embedding extraction, gene vocabulary overlap, preprocessing) are not described, so the gap may reflect implementation or adaptation choices rather than an inherent limitation. It also remains untested whether scVI or other RNA encoders would match or beat PCA.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat), at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. The RNA-only ablation (0.591) shows that RNA carries most of the signal, so the RNA representation is the most important open choice. scGPT did much worse than PCA (0.512). scVI, the remaining RNA encoder, is completely untested, and the scGPT result alone does not tell us whether learned representations in general lose to PCA. 2. What this tests: config_030 keeps config_018 fixed and swaps only PCA-2000 for scVI-200. It cleanly isolates whether a compact probabilistic latent space can match or beat PCA within the best-known setup. 3. Why now: It resolves the encoder question on the modality that matters most, in the best-performing context, with a single-factor change. If scVI wins, it is a likely new best. If it loses, the budget can confidently shift to the image encoder (ViT-L, config_024) and weighted fusion (config_019) on top of PCA.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat; llm_summary_004: val acc 0.619, F1 0.610) and swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, a one-factor test of whether a compact probabilistic latent space can match or beat PCA, given that scGPT had done much worse (0.512). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.632, about 0.013 above the PCA-2000 counterpart and the best accuracy so far, but its F1 (0.607) was slightly below PCA's (0.610). This is initial evidence that scVI-200 is at least competitive with PCA-2000 in this setup, and that the poor scGPT result does not mean learned RNA representations in general lose to PCA, but it does not show scVI is clearly better. The small accuracy gain, the opposite-direction F1 difference, single runs with uncharacterized variance, and unreported scVI details (e.g., latent training, preprocessing) mean the two encoders should be treated as roughly tied. It remains untested whether scVI's advantage, if real, holds with RNA-only models, other aggregation, weighted fusion, or stronger image encoders such as ViT-L.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best region so far is multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool and concat. Within it, scVI-200 (0.632 acc, config_030) and PCA-2000 (0.619, config_018) are roughly tied. scGPT was clearly worse, and avgpool beat transformer aggregation. Images add a small but apparently consistent increment of about 0.03 to 0.04. However, the only image encoder tested is ResNet50, which is weak on its own (0.208). The image encoder is the largest design choice not yet tested, and its effect is the biggest open uncertainty. 2) Test: Keep config_030 fixed (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swap only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This one-factor comparison asks whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal than ResNet50. A clear gain would move the remaining budget toward the image branch and fusion. No gain would suggest RNA plus aggregation dominates and the budget should go to RNA-side choices or weighted fusion. 3) Why now: It probes the highest-uncertainty factor that could plausibly give a sizable improvement, while building on the current best configuration (exploitation). Weighted fusion is the other untested factor, but its gain is likely limited while the image features stay weak, so it can be tested afterward on whichever image encoder wins. One caveat: each configuration has a single run, so a small difference should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, avgpool, concat; val acc 0.632, F1 0.607) fixed and swapped only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This one-factor test asked whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.715 (F1 0.687), about 0.08 above the ResNet50 counterpart with a similar F1 gain, and it is the best result so far. The gain is larger than the roughly 0.03 to 0.04 increment ResNet50 images had added over RNA-only models. This is initial evidence that the image encoder is a high-impact factor, which tentatively supports shifting budget toward the image branch and fusion, such as weighted fusion on ViT-L or checking ViT-L with PCA-2000. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized variance. ViT-L's standalone image-only performance and its effect with other RNA encoders or aggregation are untested. It also remains unknown whether the gain reflects richer image information or added capacity or feature dimensionality.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), with val acc 0.715 and F1 0.687. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L gave about +0.08, which suggests the image branch and how it is combined with RNA matter a lot. Every experiment so far has used concat fusion, so fusion is the only design dimension with no evidence at all. 2) Test: config_037 changes only concat to weighted fusion on the best configuration. This is a clean one-factor test of whether learned weighting of the RNA and image contributions helps, now that the image features are much stronger. 3) Budget value: it fills the largest remaining gap in the design space and also exploits the best region, since a win would likely set a new best. If it does not help, concat can be fixed as the default and the remaining budget shifted to other questions, such as ViT-L image-only or PCA with ViT-L. This is a single run with uncharacterized variance, so a small difference in either direction should be treated as a tie rather than a decision.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration fixed (llm_summary_009: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image, avgpool; val acc 0.715, F1 0.687) and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted. It was the first test of fusion, the one design dimension with no prior evidence, and asked whether learned weighting of the RNA and image contributions helps now that the image features are stronger. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.706 (F1 0.667), about 0.009 below the concat counterpart, with F1 about 0.02 lower, so it did not set a new best. Under the pre-stated rule for this single run with uncharacterized variance, the accuracy difference is best treated as roughly a tie that slightly favors concat, which tentatively supports keeping concat as the default fusion. It remains untested whether weighted fusion behaves differently with other encoders (e.g., ResNet50 or PCA-2000), other aggregation, or other weighting implementations and tuning, which are not described. Run-to-run variance is still needed to decide whether the small, consistent-direction gaps in accuracy and F1 are real.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about the absolute performance level or which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single-profile, a PCA (n=2000) encoder, and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference baseline. Later runs can then each change one factor against it: the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), the profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), the modality (image-only, multimodal), and the fusion method. 3. Why it is the best use of the next run: Starting with a simple, cheap, low-variance baseline anchors every later comparison and keeps one-factor-at-a-time attribution possible. It also guards against assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better without evidence.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration as a reference baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.4639. F1 is slightly below accuracy, which may point to some unevenness in per-class performance. No other experiments have been run, so this is only an initial baseline and tells us nothing yet about whether alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image or multimodal inputs, or fusion methods would help. It also remains unknown how much these numbers vary across seeds or splits, and what chance-level or ceiling performance is for this task.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile, PCA baseline (config_001: accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Nothing is known yet about the image modality, alternative RNA encoders, multiprofile aggregation or fusion. 2. Test: config_010 is the image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 encoder. It keeps the simplest setup (single-profile, no aggregation, no fusion) and swaps only the modality, so it is a clean comparison against config_001. It shows whether image features carry signal comparable to, weaker than, or stronger than RNA. 3. Why now: modality is the most consequential and least understood design choice. It determines whether the large multimodal portion of the search space (about two-thirds of the configurations) is worth exploring, and it is needed to interpret any later fusion result. An encoder swap (scVI or scGPT) or a multiprofile test would refine the RNA branch, but those questions are better answered once we know whether images contribute at all.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion, chosen as the closest available counterpart to the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.1718, far below the RNA-only baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). This is an initial observation that this image configuration carries less usable signal than the RNA baseline. Switching modality also switched the encoder (ResNet50 vs PCA), so the gap cannot be attributed to the image modality itself rather than to this particular encoder or feature pipeline. It remains unknown whether image features add complementary information when fused with RNA, whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would do better, how much results vary across seeds or splits, and where chance level lies, which determines how much signal the 0.21 accuracy reflects.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: we have two single-profile anchors. RNA-only PCA reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. Image alone is clearly weaker, but we do not know whether it adds information that RNA lacks. That is the central question for a multimodal study. 2) What this tests: config_016 fuses exactly the two tested encoders (PCA RNA and ResNet50 image) with simple concat, still single-profile with no aggregation. Both unimodal results act as direct controls. Accuracy above 0.485 would suggest image adds signal. Equal or lower accuracy would suggest image is redundant or adds noise under this simple fusion. F1 can also show whether image helps the weaker classes. 3) Why it is the best next use: it changes only one thing relative to existing results (adding the image branch), so the result is easy to interpret. It also decides whether the many multimodal configurations deserve further budget, or whether the search should focus on RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. Concat is the simplest fusion baseline; weighted fusion can be compared later if image proves useful.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 fused the two previously tested single-profile encoders, PCA (n=2000) RNA and ResNet50 image, by simple concatenation with no aggregation, to test whether image features add information beyond RNA. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5266 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.5104, above the RNA-only control (0.4849 / 0.4639) and well above the image-only control (0.2079 / 0.1718); the comparison with RNA-only differs only by the added image branch, so it is initial evidence that ResNet50 image features carry some signal that PCA RNA features lack. The F1 gain (~0.047) is similar to the accuracy gain (~0.042), so this single result gives no clear sign that the extra signal mainly helps weaker classes. The ~4-point improvement comes from one run, and seed/split variance is unknown, so its robustness is uncertain. It is also untested whether the benefit holds with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or alternative fusion methods such as weighted fusion. Together these results suggest multimodal configurations are worth further search budget.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: we have three runs. PCA+ResNet50 concat fusion in single-profile mode is the best so far (0.527 accuracy, 0.510 F1). It beats RNA-only (0.485) and image-only (0.208), which is initial evidence that image features add complementary signal. The profile setting (single vs. multiprofile) has not been tested in any modality, so it is one of the largest open design choices. 2) What this tests: config_018 is identical to the current best config_016 except that it switches to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles helps, using the simplest aggregator before trying a transformer. Accuracy is the main readout, with F1 as a check on whether any gain is spread across classes. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: it exploits the most promising configuration while answering one important structural question with a single change. Fusion type and RNA or image encoder swaps are also open, but profile setting affects the whole remaining grid, so resolving it early best guides later choices. A small gain or loss should still be read cautiously, since seed variance is unknown.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 took the previous best configuration (multimodal, PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, concat fusion; llm_summary_003) and changed only the profile setting, switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6186 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.6103, up from 0.5266 / 0.5104. This is the largest gain so far, and the F1 gain (~0.100) is similar to the accuracy gain (~0.092), so the improvement appears broadly spread across classes rather than concentrated in a few. Because multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, this is initial evidence that multiprofile aggregation helps in this multimodal setup, but it does not separate the effect of using multiple profiles from the choice of aggregator. The result comes from a single run with unknown seed/split variance, and it remains untested whether multiprofile helps the RNA-only or image-only settings, whether a transformer aggregator beats avgpool, and whether the benefit holds with other encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT) or other fusion methods. Since profile setting affects the whole remaining grid, multiprofile looks like the stronger default for further search.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. It improved on single-profile concat by about 9 points. However, that experiment introduced multiprofile and avgpool together, so the aggregator's own contribution is unknown. All results are single runs, so seed variance is also unknown. 2) Test: config_020 keeps everything from config_018 and changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether a learned, attention-based aggregation over profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3) Why now: Aggregation is a design choice that applies to every multiprofile configuration in the remaining grid, which is now the preferred setting. Settling avgpool versus transformer early will guide many later choices across encoders and fusion methods. It also exploits the strongest current direction with a clean one-variable comparison. Accuracy will decide the comparison, with F1 as a tiebreaker if the gap is small.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 took the current best configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, concat fusion; llm_summary_004) and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to a transformer, to test whether learned attention-based aggregation over profiles beats mean pooling. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5793 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.5631, below the avgpool counterpart (0.6186 / 0.6103) by about 4 points accuracy and 5 points F1. In this single-variable comparison, avgpool is the better aggregator for this setup, and the transformer still beat the single-profile multimodal result (0.5266 / 0.5104). That fits the idea that using multiple profiles itself helps, but it is not a direct test of that. The gap comes from single runs with unknown seed/split variance, and the transformer's hyperparameters, capacity, and training budget may not have been tuned, so it remains uncertain whether the transformer is inherently worse or only worse under these settings, and whether the ranking holds with other encoders (scVI, scGPT), other fusion methods, or the RNA-only and image-only multiprofile settings. For now, avgpool remains the stronger default aggregator.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Profile setting and aggregation each have one controlled comparison (multiprofile beat single-profile, avgpool beat transformer). Fusion method has never been tested, since every multimodal run used concat. 2) Test: config_019 changes only concat to weighted fusion on the current best setup. It directly measures whether learned modality weighting helps, which seems plausible given that the RNA branch is much stronger than the image branch (0.48 vs 0.21 alone). 3) Why now: it is a clean one-variable exploitation step from the strongest configuration, and it resolves the last unexamined design axis. That tells us whether concat or weighted fusion should be the default before spending budget on encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L). Those swaps are the logical next comparisons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 took the current best configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation; llm_summary_004) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted fusion. This was the first test of the fusion axis. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6390 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.6197, above the concat counterpart (0.6186 / 0.6103) and now the best result so far. Because only fusion changed, this is initial evidence that weighted fusion helps in this setup. However, the gain is modest (~2.0 points accuracy, ~0.9 points F1), comes from single runs with unknown seed/split variance, and could fall within run-to-run noise. The F1 gain is about half the accuracy gain, so the improvement may not be evenly spread across classes. The run also does not show whether the learned weighting actually favors the stronger RNA branch. It also remains untested whether the advantage holds with other encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) or other aggregators. For now, weighted fusion is a reasonable tentative default for the planned encoder-swap comparisons.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Profile setting, aggregation and fusion have each been tested once against this backbone. The encoder axis is still completely untested. RNA carries most of the signal (RNA-only 0.48 accuracy vs image-only 0.21), so the RNA representation is the biggest remaining unknown. 2. What this tests: config_043 keeps everything in config_019 and changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats simple PCA within the current best pipeline. 3. Why now: It is a clean single-variable comparison on the most influential modality, and it could raise performance. A null or negative result is still informative: it would tell us whether to keep PCA as the default before spending budget on scVI or ViT-L swaps.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 took the current best configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion; llm_summary_006) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n=2000 to pretrained scGPT. This was the first test of the encoder axis. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5251 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.4979, well below the PCA counterpart (0.6390 / 0.6197) by about 11 points accuracy and 12 points F1, and roughly level with the earlier single-profile concat multimodal run (0.5266 / 0.5104). In this single-variable comparison, scGPT embeddings underperformed PCA within this pipeline, so PCA remains the stronger default RNA encoder. The gap is large compared with earlier single-axis differences, but it comes from single runs with unknown seed/split variance. It also remains uncertain whether the deficit reflects scGPT itself or how it was used here (e.g., frozen vs fine-tuned embeddings, preprocessing or gene-vocabulary mismatch, embedding dimensionality, interaction with weighted fusion or avgpool), and whether scGPT would fare differently in RNA-only or concat settings. It is also untested how scVI or ViT-L swaps would compare.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Profile setting, aggregation and fusion have each had a single-variable test, and the RNA encoder axis has one data point: scGPT fell about 11 points below PCA. The image encoder axis has not been tested at all. ResNet50 image features are weak on their own (0.21 accuracy) but still added about 4 points when fused with RNA, so a stronger image representation could plausibly add more. 2. Test: config_025 swaps only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps every other setting of the best configuration. This isolates the effect of the image representation within the current best pipeline. 3. Why now: Opening an entirely untested axis reduces more uncertainty than refining one already probed. The result decides whether later runs should default to ViT-L or ResNet50, and it has a realistic chance of improving on the best result. The scVI swap (config_031) is the natural follow-up for the RNA encoder axis.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 took the current best configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion; llm_summary_006) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This was the first test of the image-encoder axis. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6352 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.6183, essentially level with the ResNet50 counterpart (0.6390 / 0.6197): about 0.4 points lower in accuracy and 0.1 points lower in F1. This is likely within run-to-run noise, so in this single-variable comparison the stronger pretrained image backbone gave no detectable benefit, and neither encoder is clearly better. The result comes from single runs with unknown seed/split variance. It remains uncertain whether ViT-L features are no more informative than ResNet50 for this task, or whether any gain is masked by how they are used (e.g., frozen features, dimensionality, weighted fusion possibly down-weighting the image branch, an RNA-dominated ceiling). An image-only ViT-L run, which could separate these explanations, is also untested. ResNet50 remains a reasonable, cheaper default, and the untested scVI RNA swap is still open.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.6390 acc / 0.6197 F1). Two encoder swaps on this base have been run. Replacing PCA with scGPT lowered performance sharply (~11 points). Replacing ResNet50 with ViT-L changed almost nothing (~0.4 points, likely noise). The scVI RNA encoder is the one remaining encoder option and has never been tested. 2) Test: config_031 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI (n=200). This finishes the RNA-encoder comparison on the best pipeline. It asks whether a compact learned latent space matches or beats PCA, or whether learned embeddings generally underperform here, as scGPT did. 3) Why now: The RNA branch appears to carry most of the signal, so the RNA encoder is the design choice most likely to move the ceiling. scVI is the only untested option on that axis. A single-variable swap on the current best base keeps the result interpretable. It also offers a real chance of a new best. Further aggregator, fusion, or modality-only ablations would be less informative until this question is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 took the current best configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion; llm_summary_006) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n=2000 to scVI n=200, completing the RNA-encoder comparison on this pipeline. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6776 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.6464, a new best. That is about 3.9 points accuracy and 2.7 points F1 above the PCA counterpart (0.6390 / 0.6197) and far above the scGPT swap (0.5251 / 0.4979). In this single-variable comparison, scVI beat PCA, so learned RNA embeddings do not underperform as a group here and scVI becomes the stronger default RNA encoder. The ~4-point gain is larger than the ViT-L difference that looked like noise, but it still comes from single runs with unknown seed/split variance. Several questions remain open: whether the gain comes from the scVI latent space itself or its lower dimensionality (200 vs 2000), whether it holds in RNA-only, concat, or other aggregator settings, and whether a smaller F1 gain than accuracy gain means the improvement is uneven across classes.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The current best is config_031 (scVI n=200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.6776 accuracy / 0.6464 F1). The only test of whether image adds value was a single-profile PCA comparison, where it gave about +4 points (0.5266 vs 0.4849). Image-only performance is weak (0.21). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L changed nothing, which suggests the image branch may contribute little in the strong setup, possibly because weighted fusion down-weights it. Multiprofile aggregation has also never been tested without images. 2) What this tests: RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool is config_031 with the image branch and fusion removed. It shows how much of the best result comes from RNA plus multiprofile aggregation alone, and whether the image modality still helps once the RNA encoder is stronger. It also gives the first evidence on whether multiprofile aggregation helps RNA-only models. 3) Why now: the result changes where the remaining budget should go. If RNA-only nearly matches 0.678, further image-encoder or fusion tuning is a poor use of experiments, and RNA-side or aggregation choices deserve more attention. If it falls well short, the multimodal direction is confirmed and fusion and image refinements around config_031 are justified. Exploitative runs like config_037 (scVI + ViT-L) are less informative given that the ViT-L swap already showed no gain.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with an scVI n=200 encoder and avgpool aggregation. This is the current best configuration (llm_summary_009) with the ResNet50 image branch and weighted fusion removed, to estimate how much of that result comes from RNA plus multiprofile aggregation alone. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6501 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.6275, about 2.8 points accuracy and 1.9 points F1 below the multimodal counterpart (0.6776 / 0.6464), yet above every PCA-based multimodal run (best 0.6390). This suggests RNA accounts for most of the best result, while the image branch with weighted fusion adds a modest increment, smaller than the ~4-point image gain seen in the single-profile PCA comparison (which differed in encoder and profile setting, so the two gains are not directly comparable). Uncertainties: the ~2.8-point gap comes from single runs with unknown seed/split variance, though it is larger than the ~0.4-point ViT-L difference judged as noise. Removing images also removed fusion, so the gap reflects the combined image-plus-fusion contribution. Without an RNA-only single-profile scVI run, this result does not isolate whether multiprofile aggregation helps RNA-only models, since the only RNA-only single-profile baseline used PCA (0.4849).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we do not know how any modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice performs. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration, with no aggregation or fusion components. It sets a reference point for validation accuracy and F1. Later experiments can each change one factor from it: swapping the RNA encoder (config_004 or config_007), switching to multiprofile with avgpool (config_002), comparing against image-only (config_010), or adding fusion (config_016). 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Without a simple baseline, no later result can show whether added complexity such as foundation-model encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or multimodal fusion actually helps. Starting at the minimal configuration keeps future comparisons clean and attributable to single design choices.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 and a validation F1 of 0.464. Because no other configurations have been completed, these numbers are only a reference point and say nothing yet about whether other encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image inputs, or multimodal fusion would help or hurt. It also remains unknown how this score compares to chance or majority-class performance (the number of classes and class balance were not provided) and how much it would vary across random seeds, so later single-factor comparisons against this baseline should be read with that variance in mind.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the only result is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). Nothing is yet known about the image modality, even though image encoders appear in 42 of the 50 remaining configurations, including every multimodal one. 2. Test: an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion gives a clean modality baseline at the same simplest profile setting. It shows whether imaging carries useful signal on its own and roughly how strong it is compared with RNA. 3. Why now: under a limited budget, this result decides how much effort the large multimodal portion of the search space deserves. If images are weak, fusion may add little; if they are competitive or complementary, multimodal fusion becomes a strong candidate. That makes it more informative than first tuning RNA encoders or aggregation within the RNA-only branch. ResNet50 is the simpler image encoder, which gives a natural reference before testing ViT-L or multiprofile variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It established the first image-modality baseline at validation accuracy 0.208 and F1 0.172, well below the RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This is an initial observation that ResNet50 image features carry weaker standalone signal than the PCA RNA features under this simple setting, but it compares only one encoder per modality. It cannot show whether images are weak in general, whether ResNet50 is a poor encoder for these data (ViT-L is untested), or whether image features add complementary information when fused with RNA. It also remains uncertain how 0.208 compares with chance or majority-class performance, since class count and balance are unknown, and how much results vary across seeds. Multimodal configurations therefore should not be ruled out on this evidence alone.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: two baselines exist. The RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile model reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. The image-only ResNet50 single-profile model reached 0.208 and 0.172. RNA looks much stronger alone, but we do not know whether image features add complementary signal or only add noise. Fusion is the most consequential untested design axis. 2) Test: config_016 changes only one thing from config_001. It adds the already-tested ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion and keeps the PCA-2000 RNA encoder and single-profile setting. Because both of its components have known standalone scores, any change from 0.485 can be attributed cleanly to adding the image modality. 3) Why now: this answers early whether the large multimodal half of the search space is worth exploring. Concat is the simplest fusion, so it isolates the modality effect before weighted fusion, ViT-L, or other RNA encoders are tested. Multiprofile aggregation and alternative RNA encoders remain good follow-ups once we know whether fusion helps.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that concatenates PCA-2000 RNA features with ResNet50 image features, with no aggregation. Its only change from the RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001) was adding the image modality through concat fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.527 and F1 0.510, compared with 0.485 / 0.464 for RNA-only and 0.208 / 0.172 for image-only. This is an initial single-run observation that adding ResNet50 image features via concat improved validation accuracy by about 4 points, with F1 moving the same way, so images may carry signal complementary to RNA despite their weak standalone performance, and the multimodal part of the search space looks worth exploring. Several things remain uncertain: whether a gain of this size exceeds seed-to-seed variance, which is unmeasured; the mechanism behind it (complementary information versus added capacity or other effects); and whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), other image encoders (ViT-L), alternative RNA encoders, or multiprofile aggregation would enlarge, shrink, or reverse this benefit.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is multimodal PCA-2000 + ResNet50 with concat fusion in single-profile mode (0.527 accuracy / 0.510 F1). That is about 4 points above RNA-only (0.485 / 0.464), with F1 agreeing. However, the profile setting (single vs. multiprofile) and aggregation have never been tested, so they are the largest unexplored design axis. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps everything in config_016 the same (PCA-2000, ResNet50, concat) and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile with the simplest aggregator, avgpool. Any accuracy or F1 difference can therefore be attributed to multiprofile aggregation in the current best setting. 3. Why now: this both exploits the most promising configuration and opens a whole untested dimension. If avgpool helps, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion become natural next steps. If it hurts or does nothing, we can focus the budget on encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) and fusion instead. A single run cannot separate a small gain from seed noise, so only a clear difference should guide the next choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best prior configuration (multimodal PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, concat fusion; llm_summary_003) and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation. Profile setting and aggregation changed together, since single-profile runs use no aggregator. Validation accuracy reached 0.619 and F1 0.610, versus 0.527 / 0.510 for the single-profile counterpart. This is about a 9-point accuracy gain, with F1 rising by a similar amount, making it the best result so far and the largest single-step improvement observed. It suggests multiprofile aggregation is a promising axis to explore further, but several points remain uncertain. This is a single run with unmeasured seed variance, although the gain is about twice the earlier multimodal-vs-RNA gain. The design cannot separate the effect of having multiple profiles from the choice of avgpool, so whether other aggregators (e.g., transformer) or other fusion methods would add to the gain is untested. It is also unknown whether a similar benefit would appear in RNA-only or image-only multiprofile settings, and how these scores compare with chance or majority-class performance.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: switching to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation gave the largest gain so far. The best config_018 reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1, against 0.527 / 0.510 for its single-profile version. However, that run changed profile setting and aggregation together, so it cannot show whether avgpool itself is a good aggregator. Transformer aggregation is untested anywhere. 2) Test: config_020 keeps everything from config_018 the same (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, concat fusion, multiprofile) and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. This isolates the aggregation choice. A gain would show that learned aggregation across profiles adds value. A tie or drop would suggest most of the benefit comes from having multiple profiles, with simple pooling being enough. 3) Why now: aggregation is the axis that has produced the biggest improvement, so refining it makes good use of the strongest evidence. The single-factor contrast is easy to interpret, and the result tells us which aggregator to carry forward when testing fusion type, image encoder and RNA encoder.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, concat fusion, multiprofile input) and swapped only the aggregator, replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation. This is a single-factor contrast. Validation accuracy fell to 0.579 and F1 to 0.563, versus 0.619 / 0.610 for avgpool, a drop of about 4 points in accuracy with F1 moving the same way. The result still sits well above the single-profile multimodal run (0.527 / 0.510). This is an initial single-run observation that learned transformer aggregation did not improve on simple pooling here, consistent with most of the multiprofile benefit coming from having multiple profiles rather than from a learned aggregator, so avgpool is the current choice to carry forward. Uncertainties remain: seed variance is unmeasured; the transformer's hyperparameters, training budget and possible overfitting were not explored, so the gap may reflect tuning rather than an inherent weakness; and whether the ranking would hold with other fusion methods, image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), RNA encoders, or unimodal multiprofile settings is untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Adding multiple profiles helped (about 9 points), adding images helped (about 4 points), and the transformer aggregator underperformed avgpool. RNA is clearly the dominant modality (0.485 RNA-only vs 0.208 image-only), yet every run so far has used PCA-2000. The RNA encoder is the least explored design choice that could plausibly have a large effect. 2) What this tests: config_042 keeps config_018 exactly and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This single-factor comparison asks whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA within the best pipeline found so far. 3) Why it is the best use of budget: Because RNA carries most of the signal, the RNA representation probably has more leverage than fusion type or image encoder. Testing it within the strongest pipeline gives both exploitation (it could raise the best result) and exploration (it addresses an untested axis). Weighted fusion (config_019) and ViT-L (config_024) remain good follow-ups once the RNA encoder question is answered.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to the pretrained scGPT representation, a single-factor contrast. Validation accuracy fell to 0.512 and F1 to 0.477, compared with 0.619 / 0.610 for PCA-2000. This is a drop of about 11 points in accuracy and 13 in F1, and it leaves the run below even the single-profile PCA multimodal run (0.527 / 0.510). This initial single-run observation suggests that scGPT embeddings, as used here, did not improve on PCA-2000 within this pipeline, and that PCA-2000 is the RNA encoder to carry forward. Uncertainties remain. Seed variance is unmeasured, though the gap is large relative to earlier differences. How scGPT was applied (frozen vs. fine-tuned, embedding extraction, gene vocabulary overlap, preprocessing) is unknown, so the drop may reflect integration or tuning rather than an inherent weakness of the representation. It is also untested whether the ranking holds in RNA-only settings, with other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), or with other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat), at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Earlier single-factor swaps favored PCA-2000 over scGPT and avgpool over a transformer aggregator. The image encoder has never been varied. ResNet50 was weak on its own (0.208 accuracy) yet still added about 4 points when fused with RNA. That leaves open whether image features are inherently weak here or ResNet50 is simply a poor fit. 2. What this tests: Swapping only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L, with everything else in config_018 kept the same, isolates the effect of the image representation. It tests whether a stronger image encoder increases the multimodal gain. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: Image representation is the main design axis still completely unexplored. A single-factor change from the best configuration keeps the comparison clean. It also has a realistic chance of a direct improvement, so it serves both exploration and exploitation. Weighted fusion (config_019) and an RNA-only multiprofile control (config_002) remain good follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and swapped only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, a clean single-factor contrast on the previously unexplored image axis. Validation accuracy rose to 0.629 from 0.619, about +1 point and nominally the new best on the primary metric. Validation F1 fell to 0.599 from 0.610, about -1 point, so the supporting evidence points the opposite way. This is an initial single-run observation that ViT-L is at least competitive with ResNet50 in this pipeline, but it gives no clear evidence that a stronger image encoder meaningfully enlarges the multimodal gain. Both differences are small relative to the earlier gains of 4 to 11 points and may lie within the unmeasured seed variance; the opposing accuracy and F1 shifts could reflect a change in per-class balance of predictions. It also remains untested how ViT-L performs on its own (image-only), whether it would benefit more from other fusion methods (e.g., weighted) or settings, and how much the multimodal model gains over an RNA-only multiprofile control.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool gave the largest gain so far, +9 points for the multimodal PCA-2000 + ResNet50 concat model (0.619 vs 0.527). The image encoders differed only slightly: ViT-L had +1 point accuracy but -1 point F1. All evidence that images help comes from the single-profile comparison (0.527 vs 0.485), a 4-point single-run gain with unmeasured seed variance. There is no RNA-only multiprofile control, so we cannot tell whether the best multimodal models (0.62-0.63) actually beat a simpler RNA-only multiprofile model. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the best RNA encoder (PCA-2000), the multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, and removes the image modality.
