Compared with config_018, it isolates the image contribution in the multiprofile regime. Compared with config_001, it isolates the multiprofile/avgpool effect for RNA alone. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It resolves a central design question in one run, namely whether multimodality is worth its cost once multiprofile aggregation is used. The answer should guide how the remaining budget is spent. If RNA-only multiprofile matches the multimodal models, further fusion and image-encoder tuning (weighted fusion, ViT-L variants) becomes less of a priority. If it falls clearly below them, that supports exploiting fusion choices next, such as weighted fusion in config_019 or config_025.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 ran the RNA-only multiprofile control: PCA-2000 RNA with avgpool aggregation and no image encoder or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.591 and F1 0.573. That is about 10.6 accuracy points above the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.485 / 0.464), which suggests the multiprofile/avgpool benefit is not specific to multimodal models, although profile setting and aggregator change together in that contrast. Removing images from the matched multimodal configuration lowered accuracy by about 3 points relative to the ResNet50 model (llm_summary_004: 0.619 / 0.610; F1 about -4) and by about 4 points relative to the ViT-L model (llm_summary_007: 0.629 / 0.599; F1 about -3). This is an initial single-run observation that images still add a modest benefit in the multiprofile regime, similar in size to the single-profile gain of about 4 points, while most of the improvement over the original baseline appears to come from multiprofile input. Seed variance is unmeasured, so it remains uncertain whether this 3-4 point image gain is robust enough to justify further fusion and image-encoder tuning (e.g., weighted fusion) over cheaper RNA-only exploration, and whether other RNA encoders or aggregators would change the gap.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation and the PCA-2000 RNA encoder are the supported choices so far. Multiprofile gave about +9 to +11 points, avgpool beat transformer by about 4, and PCA beat scGPT by about 11. Images add a modest 3-4 points over RNA-only multiprofile. ViT-L and ResNet50 are roughly tied. Fusion is the only design axis never varied: every multimodal run used concat. 2. What this tests: Swapping concat for weighted fusion in the nominal best configuration (config_024: multiprofile, PCA-2000, ViT-L, avgpool) is a clean single-factor test. It asks whether learned modality weighting extracts more from the image signal than plain concatenation, and whether it changes the accuracy/F1 imbalance seen with ViT-L. 3. Why this is the best use of budget: It exploits the strongest region of the search space while also resolving the largest remaining untested design choice. Either outcome is informative. A gain would set a new best and justify further fusion tuning. No gain would support keeping concat and redirecting budget to other axes such as scVI or seed-variance checks.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the nominal best configuration (llm_summary_007: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image, avgpool aggregation) and swapped only concat for weighted fusion, the first single-factor test of the previously unvaried fusion axis. It reached validation accuracy 0.635 and F1 0.618, versus 0.629 / 0.599 for concat. That is about +0.7 accuracy points and +1.9 F1 points, nominally the new best on both metrics, and it narrows the accuracy/F1 gap seen with ViT-L from about 2.9 to about 1.7 points. It also sits about 1.7 accuracy points above the ResNet50 concat model (0.619 / 0.610) and about 4.5 above the RNA-only multiprofile control (0.591 / 0.573). This is an initial single-run observation that weighted fusion is at least competitive with concat and may help class balance, but the accuracy gain is small relative to earlier 4 to 11 point effects and may lie within the still-unmeasured seed variance. It remains untested whether the effect holds with ResNet50 or other settings, what modality weights were learned, and whether further fusion tuning is worth more budget than seed-variance checks or other RNA encoders such as scVI.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The current best is multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool and weighted fusion (0.635 / 0.618). The largest effects so far came from multiprofile input (about +9-11 points) and from the RNA encoder (scGPT about -11 points versus PCA). The recent image-encoder and fusion changes moved results by only about 1 point, which may be within seed noise. The scVI-200 RNA encoder is the one major untested level on the axis that has shown large effects. 2. What this tests: Swapping only PCA-2000 for scVI-200 in the best configuration is a clean single-factor contrast. It shows whether a compact, count-aware latent RNA representation beats, matches or falls short of PCA, which tells us whether PCA's lead over scGPT reflects pretrained embeddings specifically or applies to learned representations generally. 3. Why this is the best use of budget: Small fusion or image-encoder refinements are unlikely to produce meaningful gains. The RNA encoder has shown large swings and leaves a genuine open question, so this experiment offers both a plausible chance of a new best and high information value about a key design choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_009: multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L image, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) and swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, a clean single-factor contrast on the axis that had shown large effects. Validation accuracy rose to 0.706 and F1 to 0.667, compared with 0.635 / 0.618 for PCA-2000. That is about +7.1 accuracy points and +4.9 F1 points, the new best on both metrics and the second-largest single-step gain after the multiprofile switch. This initial single-run observation suggests that a compact, count-aware learned RNA latent can clearly beat PCA, so PCA's earlier lead over scGPT (about 11 points) likely reflects something about the pretrained scGPT embeddings or how they were integrated, not a weakness of learned representations in general. Several points remain uncertain. Seed variance is unmeasured, though the gain is large relative to the roughly 1-point image and fusion effects. The accuracy/F1 gap widened from about 1.7 to about 3.9 points, which may indicate a shift in per-class prediction balance. It is also untested whether scVI's advantage holds with ResNet50, concat fusion, or RNA-only multiprofile settings, whether other scVI latent sizes or training choices would do better, and whether the earlier small image and fusion effects keep their ranking with the stronger RNA encoder.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters, and no reference point for judging gains. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest configuration in the space. It sets a baseline accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against. Each later comparison can then change one factor at a time: scVI or scGPT for the encoder, multiprofile avgpool for the profile setting, image-only to compare modalities, then fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, a simple anchor makes every later result easier to interpret. It also guards against assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better without evidence. Starting from a complex configuration would mix many factors and leave no reference for attributing its performance.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as the simplest, cheapest anchor configuration. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.4639 (supporting). The similar F1 suggests performance is not driven solely by majority-class predictions, though this is not certain. This is an initial reference point only. With no other experiments yet, nothing can be concluded about the effects of encoder choice (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image or multimodal fusion, or run-to-run variance. Future experiments should change one factor at a time relative to this baseline so that any differences can be attributed.

selection_reason: 1) The only evidence so far is one baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA n=2000, with 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. The effects of encoder, profile setting, aggregation, image modality and fusion are all still unknown. 2) config_002 changes exactly one factor from the baseline. It switches to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation, avgpool, and keeps the RNA-only PCA encoder fixed. Any change in accuracy can therefore be attributed to using multiple profiles rather than to encoder or modality changes. 3) Profile setting is a structural choice that affects about two thirds of the remaining search space, so learning its effect early is a high-value use of the budget. Using avgpool keeps the test cheap and avoids mixing in transformer-aggregation complexity. A natural follow-up is a single-factor encoder swap (scVI or scGPT, single-profile) or an image-only baseline.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, and no image encoder or fusion. Relative to the single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001), it changed only the profile setting, which required adding avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (primary metric, about +0.106), and F1 rose in parallel from 0.4639 to 0.5727 (supporting), so this is an initial indication that multiprofile input with avgpool helps the PCA RNA-only setup. However, these are single runs with no variance estimates, the gain cannot be separated between multiprofile input and the avgpool choice (other aggregations are untested), and it is unknown whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models, or fused multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Only RNA-only PCA models have been tested. Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, with F1 rising in parallel. This is a single comparison, and nothing is known about the image modality, even though most remaining configurations (image-only and multimodal) depend on it. 2) This experiment: It keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, avgpool, no fusion) and swaps the RNA PCA input for a ResNet50 image encoder. That gives a direct modality comparison against config_002 and shows whether image features alone carry useful signal. 3) Why now: This is the largest open uncertainty in the search space. A strong image-only result would justify exploring fusion configurations. A weak one would suggest prioritizing RNA encoder and aggregation choices, such as config_003 or config_005. Either outcome steers the remaining budget more efficiently than a smaller refinement within RNA-only models.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested an image-only, multiprofile model with a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, no RNA encoder, and no fusion. It was chosen as a direct modality comparison against the RNA-only multiprofile PCA model (llm_summary_002). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.3275 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.2884 (supporting). Both are well below llm_summary_002 (0.5907 / 0.5727) and also below the single-profile RNA baseline (0.4849 / 0.4639), giving an initial indication that, in this setup, ResNet50 image features carry less label-relevant signal than PCA RNA features. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate, only one image encoder and one aggregation were tried, and it remains unknown whether image features add complementary value when fused with RNA, so the result does not by itself rule out multimodal configurations; it does favor prioritizing RNA encoder and aggregation exploration.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002: 0.5907 acc / 0.5727 F1). It clearly beat the single-profile baseline (0.4849). Image-only ResNet50 multiprofile avgpool was much weaker (0.3275 / 0.2884). The central open question for a multimodal study is whether image features add complementary signal when combined with RNA, even though they are weak on their own. 2) Test: config_018 keeps everything from config_002 the same (multiprofile, PCA RNA, avgpool) and adds only ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Any change relative to config_002, and to config_011, can therefore be attributed to adding the image modality. 3) Why now: this single-factor comparison settles whether the large multimodal half of the search space is worth pursuing. If accuracy and F1 improve, multimodal variants (weighted fusion, ViT-L, other RNA encoders) become a priority. If not, the budget can shift to RNA encoder and aggregation exploration, such as config_005 or config_003. Concat avgpool is the simplest fusion and aggregation, so it gives a clean first read without confounding.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model that combined PCA (n=2000) RNA features and ResNet50 image features using avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Its only change from the best prior run, the RNA-only llm_summary_002, was adding the image modality. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6186 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.6103 (supporting), compared with 0.5907 / 0.5727 for llm_summary_002 (about +0.028 accuracy, +0.038 F1) and far above image-only llm_summary_003 (0.3275 / 0.2884). This is an initial indication that ResNet50 image features add some complementary signal to RNA despite being weak on their own, and it modestly supports exploring more multimodal variants. However, these are single runs with no variance estimates, so a gain of this size may fall within run-to-run noise. Also, only concat fusion, avgpool aggregation, one image encoder and one RNA encoder were tried, so it is unknown whether the benefit holds or grows with weighted fusion, ViT-L, other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or other aggregations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality. RNA-only multiprofile PCA reached 0.591 accuracy, versus 0.328 for image-only. Adding ResNet50 images gave only a modest, possibly noise-level gain to 0.619. Multiprofile avgpool helped substantially (+0.106 accuracy). Every run so far used the PCA RNA encoder, so the effect of the RNA encoder, likely the most influential remaining choice, is completely unknown. 2) Test: this run swaps PCA (n=2000) for scVI (n=200) in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup, a one-factor change from config_002 (0.591 / 0.573). It isolates whether a learned latent RNA representation beats PCA, without image or fusion effects confounding the result. 3) Why now: because RNA carries most of the signal, the RNA encoder choice will shape every later multimodal configuration. Resolving it early in the cheaper RNA-only setting tells us which encoder to carry forward into fusion experiments. It is more informative than tuning fusion, aggregation or image encoder on top of an encoder that may not be the best choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with an scVI (n=200) RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, and no image encoder or fusion. Its only change from llm_summary_002 was replacing the PCA (n=2000) encoder with scVI. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6501 (primary) and F1 of 0.6275 (supporting), compared with 0.5907 / 0.5727 for llm_summary_002 (about +0.059 accuracy, +0.055 F1), and it also exceeded the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat run llm_summary_004 (0.6186 / 0.6103). This is an initial indication that scVI is a stronger RNA representation than PCA in this setup and a reasonable candidate to carry into multimodal experiments. However, all results are single runs with no variance estimates; the encoder swap also changed latent dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so the gain cannot be attributed specifically to learned versus linear representations; scGPT and other scVI settings are untested; and it is unknown whether image features still add complementary signal when fused with scVI.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is the scVI RNA-only multiprofile avgpool model (config_005, 0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). With PCA, adding ResNet50 image features via concat gave a modest gain (+0.028 accuracy, +0.038 F1), but that gain came from a single run and may be within noise. It is unknown whether image features still add complementary signal when the RNA representation is stronger. 2. What this tests: config_030 changes only one factor from config_005 by adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion. Encoder, profile setting and aggregation stay the same, so this isolates the effect of the image modality on top of scVI. It also mirrors the earlier PCA comparison (config_002 vs config_018), which shows whether the multimodal benefit is consistent across RNA encoders. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It exploits the strongest RNA encoder and has a reasonable chance of becoming the new best configuration. Either outcome resolves a key design question that shapes the rest of the search. If the gain holds, later runs should focus on multimodal variants such as fusion type, ViT-L and aggregation. If it does not, the remaining budget should go to RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) and aggregation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model combining scVI (n=200) RNA features with ResNet50 image features via concat fusion and avgpool aggregation; its only change from the best prior run (RNA-only scVI llm_summary_005) was adding the image modality, mirroring the earlier PCA comparison (llm_summary_002 vs llm_summary_004). It reached 0.6315 validation accuracy (primary) and 0.6068 F1 (supporting), about -0.019 accuracy and -0.021 F1 below llm_summary_005 (0.6501 / 0.6275), whereas adding images to PCA had given +0.028 / +0.038, so this is an initial indication that ResNet50 concat features do not add complementary signal on top of the stronger scVI representation and that llm_summary_005 remains the best configuration. However, all results are single runs with no variance estimates, and both the PCA gain and this scVI drop are small enough to fall within run-to-run noise, so the inconsistency across RNA encoders is not firmly established. It also remains untested whether other fusion schemes (e.g., weighted), image encoders (ViT-L), or aggregations could recover a multimodal benefit, though this result modestly favors directing budget toward RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) and aggregation choices.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input (+0.106 accuracy with PCA) and scVI over PCA (+0.059) are the clearest gains so far. Adding ResNet50 images gave small, inconsistent changes (+0.028 with PCA, -0.019 with scVI), probably within noise. The best run is RNA-only scVI multiprofile with avgpool (0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Aggregation has never been varied: every multiprofile run used avgpool, so we have no evidence on it. 2. What this tests: config_006 changes only avgpool to transformer on that best configuration. It directly measures whether learned attention over profiles beats mean pooling, holding encoder, modality and profile setting fixed. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: The aggregation choice affects every multiprofile configuration, unimodal or multimodal, so the answer guides much of the remaining search. Running it on the strongest backbone also gives a real chance of a new best. The scGPT encoder comparison (config_008) is a close second and should follow, but it covers only one encoder option, while aggregation has no evidence at all.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with an scVI (n=200) RNA encoder and transformer aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. Its only change from the best prior run (llm_summary_005) was replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation, making it the first direct test of aggregation. It reached 0.6530 validation accuracy (primary) and 0.6283 F1 (supporting), versus 0.6501 / 0.6275 for llm_summary_005 (about +0.003 accuracy, +0.001 F1). This is an initial indication that learned attention over profiles performs about the same as mean pooling in this setup, and it is nominally the new best, but the difference is very small and well within plausible run-to-run noise given single runs with no variance estimates. It remains unknown whether transformer aggregation behaves differently with other encoders (PCA, scGPT), in multimodal or fused configurations, or with other transformer settings, so aggregation looks like a low-leverage factor for now compared with untested options such as scGPT.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder has been the strongest lever so far. Swapping PCA for scVI gained about +0.059 accuracy in the RNA-only multiprofile setup. Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer, +0.003) and adding ResNet50 images to scVI (-0.019) both look low-leverage or within noise. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested, which is the largest remaining gap in an important design choice. 2) Test: config_008 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT, avgpool) changes only the encoder relative to config_005 (scVI avgpool, 0.6501 / 0.6275) and config_002 (PCA avgpool, 0.5907 / 0.5727). That gives a clean three-way encoder comparison under identical profile and aggregation settings. 3) Why now: the result decides which RNA backbone to carry into later aggregation, fusion and ViT-L experiments. It does this without confounding the encoder with other factors. Avgpool is used rather than transformer because the two performed nearly the same, and avgpool keeps the comparison matched to both prior encoder baselines.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with an scGPT RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, and no image encoder or fusion. Its only change from llm_summary_005 (scVI, 0.6501 / 0.6275) and llm_summary_002 (PCA, 0.5907 / 0.5727) was the RNA encoder, which completes a matched three-way encoder comparison. It reached 0.5305 validation accuracy (primary) and 0.5152 F1 (supporting), about -0.120 accuracy versus scVI and -0.060 versus PCA, though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849). This is an initial indication that the encoder ranking in this setup is scVI > PCA > scGPT, which supports keeping scVI as the RNA backbone for later aggregation, fusion and ViT-L experiments. However, all results are single runs with no variance estimates, and the gap is large enough that noise alone seems an unlikely explanation. Encoder dimensionality and how scGPT embeddings were extracted or adapted (e.g., frozen vs fine-tuned) are uncontrolled, so this result may reflect this particular scGPT setup rather than the model's inherent quality. It also remains untested whether scGPT behaves differently with transformer aggregation or in multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI is the strongest RNA encoder tested (about 0.650 to 0.653 accuracy). Concat-fusing ResNet50 image features with scVI gave 0.632 accuracy, slightly worse than scVI alone. The same addition gave a small gain with PCA (+0.028). Fusion type is entirely untested, and only concat has been tried. One plausible explanation is that concat lets weak image features (image-only accuracy 0.328) dilute a strong RNA signal. 2) Test: config_031 changes only concat to weighted fusion relative to config_030 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates the effect of fusion and asks whether a learned modality weighting can recover a multimodal benefit on top of scVI. 3) Why now: aggregation looked low-leverage (+0.003) and scGPT underperformed, so fusion and image encoder are the main open questions. A one-factor fusion comparison against an existing matched run uses the budget efficiently. It also tells us whether weighted fusion should be carried into later ViT-L multimodal experiments. Validation F1 will be checked as supporting evidence if the accuracy difference is small.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model that combined scVI (n=200) RNA features with ResNet50 image features using avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion. Its only change from llm_summary_006 was replacing concat fusion with weighted fusion, which makes it the first isolated test of fusion type. It reached 0.6776 validation accuracy (primary) and 0.6464 F1 (supporting), versus 0.6315 / 0.6068 for the matched concat run (about +0.046 accuracy, +0.040 F1). It also exceeded the best RNA-only runs, llm_summary_005 (0.6501 / 0.6275) and llm_summary_007 (0.6530 / 0.6283), by about +0.025 to +0.028 accuracy, making it the new best configuration and an initial indication that weighted fusion can recover a multimodal benefit on top of scVI where concat did not. However, all results are single runs with no variance estimates. The learned modality weights were not reported, so the proposed mechanism (concat letting weak image features dilute the RNA signal) is plausible but unconfirmed. It also remains untested whether weighted fusion helps similarly with PCA, transformer aggregation, or ViT-L image features, though this result supports carrying weighted fusion into those experiments.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the current best run is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.6776 accuracy / 0.6464 F1). Weighted fusion appears to recover a multimodal gain that concat did not. The image encoder, however, has never been varied: every image-containing run used ResNet50, which was weak on its own (0.3275 image-only). Aggregation looked low-leverage (transformer vs avgpool gave about +0.003). 2) What this tests: config_037 changes only the image encoder, ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, while keeping the best scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted-fusion setup. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal under weighted fusion. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: it both exploits the leading configuration and resolves the largest untested design factor. A gain would point to a new best direction for later aggregation tests. No gain would suggest image features have limited value, so the remaining budget should go to RNA or aggregation choices. Single runs carry noise, so small differences should be read cautiously, and F1 should be checked as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model combining scVI (n=200) RNA features with ImageNet ViT-L image features using avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion. Its only change from the prior best run, llm_summary_009, was swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L, which makes it the first isolated test of the image encoder. It reached 0.7062 validation accuracy (primary) and 0.6671 F1 (supporting), versus 0.6776 / 0.6464 for llm_summary_009 (about +0.029 accuracy, +0.021 F1), and about +0.053 accuracy over the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_007, 0.6530). This makes it the new best configuration and is an initial indication that a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal under weighted fusion, which supports carrying ViT-L forward. However, all results are single runs with no variance estimates, so a gain of this size may partly reflect run-to-run noise. ViT-L was never run image-only, so its standalone strength relative to ResNet50 (0.3275) is unknown, and the learned modality weights were not reported. ViT-L also differs from ResNet50 in architecture, feature dimensionality and pretraining, so it is unclear which property drives the gain. Untested combinations include ViT-L with concat fusion, ViT-L with transformer aggregation, and ViT-L with other RNA encoders.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 for unimodal RNA performance and serves as the anchor for one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. Changing only the RNA encoder gives config_004 and config_007. Adding multiprofile aggregation gives config_002 and config_003. Adding an image encoder gives config_016 and config_022. 3. Under a limited budget, a simple, cheap baseline is the most informative first step. Gains from complex multimodal or multiprofile models are only interpretable against it, and it avoids assuming that complexity helps before any evidence exists.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a validation F1 of 0.464, which is consistent with roughly balanced performance across classes. This is a reference point for one-factor-at-a-time comparisons: changing only the RNA encoder (config_004, config_007), adding multiprofile aggregation (config_002, config_003), or adding an image encoder (config_016, config_022). Because no other configurations have been evaluated, it is not yet known whether alternative RNA encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image features, or fusion would improve or hurt performance, and the run-to-run variability of this result is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Every other design choice is untested, and we do not know how much results vary from run to run. 2) This experiment changes one thing from the baseline: it switches from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). The RNA modality and PCA encoder stay the same. That isolates whether combining multiple profiles per sample helps, which is a structural choice affecting roughly two-thirds of the search space. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: profile setting and aggregation apply to every modality and encoder, so this answer has the widest reach. Avgpool is the cheapest, lowest-variance way to test it. Its result will guide whether to try transformer aggregation next (config_003) and whether multiprofile options are worth pursuing for image and multimodal models. Encoder swaps (config_004/007) and adding images (config_016) remain natural one-factor follow-ups.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 changed one factor from the llm_summary_001 baseline. It kept the RNA-only model and PCA-2000 RNA encoder but switched from single-profile to multiprofile input, aggregated with avgpool. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (+0.106) and validation F1 from 0.464 to 0.573 (+0.109), so the two metrics moved together. This is an initial signal that multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation may substantially help RNA-only models, though multiprofile and avgpool are bundled here and cannot be separated. It remains uncertain whether the gain exceeds run-to-run variance (each configuration has a single run), whether other aggregators such as the transformer in config_003 would do better or worse, and whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders, image models or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool improved accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591 and F1 from 0.464 to 0.573. That makes multiprofile input the most promising direction so far. However, multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation were changed together, so it is unknown whether a different aggregator would do better or worse. Each result also comes from a single run. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation. It also checks whether the multiprofile gain holds under a different pooling scheme. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: aggregation applies to most remaining configurations, including multiprofile RNA, image and multimodal ones. Settling it now with a cheap, controlled comparison makes later encoder, modality and fusion experiments easier to interpret. It also builds on the strongest current lead rather than changing several factors at once.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 changed only the aggregator from the llm_summary_002 setup (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile), replacing avgpool with a transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 (-0.072) and F1 from 0.573 to 0.480 (-0.093), though both stayed slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1). This controlled comparison is initial evidence that avgpool suits this RNA-only multiprofile setting better than the transformer aggregator, and that some multiprofile benefit may persist across aggregators, but the benefit appears much smaller with the transformer. Each configuration has a single run, so the differences may partly reflect run-to-run variance. It is also unknown whether the transformer was under-tuned or is affected by data size, and whether this aggregator ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image models or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation is the best setting so far (config_002: 0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). It beats the single-profile baseline (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519). Each result is a single run, though, and the image modality has not been tested at all. That leaves the biggest open design question unresolved. 2) Test: config_018 keeps the best configuration fixed (RNA PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. This isolates whether image features add value on top of the strongest RNA-only baseline. It is a cleaner modality test than jumping to an image-only model or changing several factors at once. 3) Why now: Whether multimodality helps decides which half of the search space (33 multimodal configurations) deserves budget. An improvement would also be a direct exploitation gain. If performance does not improve or drops, that is equally useful, because it suggests concentrating on RNA encoder choices in the multiprofile avgpool setting (e.g., config_005 and config_008) instead.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 fixed (PCA-2000 RNA encoder, multiprofile input, avgpool aggregation) and changed only one factor, adding a ResNet50 image branch fused by simple concatenation. This was the first test of the image modality. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619 (+0.028) and F1 from 0.573 to 0.610 (+0.038), the best results so far, with F1 gaining slightly more. This is initial evidence that image features may add modest value on top of the strongest RNA-only configuration and that multimodal configurations deserve further budget. However, each configuration has a single run, and this gain is much smaller than the multiprofile gain (+0.106), so it may partly reflect run-to-run variance. It also remains unknown how an image-only model would perform, whether other image encoders or fusion methods would do better than ResNet50 with concat, and whether the benefit holds with other RNA encoders or aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile input with avgpool gave the largest gain so far (+0.106 accuracy for RNA-only). Adding a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion (config_018) added only a modest +0.028 accuracy and +0.038 F1. Each result comes from a single run, so the image gain could partly be run-to-run variance. We still have no image-only result, so we do not know how much signal the image modality carries on its own. 2) Test: config_011 is the image-only counterpart of config_018, keeping ResNet50, multiprofile input and avgpool. Comparing it with config_002 (RNA-only), config_018 (multimodal) and config_001 (baseline) will show whether images are strong, weak or complementary to RNA, and whether the multiprofile and avgpool advantage carries over to images. 3) Why now: The search space contains many multimodal configurations that vary the image encoder and fusion method. Knowing whether the image modality is informative on its own is the key uncertainty for allocating the remaining budget. If image-only is weak, effort should shift toward RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT. If it is strong, comparing image encoders (ViT-L) and fusion methods becomes the priority.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 tested the first image-only model, the image-only counterpart of llm_summary_004: a ResNet50 image encoder with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation, and no RNA encoder or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 and a validation F1 of 0.288. This is well below the single-profile RNA-only baseline (0.485), the multiprofile avgpool RNA-only model (0.591) and the multimodal concat model (0.619), and its accuracy–F1 gap (0.039) is somewhat wider than in the RNA-only runs. This is initial evidence that ResNet50 image features carry much weaker standalone signal than PCA-2000 RNA features in this setup, while the modest multimodal gain (+0.028 accuracy) suggests images may play at most a small complementary role, so RNA-side improvements (for example scVI or scGPT encoders) look like a reasonable budget priority. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has a single run, so variance is unknown; no single-profile image-only run exists, so it is not known whether the multiprofile/avgpool benefit transfers to images; chance-level performance is not reported; and it is unclear whether a stronger image encoder such as ViT-L would change this picture.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the signal. The RNA-only multiprofile avgpool model reached 0.591, while image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.328, and adding images gave a small +0.028. Multiprofile with avgpool gave the largest gain so far (+0.106). The RNA encoder is still completely untested beyond PCA-2000, so it is the largest open design choice. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, within the best RNA-only setup (multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates whether a learned latent representation beats PCA. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: because RNA dominates, the RNA encoder choice is likely to shape every later multimodal experiment. Testing it in the simpler RNA-only setting avoids confounding with image or fusion effects. The result will tell us whether later multimodal runs should use scVI or stay with PCA, and whether scGPT (config_008) is worth testing next.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder from the llm_summary_002 setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool), replacing PCA-2000 with scVI-200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 (+0.059) and F1 from 0.573 to 0.628 (+0.055), so the two metrics moved together. This also exceeds the multimodal PCA-2000 + ResNet50 concat model (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1), making it the best configuration so far. Because only the encoder changed, this is initial controlled evidence that the scVI-200 latent representation outperforms PCA-2000 in this setting. However, each configuration has a single run, so variance is unknown, and the comparison also changes dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so it is unclear whether the gain comes from the learned latent space itself. It also remains untested whether the scVI advantage carries over to multimodal fusion with images, other aggregators or single-profile input, and whether scGPT (config_008) would do better still.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: the RNA encoder is one of the strongest levers. Swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 and F1 moved similarly, making it the current best. Adding ResNet50 images gave a smaller gain (+0.028), and image-only performance was weak (0.328). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested, which is the largest remaining uncertainty on the most impactful axis. 2) This experiment changes only the RNA encoder (scGPT) relative to config_002 and config_005, keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. That gives a clean three-way encoder comparison under the best known profile and aggregation setting, and shows whether a foundation-model embedding beats scVI. 3) Knowing which RNA encoder is best should come before spending budget on multimodal extensions such as scVI with ResNet50 (config_030). Those combine factors, and their value depends on which RNA backbone multimodal runs should be built on. The test reduces key uncertainty and could also directly yield a new best.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 changed only the RNA encoder from the llm_summary_002 and llm_summary_006 setups (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool), using scGPT embeddings. This completes a controlled three-way encoder comparison. Validation accuracy was 0.530 and F1 was 0.515, well below scVI-200 (0.650 / 0.628) and PCA-2000 (0.591 / 0.573), though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This is initial evidence that the scGPT embeddings, as used here, underperform both scVI-200 and PCA-2000 in this setting, so scVI-200 remains the strongest RNA backbone for multimodal extensions such as scVI + ResNet50. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run, so variance is unknown. It is also unclear whether scGPT's weaker result reflects the embedding itself or factors such as embedding dimensionality, a lack of fine-tuning or preprocessing compatibility. Finally, it is untested whether this encoder ranking holds with other aggregators, single-profile input or image fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is scVI-200 RNA-only with multiprofile input and avgpool (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Separately, adding a ResNet50 branch with concat fusion to the PCA-2000 multiprofile avgpool model gave a modest gain (+0.028 accuracy, +0.038 F1). Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.328), so it is uncertain whether images add anything beyond a stronger RNA representation. 2) Test: config_030 adds ResNet50 with concat fusion to the best scVI-200 multiprofile avgpool setup, changing only one factor. This mirrors the earlier PCA comparison (config_002 → config_018). It shows whether the small image benefit persists, shrinks or reverses once the RNA encoder is stronger. 3) Why now: This is both the most promising exploitation step, since it combines the two components that have each helped so far, and a controlled test of whether the image modality contributes at all. That answer determines whether to spend further budget on image encoders (ViT-L) and fusion variants, or on RNA-side and aggregation choices. Since each configuration has a single run, a small difference should be read cautiously, with F1 as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 added a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best configuration so far, the scVI-200 RNA-only model with multiprofile avgpool input (llm_summary_006), and changed only this one factor. It mirrors the earlier PCA-2000 comparison (llm_summary_002 → llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy fell from 0.650 to 0.632 (-0.019) and F1 from 0.628 to 0.607 (-0.021). This reverses the modest image gain seen with PCA-2000 (+0.028 accuracy), leaves scVI-200 RNA-only as the best configuration, and ranks just above PCA-2000 + ResNet50 on accuracy (0.632 vs 0.619) but slightly below it on F1 (0.607 vs 0.610). Together with the weak image-only result (0.328), this is initial evidence that ResNet50 features with concat fusion add little or nothing once the RNA representation is stronger, which tentatively favors spending budget on RNA-side and aggregation choices over more ResNet50/concat variants. However, each configuration has a single run, and both the earlier gain and this drop are small enough that they may reflect run-to-run variance. It also remains untested whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or a different fusion method would extract complementary image signal that concat with ResNet50 does not.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: scVI-200 RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool is the best run so far (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion slightly hurt it (0.632 / 0.607), but helped the weaker PCA backbone (+0.028). ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.328). So it is unclear whether the image branch has no complementary value or whether concat fusion fails to use it, for example by letting noisy image features dilute a strong RNA signal. Fusion method is the one major design factor not yet tested at all. 2) What this tests: config_031 changes only concat to weighted fusion relative to config_030, keeping scVI-200, ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion matches or exceeds the RNA-only result, the earlier drop was a fusion problem and multimodal models stay worth exploring. If it still falls below RNA-only, that strengthens the case for putting budget into RNA-side and aggregation choices, or into testing ViT-L as a last image check. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: it is a clean single-factor comparison on the strongest backbone, it tests a factor with zero evidence so far, and it has a realistic chance of becoming the new best. In contrast, the transformer aggregator already underperformed with PCA, and scGPT variants look weak.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 changed only the fusion method from llm_summary_008 (scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool), replacing concat with weighted fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.632 to 0.678 (+0.046) and F1 from 0.607 to 0.646 (+0.040), making this the best configuration so far, ahead of the scVI-200 RNA-only model (0.650 / 0.628; +0.027 accuracy, +0.019 F1). This controlled comparison is initial evidence that the earlier multimodal drop with scVI-200 may have reflected concat fusion rather than a lack of image value, so multimodal configurations with weighted fusion remain worth exploring. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run, and the margin over RNA-only is small enough that it may partly reflect run-to-run variance. It is also unknown whether weighted fusion draws complementary image signal or mainly down-weights the weak image branch (image-only scored 0.328; learned weights are not reported), and whether the benefit holds with PCA-2000, a stronger image encoder such as ViT-L, or other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI-200 is the strongest RNA encoder so far, ahead of PCA-2000 and scGPT. Multiprofile avgpool beats both single-profile input and the transformer aggregator. Weighted fusion with ResNet50 gave the best result (0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1), whereas concat fusion fell below the RNA-only model. The image branch is still the weak, uncertain part: ResNet50 image-only scored only 0.328, and the ViT-L encoder has never been tested. 2) Test: config_037 keeps the best configuration fixed (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds complementary signal beyond what weighted fusion extracts from ResNet50. 3) Value: the experiment both exploits the current best direction and explores a design dimension that has had no evaluations at all. A gain would point to the image representation as the bottleneck. No gain or a loss would suggest the images add little and the remaining budget should go to RNA-side or aggregation choices. Either outcome is informative under the limited budget.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 changed only the image encoder from the previous best configuration, llm_summary_009 (scVI-200 RNA encoder, multiprofile input, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion), replacing ResNet50 with ImageNet ViT-L. This was the first ViT-L evaluation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.678 to 0.706 (+0.029) and F1 from 0.646 to 0.667 (+0.021), making it the best configuration so far and widening the margin over the scVI-200 RNA-only model (0.650 / 0.628) to +0.056 accuracy. This controlled comparison is initial evidence that the image representation was a bottleneck and that a stronger image encoder can add complementary signal under weighted fusion. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run, so a gain of this size may partly reflect run-to-run variance; no ViT-L image-only run exists, so ViT-L's standalone signal is unknown; learned fusion weights are not reported; and it is untested whether the ViT-L benefit holds with concat fusion, PCA-2000, or other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so we have no information about how well any modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice performs. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration. It sets a reference point for validation accuracy and F1. Later experiments can then be built as one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against it: scVI or scGPT for representation (config_004/007), multiprofile avgpool for profile setting (config_002), and multimodal concat for fusion (config_016). 3. Why it is the best first use of the budget: it is cheap, easy to interpret, and makes no assumption that complex or multimodal models will help. Every later gain from added complexity can be measured against this baseline, which makes the rest of the budget more informative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration as a first baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. Because no other experiments have been run, this is only an initial reference point and says nothing yet about whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or multimodal fusion would help or hurt. Open questions include run-to-run variance and how this accuracy compares with chance level for the task. Later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against this baseline are needed before attributing any performance difference to a specific design choice.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Only one baseline exists so far: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000, at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. No design factor has been isolated yet. 2) Test: config_002 changes a single factor, moving from single-profile to multiprofile. It uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and keeps the same RNA-only PCA setup. This isolates whether pooling several profiles per sample helps, without confounding it with encoder or modality changes. 3) Why now: Profile setting runs through most of the remaining search space, since multiprofile appears in most RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations. Measuring its effect early, with the cheapest aggregator, tells us whether to prioritize multiprofile options. A follow-up can then test the transformer aggregator (config_003). Encoder and modality comparisons can follow against the same baseline.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 changed only the profile setting relative to the llm_summary_001 baseline, moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, while keeping the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) setup with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (about +0.106), and validation F1 rose from 0.4639 to 0.5727 (about +0.109), so the two metrics agree. This is the first one-factor comparison in the study, and it suggests that pooling multiple profiles per sample may substantially help RNA-only PCA models. However, the evidence is a single run per configuration with unknown run-to-run variance, and the multiprofile change is bundled with the avgpool aggregator, so it remains open whether the gain is robust, whether other aggregators such as the transformer would do better or worse, and whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile avgpool raised RNA-only PCA accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose by a similar amount. The best current setting is therefore RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA, avgpool. The image modality, which drives most of the remaining search space, is still completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the best setting fixed and changes one thing, adding a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion. This directly measures whether imaging adds information beyond RNA under the current best profile and aggregation choice. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Most remaining configurations (36 of 49) are multimodal. Learning early whether adding images helps or hurts will decide whether to pursue the fusion and image-encoder branches or focus on RNA encoders and aggregators. The aggregator question (config_003) is narrower and can follow.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the best prior setting (multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation) and added a ResNet50 image encoder with concat fusion, making it the study's first multimodal run and a direct comparison against the RNA-only llm_summary_002. Validation accuracy rose modestly from 0.5907 to 0.6186 (about +0.028), and validation F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6103 (about +0.038), so the metrics agree. This is an initial signal that imaging may add information beyond RNA, making it the current best configuration. However, the gain is small, comes from a single run with unknown variance, and bundles the image modality with one specific encoder (ResNet50) and fusion method (concat); it also remains unknown how image-only models perform and whether other image encoders, fusion strategies, or aggregators would increase or erase this improvement.

selection_reason: Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile for RNA-only PCA (0.485 to 0.591). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave a smaller further gain (0.591 to 0.619), with F1 agreeing. That modest multimodal gain is hard to interpret without knowing how images perform alone. The images might carry most of the signal, or very little. Test: config_011 is image-only ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool. It is the image-only counterpart of the current best (config_018) and of RNA-only config_002, so only the modality changes. This completes a clean three-way modality comparison under identical profile and aggregation settings. Why now: knowing whether imaging is weak, comparable to RNA, or stronger tells us where to spend the remaining budget. It shows whether to prioritize image encoders (ViT-L vs ResNet50) or RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), and whether fusion choices are worth exploring. It also guards against assuming multimodal is better, which matters more right now than a small exploitative tweak.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool aggregation, the image-only counterpart of RNA-only llm_summary_002 (PCA n=2000) and multimodal llm_summary_003 (PCA + ResNet50, concat). This completes a three-way modality comparison under identical profile and aggregation settings. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.3275 (F1 0.2884), far below RNA-only (0.5907 / 0.5727) and multimodal (0.6186 / 0.6103), so under this setup ResNet50 image features appear much weaker on their own than RNA PCA features, even though adding them to RNA gave a small gain. Uncertainties remain. Each configuration was run only once, so run-to-run variance is unknown. The weak image result is tied to the ResNet50 encoder and may not reflect the imaging modality in general; a ViT-L encoder could differ. It is unclear how far 0.3275 sits above chance. The modest multimodal gain could reflect a real complementary signal or noise.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only PCA multiprofile reached 0.591, image-only ResNet50 only 0.328, and adding images gave a small gain to 0.619. Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile (+0.106 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). The RNA encoder is still untested: every RNA run so far used PCA n2000, yet it is the strongest modality. 2. Test: config_005 swaps PCA for scVI (n200) and keeps the rest of config_002 fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates the RNA representation effect in a clean one-factor comparison. 3. Why now: because RNA dominates performance, the RNA encoder is likely the design choice with the largest remaining impact. A one-factor result here tells us whether later multimodal runs should build on PCA or scVI, before spending budget on smaller factors like fusion or aggregation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 changed only the RNA encoder relative to llm_summary_002, swapping PCA (n=2000) for scVI (n=200) while keeping the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6501 (about +0.059), and F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6275 (about +0.055), so the two metrics agree. This one-factor comparison suggests scVI may give a stronger RNA representation than PCA in this setting. The RNA-only scVI run also exceeds the current multimodal PCA + ResNet50 result (0.6186 / 0.6103), which suggests later multimodal runs may be better built on scVI. However, each configuration was run only once and run-to-run variance is unknown, and the encoder swap also changes latent dimensionality (2000 to 200), so the effect of the method cannot be separated from the effect of dimensionality. It also remains untested whether the scVI advantage holds in single-profile, multimodal, or other-aggregator settings, and whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) would do better.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Each of the following is a single run with unknown variance. Multiprofile avgpool beat single-profile (+0.106 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion to PCA RNA gave a small gain (0.591 to 0.619). Swapping PCA for scVI in the RNA-only setting gave a larger gain (0.591 to 0.650). Image-only ResNet50 is weak (0.328). The open question is whether the small image gain is a real complementary signal or whether a stronger RNA representation makes it disappear. 2. Test: config_030 combines scVI and ResNet50 under multiprofile avgpool with concat fusion. It differs by one factor from two completed runs: it adds images to RNA-only scVI (config_005), and it swaps PCA for scVI in multimodal config_018. This tests whether the scVI advantage holds in the multimodal setting and whether images still help on top of the best RNA encoder. 3. Why now: It is the most plausible candidate for a new best accuracy, and it answers an important modality question with a clean comparison against two existing runs. Tests of scGPT, ViT-L, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion can then build on whichever base wins.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 combined the scVI (n=200) RNA encoder with ResNet50 images (multiprofile, avgpool, concat fusion). It differs by one factor from two earlier runs: it adds images to RNA-only scVI (llm_summary_005), and it swaps PCA for scVI in multimodal llm_summary_003. It reached validation accuracy 0.6315 (F1 0.6068), which is below RNA-only scVI (0.6501 / 0.6275, about -0.019 accuracy and -0.021 F1), so adding ResNet50 images with concat did not help on top of scVI and may slightly hurt. Against multimodal PCA (0.6186 / 0.6103), accuracy rose about +0.013 but F1 fell slightly (about -0.004), so the scVI advantage seen in the RNA-only setting appears much weaker here and the metrics do not clearly agree. RNA-only scVI therefore remains the best configuration so far, but every comparison rests on single runs with unknown variance and small differences. It is still unclear whether the earlier small image gain with PCA was real complementary signal or noise, and whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), a different fusion method (e.g., weighted), or a transformer aggregator would let images add value beyond scVI.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA drives most of the performance. Moving to multiprofile gave about +0.106 accuracy, and swapping PCA for scVI gave about +0.059. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion did not help on top of scVI (0.6315 vs 0.6501). The best configuration so far is RNA-only scVI, multiprofile, avgpool (0.6501 accuracy, 0.6275 F1). Aggregation is the one major design axis never tested: every multiprofile run so far used avgpool. 2) What this tests: config_006 changes only avgpool to transformer on the current best configuration. This isolates whether learned attention over profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: it is a clean one-factor comparison against the strongest baseline, so it has a real chance of improving the best result. Whichever way it turns out, the answer will guide all later multiprofile runs, both RNA-only and multimodal. That makes it more informative under the limited budget than further tweaks to fusion or the image encoder, where images have so far added little. Testing scGPT (config_008) is a strong next candidate after this.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the aggregation of the best configuration so far, the RNA-only, multiprofile scVI (n=200) setup from llm_summary_005, from avgpool to transformer, making it the study's first test of a learned aggregator. Validation accuracy was 0.6530 versus 0.6501 (about +0.003) and F1 was 0.6283 versus 0.6275 (about +0.001); the metrics agree in direction, and this run is now nominally the best configuration. The gains are very small and rest on single runs with unknown run-to-run variance, so the evidence does not show that transformer aggregation is meaningfully better than mean pooling; the two look roughly equivalent in this RNA-only scVI setting. It remains untested whether the transformer aggregator matters more with PCA features, in multimodal runs where it might help images add value, or with other RNA encoders such as scGPT.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA encoder has been one of the largest levers so far. Swapping PCA for scVI gave about +0.059 accuracy in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting, and the F1 change agreed. Other choices had smaller effects: transformer aggregation added only about +0.003, and ResNet50 images added little or even hurt with scVI. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is entirely untested. 2. Test: Config_008 changes only the RNA encoder (scVI to scGPT) relative to config_005, keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. It also directly matches the PCA run (config_002), giving a clean three-way encoder comparison. This shows whether a foundation-model RNA representation beats scVI and which RNA backbone later multimodal or aggregator runs should use. 3. Why now: Image encoder and fusion questions (ViT-L, weighted fusion) remain open. But the evidence so far points to RNA representation as the main driver of accuracy, so settling the RNA backbone first is the best use of the next run. It avoids spending many multimodal runs on a possibly weaker encoder, and it is both exploratory (an unseen encoder) and plausibly high-performing.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed only the RNA encoder of the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup, swapping in scGPT, which completes a three-way encoder comparison with PCA n=2000 (llm_summary_002) and scVI n=200 (llm_summary_005). scGPT reached validation accuracy 0.5305 (F1 0.5152), well below both scVI (0.6501 / 0.6275; about -0.120 accuracy and -0.112 F1) and PCA (0.5907 / 0.5727; about -0.060 and -0.058); the two metrics agree. Under this setup, the scGPT representation was therefore the weakest of the three, and scVI remains the preferred RNA backbone for later multimodal or aggregator runs, with RNA-only scVI plus transformer (0.6530) still nominally best overall. Each configuration was run only once, so run-to-run variance is unknown. The encoders also differ in embedding dimensionality and in how the embeddings are produced (e.g., scGPT pretrained versus fine-tuned, unspecified), so this result may reflect this particular scGPT usage rather than foundation-model representations in general. It is also untested whether the ranking holds with single-profile, transformer aggregation, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.650 vs 0.591 for PCA and 0.530 for scGPT). Transformer and avgpool aggregation look about equal (+0.003). Images have not clearly helped. ResNet50 image-only scored 0.328. Adding ResNet50 to scVI with concat fusion lowered accuracy slightly (0.632 vs 0.650), although adding it to PCA raised accuracy a little. The largest untested design choice is the image encoder, since ViT-L has never been run. It is therefore unclear whether the weak image results reflect the imaging modality itself or just ResNet50. 2) What this tests: config_036 changes only the image encoder relative to config_030 (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, concat). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L isolates whether a stronger image representation lets images add value on top of the best RNA backbone. Comparing it with RNA-only scVI (config_005) also shows directly whether multimodality beats the current best. 3) Why this is the best use of the next run: it tackles the most important open question, whether images are worth including, in the setting that matters most for the final model. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best result. Weighted fusion and transformer-aggregated multimodal runs can be judged better once the image encoder question is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 swapped the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L in the multimodal, multiprofile scVI (n=200) setup with avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, changing only this one factor relative to llm_summary_006. It also gives a direct comparison against RNA-only scVI (llm_summary_005). It reached validation accuracy 0.7150 (F1 0.6872), well above scVI + ResNet50 (0.6315 / 0.6068; about +0.084 accuracy and +0.080 F1) and above RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.6501 / 0.6275; about +0.065 / +0.060) or with transformer aggregation (0.6530 / 0.6283), with both metrics agreeing. This makes it the new best configuration and suggests that the earlier weak image contribution was tied to ResNet50 rather than to the imaging modality itself, so ViT-L image features appear to add complementary value beyond the scVI RNA features. Uncertainties remain: each configuration was run only once with unknown run-to-run variance, though this gain is larger than earlier small differences. ViT-L has not been tested image-only or combined with the PCA backbone. It is also untested whether weighted fusion or transformer aggregation would add further gains in this multimodal ViT-L setting.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The current best is config_036 (multimodal scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. It clearly beats RNA-only scVI (about 0.650), which suggests ViT-L images add complementary signal. Fusion method has never been varied; every multimodal run used concat. Aggregation was tested once, in RNA-only scVI, where transformer and avgpool were roughly equivalent (+0.003). 2. What this tests: config_037 changes only fusion, from concat to weighted, on the best configuration. This isolates the effect of the fusion strategy, a design dimension that is still completely untested. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It explores an unknown factor while exploiting the strongest configuration, so it can both improve performance and show whether fusion matters. The transformer-aggregator variant (config_038) is less informative because prior evidence suggests a small aggregation effect. Image-only ViT-L (config_014) is a useful diagnostic, but it is unlikely to improve the best result and can come later.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 changed only the fusion method of the best configuration so far, llm_summary_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n=200 + ViT-L, avgpool), from concat to weighted. This is the study's first test of fusion strategy. It reached validation accuracy 0.7062 (F1 0.6671) versus 0.7150 (F1 0.6872) for concat, about -0.009 accuracy and -0.020 F1. The metrics agree in direction, so weighted fusion gave no improvement and may be slightly worse here, while still clearly beating RNA-only scVI (0.6501 / 0.6275); concat with ViT-L remains the best configuration. Each configuration was run only once and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the accuracy gap in particular may be within noise. It also remains untested whether the fusion ranking holds with transformer aggregation, other encoders, or different weighted-fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so we have no information about any design choice: modality, RNA or image encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. 2. What this tests: The simplest model (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 features, no aggregation or fusion) sets a baseline accuracy and F1. Each later experiment can then change one factor from this anchor, such as swapping the encoder to scVI or scGPT, switching to multiprofile with avgpool, or adding image features. That makes the effect of each change easy to attribute. 3. Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting with a complex multimodal configuration would bundle several untested choices together, so any result would be hard to interpret. A cheap, interpretable baseline makes all subsequent comparisons informative. It also checks whether added complexity is needed at all.
experiment_summary: This first experiment set a baseline with the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model using PCA features (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.464. The similar accuracy and F1 suggest no severe class imbalance in performance, but this is an initial observation only. With no other experiments to compare against, it is unknown whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or adding image features would improve results, so this run should serve as the reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.485 validation accuracy and 0.464 F1. Nothing yet shows whether representation, profile setting, aggregation, or modality matters. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the RNA-only PCA encoder and changes one factor, single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles helps. The design choice applies to every modality and encoder, and avgpool gives a clean, low-complexity check before trying transformer aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: a one-factor comparison against the baseline reduces uncertainty about a structural axis that shapes most of the remaining search space (36 of the 50 untested configurations are multiprofile). Comparing RNA encoders (config_004 or config_007) would be similarly informative, but the profile-setting result tells us more about which branch of the space to prioritize.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the RNA-only pca_n2000 baseline (llm_summary_001) fixed and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile, using average pooling across profiles. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (+0.106), and validation F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573, so the gain is consistent across both metrics. Because this is a one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that multiprofile input helps for this RNA-only PCA setup. Uncertainties remain: each setting has only one run with no variance estimate, multiprofile cannot be separated from the avgpool choice, and it is untested whether the gain holds with other RNA encoders, other aggregators such as transformers, or image and fused modalities.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573. This makes multiprofile the most promising direction so far. However, the multiprofile effect is currently tied to one aggregator, so we cannot yet tell whether avgpool is a good choice or merely adequate. 2. Test: config_003 keeps everything from the current best (config_002: rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation. If the transformer helps, profile interactions matter and later multiprofile runs should use it. If it does not, the simpler avgpool becomes the default. 3. Why now: it extends the strongest evidence with a clean one-factor comparison. Its answer also shapes many remaining configurations, both RNA-encoder and multimodal ones, that depend on the aggregation choice. That makes it more informative per experiment than changing encoder or modality at this point. Encoder (scVI/scGPT) and image modality comparisons can follow with the aggregator settled.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the current best configuration (llm_summary_002: rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) fixed and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 (-0.072), and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480. Both metrics moved the same way, so this one-factor comparison is initial evidence that avgpool works better than this transformer aggregator in the RNA-only PCA multiprofile setting, and it supports keeping avgpool as the default for now. The result is still uncertain: each configuration has a single run with no variance estimate, and the transformer may be undertuned or less suited to this data size (its hyperparameters and training details are not reported). It is also unknown whether the ranking holds with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or with image and fused modalities.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: all three runs used the RNA-only pca_n2000 encoder. Multiprofile with avgpool is the best result (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It beat single-profile by about 0.106 and beat transformer aggregation by about 0.072, with F1 moving the same way both times. The RNA encoder choice is still untested, and so is the image modality. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. It is a clean one-factor test of whether the representation matters. It also checks whether the multiprofile/avgpool gain carries over to a different encoder. 3) Why this is the best next step: it builds on the strongest evidence so far while resolving a major open design choice. The answer decides which RNA encoder to carry into the many later multimodal configurations, all of which are paired with a specific RNA encoder. That makes it a high-value use of limited budget. Image-only baselines (for example config_011) remain an important next step after this.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_002: rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 (+0.059) and validation F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.628, making this the new best result. Because this is a one-factor comparison with both metrics moving the same way, it is initial evidence that the scVI representation outperforms PCA in this setup, and it suggests the multiprofile/avgpool setup still works with a different encoder, though single-profile and transformer variants were not rerun with scVI. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with no variance estimate, scVI also differs from PCA in dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so the source of the gain cannot be isolated, other encoders such as scGPT are untested, and it is unknown whether the advantage holds once image or fused modalities are added.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: In the RNA-only multiprofile setting, avgpool beat the transformer with PCA (0.591 vs 0.519). Swapping PCA for scVI under avgpool gave the current best result (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is untested. Every multimodal configuration depends on which RNA encoder is chosen. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from scVI to scGPT. That completes the encoder comparison in one clean step and shows whether a foundation-model embedding beats scVI. 3) Under a limited budget, settling the best RNA encoder first is efficient, because it narrows the large multimodal space before image and fusion runs are spent. Either result is useful: scGPT becomes the new best, or scVI is confirmed as the anchor for later image and fusion comparisons. Image-only and multimodal runs remain important next steps once the RNA backbone is settled.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_004: rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from scvi_n200 to scGPT. Validation accuracy fell from 0.650 to 0.530 (-0.120) and validation F1 fell from 0.628 to 0.515. That puts scGPT below both scVI and PCA (0.591 under the same setup). Both metrics moved the same way, so this one-factor comparison is initial evidence that scVI is the strongest of the three RNA encoders here and supports keeping scVI as the RNA anchor for later image-only and multimodal runs. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with no variance estimate, and the scGPT embedding's dimensionality, preprocessing, and whether it was fine-tuned or frozen are not reported, so scGPT may be suboptimally configured rather than inherently weaker. It is also unknown whether the encoder ranking holds with other aggregators, single-profile input, or image and fused modalities.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA side is now fairly well mapped, though each result is a single run. Multiprofile beat single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485), avgpool beat transformer (0.591 vs 0.519), and scVI was the best RNA encoder (0.650), ahead of PCA (0.591) and scGPT (0.530).
