A clean early answer on whether multiprofile adds value will therefore guide many later choices. Avgpool is the lowest-complexity way to get that answer, so it avoids mixing the profile effect with transformer aggregation. Image-only and alternative-encoder baselines remain natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 changed one factor from the llm_summary_001 baseline. It kept the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) encoder with no image input or fusion, and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with average-pooling aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (about +0.106), and F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573, which suggests that pooling across multiple profiles helps in this RNA-only PCA setting. The comparison treats 'multiprofile with avgpool' as a single change, so it cannot separate the benefit of multiple profiles from the choice of pooling. It also does not show whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders, image or multimodal inputs, or transformer aggregation. Each configuration has only one run and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the size of the gain should be confirmed before it is relied on.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: only RNA-only PCA models have been tested. Multiprofile input with avgpool gave a large gain over single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485 accuracy, with F1 rising similarly), so multiprofile avgpool is the strongest setting so far. The image modality is entirely untested, yet it underlies most of the remaining search space (image-only and all multimodal configurations). 2) Test: config_011 keeps the best-known profile and aggregation setting (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the modality, from RNA (PCA) to image (ResNet50). This shows whether image features alone carry useful signal, roughly how they compare with RNA, and whether the multiprofile benefit appears for images too. 3) Why now: the result decides whether the large multimodal and image branches deserve budget. If images are weak, effort can shift to RNA encoders and aggregation. If they are competitive, fusion experiments become well motivated. That makes it a more valuable next step than refining aggregation (config_003) or the RNA encoder (config_005).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 changed one factor from the best configuration so far (llm_summary_002). It kept multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation and no fusion, but replaced the RNA PCA (n=2000) input with image-only ResNet50 features, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.328 and F1 of 0.288, well below the RNA-only multiprofile result (0.591 / 0.573) and also below the single-profile RNA baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This is the first image observation and suggests that, in this setup, ResNet50 image features alone carry less usable signal than RNA PCA features, so images may be better suited as a complementary input in fusion than as a standalone modality. Uncertainties remain: the change swaps modality and encoder together, so weak image signal cannot be separated from a poor fit of ResNet50 features or avgpool to images; no single-profile image run exists to show whether multiprofile pooling helps images; and with single runs and unknown chance level and variance, it is unclear how far above chance this result is or whether adding images could still improve multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1). Image-only ResNet50 under the same multiprofile avgpool setting is much weaker (0.328 / 0.288). It is still unknown whether image features add complementary signal when combined with RNA, or only add noise. 2) Test: config_018 keeps everything from the best configuration (PCA n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features through the simplest fusion, concat. This isolates one question: does adding the image modality help, hurt, or do nothing relative to the 0.591 RNA-only anchor? 3) Value: Whether to use multimodal input decides which part of the large remaining space is worth exploring, since most untested configurations are multimodal. One clean comparison against the strongest anchor answers that before budget goes to fusion-type, image-encoder or aggregation variants. Encoder (scVI/scGPT) and transformer-aggregation tests can follow once the value of multimodality is clearer.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 changed one factor from the best configuration so far (llm_summary_002, RNA-only multiprofile PCA n2000 with avgpool, 0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1). It added ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion and kept the RNA encoder, multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation fixed. Validation accuracy rose to 0.619 (about +0.028) and F1 to 0.610 (about +0.038), which gives an initial indication that images add some complementary signal to RNA even though image-only performance was weak (0.328 / 0.288). Each configuration has a single run and run-to-run variance is unknown, so this modest gain may not exceed noise and should be confirmed with repeats. It is also not yet known whether other fusion methods, image encoders, RNA encoders (scVI/scGPT) or transformer aggregation would enlarge, shrink or reverse the multimodal benefit.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is the dominant signal source. RNA-only multiprofile PCA reached 0.591 accuracy, image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.328, and adding images by concat gave a modest gain to 0.619 accuracy / 0.610 F1 (config_018, the best so far). Multiprofile avgpool clearly helped over single-profile. The RNA encoder, however, has only ever been PCA n2000, so the choice of RNA representation is the largest untested factor for the modality that drives performance. 2) Test: this run keeps config_018 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scVI n200. That isolates whether a learned, compact RNA representation improves on PCA within the best pipeline. 3) Why now: because RNA carries most of the signal, the RNA encoder is likely to matter more than fusion type or image encoder. A one-factor change from the current best gives a clean comparison and a realistic chance of a new best result. If scVI helps, the next steps can test scGPT and the aggregation and fusion choices on top of it. If it does not, it supports PCA as the RNA encoder. With single runs, a small difference in either direction should be treated as tentative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 changed one factor from the previous best (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion, PCA n2000 RNA encoder, 0.619 accuracy / 0.610 F1) by replacing the RNA encoder with scVI n200, the first test of a non-PCA RNA representation. Validation accuracy rose to 0.632 (about +0.013), making this the new best on the primary metric, but F1 fell slightly to 0.607 (about -0.004), so the evidence is mixed: scVI may give a small accuracy gain without a matching improvement in class-balanced performance. Because each configuration has a single run and run-to-run variance is unknown, this small difference is tentative and may be within noise. It is also untested whether scVI's effect holds in RNA-only or single-profile settings, under other aggregation or fusion choices, or relative to scGPT or other scVI latent sizes.

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: The current best is config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool, concat), at 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. Adding images helped modestly: 0.591 to 0.619 with PCA. But image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.328), so the image encoder may be limiting how much the image modality contributes. The image encoder has never been varied, which makes it one of the largest untested design choices.
2. What this tests: Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L in the best configuration, with everything else fixed, isolates the image representation. If accuracy and F1 rise clearly, the image encoder was a bottleneck and ViT-L should become the default image backbone for later fusion and aggregation tests. If performance is flat or worse, image features are likely only a minor complement and the budget should go to RNA encoder, aggregation or fusion choices.
3. Why this is the best next use of budget: It is a clean one-factor comparison against the strongest configuration, so it has reasonable odds of a new best. Whatever the result, it settles an important open design axis. Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion are also untested, but each is a further refinement whose value depends on which image features are being fused. Fixing the image encoder first makes those later comparisons easier to interpret. With single runs and unknown variance, a small difference should be treated as tentative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed one factor from the previous best (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 RNA, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion, 0.632 accuracy / 0.607 F1), replacing the ResNet50 image encoder with ImageNet ViT-L. This was the first test of an alternative image backbone. Validation accuracy rose to 0.715 (about +0.084) and F1 to 0.687 (about +0.080), making it the new best on both metrics. Because only the image encoder changed, the gain is attributable to that swap in this configuration, and it suggests that ResNet50 features were limiting the image contribution. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run and variance is unknown, though this gain is much larger than earlier increments. No image-only ViT-L run exists to show how much standalone signal ViT-L carries. It is also untested whether the benefit holds with PCA RNA, transformer aggregation, other fusion methods or other image encoders, which makes ViT-L a reasonable but provisional default image backbone for later experiments.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Moving to multiprofile with avgpool gave one of the largest gains seen (+0.106 for RNA-only PCA). However, every multiprofile run has used avgpool. Whether the aggregation method itself matters, beyond simply having multiple profiles, is completely untested. Fusion (weighted) and scGPT are also untested, but those are encoder- and fusion-level choices. Aggregation sits directly on the axis that produced the biggest gain. 2. Test: Changing only the aggregation of the current best from avgpool to transformer isolates the effect of learned, attention-based pooling over profiles. All other settings stay fixed: scVI, ViT-L, concat fusion and multiprofile input. 3. Why now: This one-factor change both exploits the strongest configuration and resolves a major open design question. If transformer aggregation helps, it may give the next large improvement. If it does not, avgpool can be kept as the default and later experiments can focus on fusion (config_037) or the RNA encoder (scGPT, config_048). Single runs with unknown variance mean small differences should still be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed one factor from the previous best (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, concat fusion, avgpool, 0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1) by replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation. This was the first test of learned, attention-based pooling over profiles. Validation accuracy rose slightly to 0.721 (about +0.006), technically a new best on the primary metric, but F1 fell to 0.681 (about -0.006). The evidence is therefore mixed and suggests that transformer aggregation gives at most a marginal benefit over avgpool in this configuration, not a large new gain. Each configuration has a single run and variance is unknown, so these small opposite-direction changes may be within noise. It is also still untested whether transformer aggregation matters more with other RNA encoders (e.g., PCA, scGPT), other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), or RNA-only settings, so avgpool and transformer should currently be treated as roughly equivalent choices.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the leading configurations are both multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 plus ViT-L with concat fusion. Avgpool scored 0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1 and transformer scored 0.721 / 0.681, so the two aggregations look roughly equivalent and may differ only by noise. The fusion method is the one major design dimension never tested, since every multimodal run has used concat. The gain from adding images (+0.03 with ResNet50) and the large gain from switching to ViT-L (+0.08) suggest that how the two modalities are combined could matter. 2. What this tests: config_037 changes only concat to weighted fusion, starting from config_036 (scVI, ViT-L, avgpool). That isolates the fusion effect against the simpler, best-F1 baseline. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it gives a clean one-factor answer on a completely unexplored dimension. It is also plausibly competitive with the current best, so it balances exploration and exploitation. Testing scGPT (config_048) or transformer plus weighted fusion (config_039) would follow naturally once the fusion effect is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed one factor from llm_summary_006 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool; 0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1), replacing concat fusion with weighted fusion. This was the first test of a non-concat fusion method. Validation accuracy fell slightly to 0.706 (about -0.009) and F1 fell to 0.667 (about -0.020), so in this configuration weighted fusion gave no benefit and may be slightly worse than concat, with the F1 drop the clearer of the two signals. Each configuration has a single run and variance is unknown, so the accuracy difference may be within noise. It is also untested whether weighted fusion behaves differently with transformer aggregation, PCA or scGPT RNA encoders, or other image encoders, so concat remains the provisional default rather than a demonstrated optimum.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best results so far come from the multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 + ViT-L, concat setup. Avgpool gave 0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1. Transformer aggregation gave 0.721 / 0.681, which is roughly equivalent. Weighted fusion did not help. The image encoder swap gave by far the largest gain. Fusion and aggregation now look like secondary choices. The RNA encoder axis is still open, because scGPT has never been tested in any setting. 2. What this tests: config_048 changes only the RNA encoder, from scVI n200 to scGPT, relative to config_036. This gives a clean one-factor test of whether a foundation-model RNA representation beats scVI in the strongest pipeline. I chose avgpool over transformer as the base because it is the simpler choice, gave the better F1, and has a cleaner comparison chain. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: It addresses the largest untested design choice and could plausibly produce a new best. Further tweaks to fusion or aggregation in the current setup look likely to give only marginal changes within noise.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 was a one-factor test against the best avgpool pipeline (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool, concat; 0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1), replacing the scVI n200 RNA encoder with scGPT, the first scGPT run in any setting. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.518 (about -0.197) and F1 to 0.484 (about -0.204). This is below even the RNA-only multiprofile PCA result (0.591 / 0.573) and close to the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485 / 0.464), so in this configuration scGPT embeddings performed much worse than scVI and appear to have degraded the multimodal model rather than simply adding less signal. Because only the RNA encoder changed, the drop is attributable to that swap here, and it is far larger than earlier noise-level differences. However, with a single run, no RNA-only scGPT run, and no scGPT tests under other aggregation or fusion choices, it remains unclear whether the cause is the scGPT representation itself or how its embeddings were extracted, normalized or integrated with concat fusion. Until that is checked, scVI n200 should remain the default RNA encoder.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best results (about 0.715–0.721 accuracy) come from multimodal scVI + ImageNet ViT-L. The largest single gain in the search (+0.084) came from swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L. Image-only has only been tested with ResNet50 (0.328), so we do not know how much standalone signal ViT-L carries. We also do not know whether RNA still adds much once a strong image encoder is used. 2. What this tests: config_014 is image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool. It differs from config_011 only in the image encoder, which isolates ViT-L's standalone image signal. It differs from config_036 only by removing RNA, which shows how much RNA and fusion add on top of ViT-L images. 3. Why now: This directly checks the assumption that multimodal fusion is needed. If image-only ViT-L comes close to 0.715, the simpler model may be enough and later experiments should focus on image-side choices. If it falls well short, that confirms the two modalities complement each other and justifies further fusion and RNA-encoder work. Either outcome informs the remaining budget more than another small aggregation or fusion tweak.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested image-only ImageNet ViT-L features with multiprofile avgpool aggregation and no RNA or fusion. It differs by one factor from llm_summary_003 (image encoder: ResNet50 to ViT-L) and from llm_summary_006 (RNA and concat fusion removed). Validation accuracy was 0.332 (F1 0.315), essentially the same as image-only ResNet50 (0.328 / 0.288; about +0.004 accuracy, +0.027 F1) and far below multimodal scVI + ViT-L (0.715 / 0.687; about -0.383). This suggests that ViT-L's large gain in the multimodal setting did not come from much stronger standalone image signal, that RNA supplies most of the usable signal, and that multimodal fusion remains necessary, since image-only ViT-L is not a viable simpler alternative. It remains unclear why ViT-L helped so much in fusion but not alone (for example, complementarity with scVI, or limits of the image-only head or pooling), and no RNA-only scVI multiprofile run exists to measure how much images add on top of scVI. All results are single runs with unknown variance and unknown chance level, so the small image-only differences may be noise.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest baseline. It has no aggregation or fusion and uses a standard, non-learned RNA representation. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 that later changes can be compared against one factor at a time: scVI or scGPT encoders (config_004, config_007), multiprofile pooling (config_002), image-only models (config_010), and multimodal fusion (config_016). 3) With a limited budget, a cheap and interpretable anchor is worth more as a first run than a complex multimodal configuration. If a complex model were run first and did well or badly, we could not tell which of its design choices was responsible. The baseline also shows whether added complexity is needed at all.
experiment_summary: The first completed experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA-2000 RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.464. Because no other configurations have been run, this is an initial reference point only. It does not show whether alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile pooling, image-based inputs, or multimodal fusion would help or hurt. Also unknown are the number of classes, the chance level, and run-to-run variance, so the absolute quality of this baseline and how large a later difference must be to count are uncertain. Future comparisons should change one factor at a time relative to this anchor.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: There is only one data point so far. The RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 baseline reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We do not yet know which design axis matters most. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes one factor relative to that anchor. It switches from single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), and keeps the same RNA-only PCA-2000 setup. Any difference is therefore attributable to profile setting rather than to encoder or modality. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: Profile setting is a high-leverage choice. Most remaining configurations, both unimodal and multimodal, are multiprofile, so learning early whether pooling multiple profiles helps will shape where the rest of the budget goes. Avgpool is the cleanest first test because it adds no learned aggregation parameters. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and image-only or multimodal anchors remain natural follow-ups. A single small difference should be read cautiously, since run-to-run variance is unknown.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup from the llm_summary_001 baseline and changed one thing: it switched from single-profile to multiprofile input, aggregated with parameter-free average pooling. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591, and validation F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573, so multiprofile pooling looks promising for this RNA-only PCA setting. Because this is one run per configuration with unknown run-to-run variance, chance level and class count, the size and reliability of the roughly 0.11 gain are uncertain. The test also cannot separate the benefit of multiple profiles from the choice of avgpool, and it says nothing about whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-based models, multimodal fusion, or learned aggregation methods.

selection_reason: Evidence: we have only two runs, both RNA-only with PCA-2000. Switching from single-profile to multiprofile avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591 (F1 0.464 to 0.573). That is promising but comes from one run each. The image modality, which is about half of the search space (image-only and all multimodal configurations), is completely untested. This experiment keeps the profile setting (multiprofile) and aggregation (parameter-free avgpool) the same as the current best, config_002. It replaces the RNA input with the ResNet50 image encoder. That gives a direct test of whether image features alone carry useful signal compared with RNA. Changing the modality necessarily changes the encoder too, so it is the cleanest available test of the image side. It is a better use of budget than small RNA refinements such as transformer aggregation or scVI. The result decides whether the many image-only and multimodal configurations are worth pursuing, and it shows whether the multiprofile pooling gain may extend beyond RNA.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 was the first test of the image modality. It used an image-only, multiprofile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and parameter-free avgpool aggregation, matching the profile and aggregation settings of the current best run (llm_summary_002) but replacing the RNA PCA-2000 input. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 (F1 0.288), well below the multiprofile RNA-only run (0.591) and the single-profile RNA-only baseline (0.485). In this setup, ResNet50 image features alone look weaker than PCA RNA features. Because modality and encoder changed together, this cannot be read as a statement about images in general: another image encoder, learned aggregation, or a single-profile image run (needed to check whether multiprofile pooling helps images) might behave differently. Each configuration has one run, and variance, class count and chance level are unknown, so the size of the gap and how much useful signal the image features carry are uncertain. Whether image features add complementary value when fused with RNA also remains untested, so this result alone should not rule out multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the RNA-only PCA-2000 model improved from 0.485 to 0.591 accuracy when switched to multiprofile avgpool (config_002). ResNet50 image-only multiprofile avgpool was much weaker at 0.328 (config_011). That weak result does not tell us whether image features add complementary signal when combined with RNA, and over half of the remaining search space is multimodal. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration's settings fixed (RNA-only PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only the ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Any difference from config_002 can therefore be attributed to adding the image modality. 3) This is the best use of the next run because whether fusion helps or hurts decides whether the large block of multimodal configurations deserves budget. If fusion does not help, the search can focus on RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation choices. If it helps, fusion type and image encoder become worth exploring. Concat is the simplest fusion and reuses components already tested, which keeps the comparison clean.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_002: RNA-only PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619, and validation F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.610, making this the best run so far even though ResNet50 image features alone were weak (0.328 in llm_summary_003). This is initial evidence that the image features may add complementary signal to RNA, which tentatively justifies some budget for multimodal configurations. However, the gain is modest (about 0.03 accuracy) and comes from a single run with unknown variance, class count and chance level, so it may fall within run-to-run noise; it also cannot separate image information from added model capacity or the concat choice, and it does not show how other fusion methods, image encoders, RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or learned aggregation would perform.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The largest effect so far came from switching single-profile to multiprofile in the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup (0.485 to 0.591 accuracy, with F1 rising in step). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave a smaller gain (0.619), which may be within noise given single runs. All multiprofile runs used parameter-free avgpool, so we cannot tell whether the multiprofile benefit is limited by the aggregation choice. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 setup of config_002 and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a learned transformer. This directly isolates the aggregation effect and shows whether the strongest observed lever can be pushed further. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: Aggregation is a design choice that applies to nearly every remaining multiprofile configuration, whether RNA-only, image-only or multimodal. Resolving it in the simplest, strongest RNA-only setting, without confounding from the image branch or fusion, will efficiently prune or prioritise a large part of the remaining search space.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregation, from parameter-free avgpool to a learned transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480. This leaves the transformer only slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464) and well below the best multimodal avgpool run (0.619). Because aggregation was the only factor changed, this is direct initial evidence that the transformer aggregator underperformed avgpool in this setting, so avgpool should remain the default and transformer aggregation should be deprioritised for now. However, it is a single run with unknown variance, class count and chance level, and the cause is unclear: it could reflect undertraining, overfitting or untuned hyperparameters for the added parameters. The result also does not show whether other learned aggregators (e.g., attention pooling) or transformer aggregation in image-only or multimodal configurations would behave the same way.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591, image-only ResNet50 reached 0.328, and adding images gave only a modest gain to 0.619. Multiprofile with avgpool is the best-supported profile and aggregation setting, and the transformer aggregator underperformed it. The RNA encoder has only been tested as PCA-2000, so it is the largest untested factor for the strongest modality. 2) Test: config_008 keeps RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed, matching config_002, and swaps PCA-2000 for scGPT. This isolates the RNA representation effect with a clean one-factor comparison. 3) Why now: a large difference here, in either direction, would redirect the whole multimodal search, since the scGPT-based multimodal configurations depend on it. Tweaks like weighted fusion or a different image encoder probably affect the smaller image contribution and can be tested later on the best RNA backbone.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 kept the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_002: multiprofile, avgpool, no image branch) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scGPT, making this a clean one-factor comparison. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.530, and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.515. This is initial evidence that scGPT embeddings underperformed PCA-2000 in this configuration, so PCA-2000 should remain the default RNA backbone and scGPT-based multimodal configurations should be deprioritised for now. However, this is a single run with unknown variance, class count and chance level, and the cause is unclear (for example, frozen versus fine-tuned embeddings, embedding dimensionality or preprocessing mismatch). The result also does not show how other RNA encoders such as scVI would perform, or whether scGPT would behave differently when fused with image features.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best run so far is config_018 (PCA-2000 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; 0.619 acc, 0.610 F1). It beat RNA-only (0.591), which suggests image features add some complementary signal. ResNet50 alone was weak, though (0.328), so the image branch is the clearest likely bottleneck. Earlier one-factor tests favoured PCA-2000 over scGPT and avgpool over transformer, so those choices can stay fixed. The image encoder dimension (ResNet50 vs ImageNet ViT-L) is completely untested and affects about half of the remaining configurations. 2) Test: config_024 keeps config_018 identical and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain. It also helps show whether the small 0.03 improvement from adding images is real signal that grows with better features, or likely noise or extra capacity. 3) Why now: It is a clean single-factor extension of the current best. It has a plausible chance of producing a new best, and it resolves an important design choice that prunes much of the search space. Concat vs weighted fusion (config_019) and scVI (config_005) remain good next checks.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the previous best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, avgpool, concat fusion) fixed and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, making this a clean one-factor comparison. Validation accuracy rose slightly, from 0.619 to 0.629, making this nominally the best run so far. Validation F1, however, fell from 0.610 to 0.599, so the evidence is mixed rather than a clear win for ViT-L. It may mean the gain in correct predictions is concentrated in larger classes, or the two encoders may simply be equivalent within noise. Because each configuration has a single run and run-to-run variance, class count and chance level are unknown, the roughly 0.01 differences cannot be distinguished from noise. It therefore remains unresolved whether stronger image features increase the multimodal gain, whether ViT-L would beat ResNet50 in an image-only setting (untested), and how ViT-L would interact with other fusion methods (e.g., weighted fusion) or RNA encoders such as scVI.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The two best runs are multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 and avgpool, using concat fusion. These are config_024 with ViT-L (accuracy 0.629, F1 0.599) and config_018 with ResNet50 (0.619 / 0.610). This setup is consistently better than RNA-only multiprofile (0.591). Avgpool beat the transformer aggregator, and PCA beat scGPT, so those defaults look settled for now. The main design choice not yet tested is fusion: weighted fusion has never been tried, and every multimodal gain so far comes from concat alone. 2. Test: config_025 keeps the current best configuration (config_024) fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion. It is a clean one-factor test of whether learned modality weighting adds value. It could down-weight the weaker image branch and preserve the RNA signal. It may also help F1, which dropped with ViT-L. 3. Why now: This tests an important open design choice while exploiting the strongest region of the search space found so far. The result will guide whether later multimodal runs (scVI or ResNet50 variants) should use weighted or concat fusion. Single runs with unknown variance mean only a clear difference should be read as meaningful.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept the previous best configuration (llm_summary_007: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool) fixed and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, a clean one-factor test of learned modality weighting. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.629 to 0.635, making this nominally the best run so far. Supporting F1 rose more clearly, from 0.599 to 0.618, recovering the F1 drop seen with ViT-L under concat and edging past the ResNet50 concat run (0.610). This is initial, mildly favourable evidence for weighted fusion in this setting, but the accuracy gain is under 0.01 from single runs with unknown variance, class count and chance level, so it may be noise. It is also unknown what modality weights were learned, whether the image branch was actually down-weighted, and whether weighted fusion would help with ResNet50 or other RNA encoders such as scVI.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA features drive most of the performance. RNA-only PCA multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591, image-only only 0.328, and adding images gave about +0.03–0.04 on top of RNA. Among RNA encoders, PCA-2000 beat scGPT (0.591 vs 0.530). scVI, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested, so it is the largest remaining unknown in the most influential part of the model. By contrast, the image encoder and fusion comparisons so far show differences of 0.01 or less, likely within noise. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder, to scVI, relative to config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool). This gives a direct three-way comparison of PCA, scGPT and scVI under identical conditions. Running it without the image branch keeps the comparison free of fusion or image-encoder effects. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: the result decides whether scVI-based multimodal configurations (e.g., config_037) are worth testing. If scVI matches or beats PCA, those become the logical next exploitation step. If it underperforms, PCA can be locked in as the RNA backbone and the remaining budget spent on other refinements. Either way, one cheap, cleanly isolated run settles an important design choice.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_002: multiprofile, avgpool, no image branch) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI (n200), completing a clean three-way RNA encoder comparison. It reached validation accuracy 0.650 (F1 0.628), above PCA-2000 (0.591 / 0.573) and scGPT (0.530 / 0.515). It is also the best run overall, beating even the best multimodal PCA run (llm_summary_008, weighted fusion with ViT-L: 0.635 / 0.618) without any image branch. This is initial evidence that scVI embeddings outperform PCA-2000 here, and it makes scVI-based multimodal configurations (e.g., config_037) the logical next test. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with unknown variance, class count and chance level, so the roughly 0.06 gain over PCA may be partly noise. The cause of the gain is unclear (for example, lower dimensionality, learned denoising or batch correction). It is also untested whether adding image features or weighted fusion still helps on top of scVI, given that the image gain with PCA was only about 0.03–0.04.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scVI-200 is the best RNA encoder so far. In the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting it reached 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1, against 0.591 for PCA and 0.530 for scGPT. It even beats the best PCA multimodal run (ViT-L, weighted fusion: 0.635 / 0.618). With PCA, adding images helped only modestly, about 0.03–0.04. The key open question is whether image features still add complementary signal on top of a stronger RNA representation, or whether scVI already captures that signal. 2. What this tests: config_037 keeps the best RNA-only setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds the best-performing image branch and fusion seen so far (ViT-L, weighted). Compared with config_005, it isolates the effect of adding the image modality with scVI. It also directly mirrors the PCA pair config_002 vs config_025, which lets us check whether the multimodal gain carries over across RNA encoders. Weighted fusion is the better choice here because it can down-weight a weak image branch, and it gave better F1 than concat with PCA. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: it answers the most decision-relevant question, whether the remaining budget should go to multimodal scVI configurations or to scVI-only variants. It is also the most likely candidate for a new best. Other options address lower-priority questions: transformer aggregation and scGPT have already underperformed, and the single-profile and image-only ablations matter less right now.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 kept the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_009: scVI-n200, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and added an ImageNet ViT-L image branch with weighted fusion, a one-factor test of adding the image modality on top of scVI. Validation accuracy rose from 0.650 to 0.706 and F1 from 0.628 to 0.667, making this the best run so far. The roughly 0.056 accuracy gain is similar to or slightly larger than the image gain seen with PCA (about 0.045, llm_summary_002 to llm_summary_008), which is initial evidence that image features still add complementary signal with a stronger RNA representation and that budget for multimodal scVI variants is justified. Uncertainties remain: these are single runs with unknown variance, class count and chance level; the gain cannot be separated from added model capacity; the learned modality weights are unknown; and it is untested with scVI whether weighted fusion beats concat or whether ViT-L beats ResNet50. The accuracy–F1 gap also widened slightly (0.039 vs 0.022), so gains may be uneven across classes.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference baseline that later changes can be compared against one at a time: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile avgpool or transformer aggregation, image-only models, and fusion. 3. Why now: under a limited budget, starting with a cheap, interpretable baseline is the most useful first step. Every later result becomes informative relative to it, and if complex multimodal models are run first, their gains cannot be attributed to any single design choice. A natural next step is an image-only single-profile baseline (config_010) to compare modalities.
experiment_summary: This first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single-profile input with a PCA-2000 RNA encoder, and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. The closeness of the two metrics loosely suggests performance is not driven mainly by majority-class predictions, though this cannot be confirmed without class-level or chance-level information. Because no other experiments have been run, this result is only a baseline. It says nothing yet about whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image modalities, or fusion would help, and the result's sensitivity to seed or run variance is also unknown. The planned next step is a matched image-only single-profile baseline (config_010) for a direct modality comparison.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: Only one experiment has been run. The RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 baseline reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We have no information yet about whether the image modality is informative, and that is the largest open question in the design space, since all 36 multimodal configurations depend on it. 2) What this tests: config_010 is a matched image-only, single-profile baseline with ResNet50 and no aggregation or fusion. Comparing it with config_001 isolates the effect of modality while holding the profile setting and model simplicity fixed. It shows whether images alone are weaker than, similar to, or stronger than RNA, which tells us whether fusion is likely to add complementary signal. 3) Why now: this one cheap, single-variable comparison tells us how to prioritize the next experiments. If images are informative, multimodal and image-encoder comparisons become worthwhile. If not, the budget is better spent on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and multiprofile aggregation. Testing an encoder or aggregation variant first would leave the fundamental question of modality value unanswered.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile baseline with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion, as a matched comparison to the RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2079 (F1 0.1718), well below the RNA-only result (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). This is an initial observation that, in this single-profile setting, the image pathway alone is substantially weaker than the RNA pathway. However, modality is confounded with encoder choice (ResNet50 vs. PCA-2000), each result comes from a single run with unknown seed variance, and without a chance-level reference it is unclear whether images carry meaningful signal or whether they could add complementary information under fusion or multiprofile aggregation.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: two single-run, single-profile baselines. RNA-only with PCA-2000 reached 0.485 accuracy (F1 0.464). Image-only with ResNet50 reached 0.208 (F1 0.172). This tentatively points to RNA as the stronger modality. However, the profile setting, aggregation, RNA encoder and fusion axes remain completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the strongest known setup fixed (RNA-only, PCA-2000) and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregator (avgpool). It therefore isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles improves accuracy and F1. 3) Profile setting is a design choice that affects nearly every remaining configuration (most are multiprofile), so resolving it early has high value under a limited budget. Building on the stronger RNA pathway also makes the effect easier to detect. Avgpool is a clean first test before the more complex transformer aggregator, and a gain would also be a plausible step toward higher performance. A matched single-profile multimodal test (config_016) is a natural follow-up once the value of multiprofile input is known.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested RNA-only input with the PCA-2000 encoder under a multiprofile setting with avgpool aggregation. It changed only the profile setting (plus the aggregator it requires) relative to the single-profile RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5907 (F1 0.5727), up from 0.4849 (F1 0.4639), an improvement of about 10.6 points in accuracy with a consistent F1 gain. This is initial evidence that multiprofile input with simple mean pooling helps the RNA pathway. However, each result is a single run with unknown seed variance, and multiprofile input is inherently paired with an aggregator, so the gain cannot yet be attributed to multiple profiles per se rather than to avgpool specifically. It also remains unknown whether the benefit transfers to the image or multimodal settings, other RNA encoders, or the transformer aggregator.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multiprofile RNA-only with PCA-2000 and avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1) clearly beat the single-profile RNA baseline (0.485 acc). However, the gain is tied to one aggregator, so it is unclear how much comes from having multiple profiles and how much from mean pooling specifically. Image-only ResNet50 was much weaker (0.208 acc). 2. Test: config_003 keeps everything from the current best (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000) and changes only the aggregator from avgpool to a transformer. This shows whether aggregation choice matters, and whether a learned aggregator adds to or loses some of the multiprofile gain. If both aggregators land near 0.59, that supports attributing the gain to multiprofile input itself. 3. Why now: Aggregation is a design axis shared by many remaining configurations, including the multimodal and alternative-encoder ones. Settling it with a clean one-factor comparison on the strongest pathway makes later encoder and fusion comparisons more efficient and easier to interpret. It is also a reasonable bet for matching or beating the current best.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested RNA-only, multiprofile input with the PCA-2000 encoder and a transformer aggregator. It changed only the aggregator relative to the current best (llm_summary_003, avgpool: 0.5907 acc, 0.5727 F1) and reached 0.5191 validation accuracy (F1 0.4797), about 7.2 points lower in accuracy with a consistent F1 drop. This is still about 3.4 points above the single-profile RNA baseline (0.4849 acc). As a single-run, one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that aggregation choice matters on this pathway: in this setup, simple mean pooling outperformed the learned transformer aggregator, which kept only part of the multiprofile gain. It remains uncertain whether this gap exceeds seed variance, whether it reflects transformer under-training or tuning (capacity, data size, hyperparameters) rather than an inherent limitation, and whether the avgpool advantage holds for other RNA encoders, image, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 with avgpool (0.5907 acc, 0.5727 F1). Multiprofile with mean pooling beat both the single-profile baseline and the transformer aggregator. Image-only ResNet50 was much weaker (0.2079 acc), but that was single-profile and standalone, so it is still unknown whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA. Whether to include the image modality at all is the largest untested design choice. 2) What this tests: config_018 adds the ResNet50 image pathway with simple concat fusion and keeps everything else identical to the current best (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool). That makes it a clean one-factor test of multimodal fusion, with RNA-only multiprofile avgpool as the matched reference. Concat is the simplest fusion option, which makes it a sensible first probe before comparing it with weighted fusion. 3) Why now: under a limited budget, this result decides whether the large multimodal half of the search space deserves further budget. If fusion helps or matches, later steps can tune fusion type and image encoder. If it hurts, the search can focus on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) in the multiprofile avgpool setting. Either outcome is informative, and the experiment also has a reasonable chance of improving on the current best.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 tested multimodal input by adding the ResNet50 image pathway with simple concat fusion to the current best configuration (PCA-2000 RNA encoder, multiprofile, avgpool), keeping everything else fixed. It is a one-factor comparison against the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reference (llm_summary_003: 0.5907 acc, 0.5727 F1). It reached 0.6186 validation accuracy (F1 0.6103), about 2.8 points higher in accuracy and about 3.8 points higher in F1, making it the new best. This is initial evidence that image features may add complementary signal when fused with RNA, despite the weak standalone image-only single-profile result (0.2079 acc). However, both results are single runs with unknown seed variance, so a gain of this size may not exceed run-to-run noise. It also remains untested whether the benefit holds with weighted fusion, other image encoders, other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or other aggregators, and whether it reflects true complementarity or simply added capacity.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The current best is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.6186 accuracy and 0.6103 F1. Every completed run used the PCA-2000 RNA encoder, so RNA encoder choice is still completely untested. RNA is clearly the dominant modality (0.48 vs 0.21 single-profile accuracy), and multiprofile avgpool has given consistent gains, so this setting is reasonably well supported. 2. Test: This run swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to the pretrained scGPT model and keeps everything else in the best configuration fixed. It is a one-factor comparison that shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation of the strongest modality improves on a linear PCA baseline. 3. Why now: Encoder choice for the dominant modality likely has more headroom than refining fusion (weighted vs concat) or the weaker image pathway. Running it in the best-known context also exploits current evidence, since a gain would likely set a new best. If scGPT does not help, that is also informative and justifies keeping PCA while exploring other axes such as scVI, ViT-L, or weighted fusion. Because this is a single run, a small difference in either direction should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to pretrained scGPT within the current best configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat), making it a one-factor comparison against llm_summary_005 (0.6186 acc, 0.6103 F1). It reached 0.5121 validation accuracy (F1 0.4771), about 10.7 points lower in accuracy and 13.3 points lower in F1. This also puts it below the RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 run (0.5907 acc), so this is initial evidence that, in this setup, scGPT embeddings underperform the simple PCA-2000 representation, with the larger F1 drop hinting at worse class balance. It remains uncertain whether this gap exceeds seed variance (the drop is large, but this is a single run), whether it reflects scGPT itself or how it was used (frozen vs. fine-tuned, preprocessing or gene-vocabulary mismatch, embedding dimensionality, interaction with avgpool or concat), and whether scGPT would fare differently in RNA-only or single-profile settings; scVI, ViT-L, and weighted fusion remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The current best is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat), at 0.6186 accuracy and 0.6103 F1. The RNA pathway carries most of the signal: RNA-only multiprofile reached 0.5907, while image-only single-profile reached only 0.2079. The RNA encoder choice has a large effect: swapping PCA-2000 for scGPT cost about 10.7 accuracy points and 13.3 F1 points. scVI, the third RNA representation, is still untested. ViT-L and weighted fusion are also untested. 2. Test: config_030 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, in the current best setup. This one-factor comparison asks whether a compact, count-aware latent representation can match or beat PCA-2000. It also shows whether scGPT's poor result reflects a general weakness of learned embeddings or something specific to scGPT. 3. Why now: Representation is the design choice with the largest observed effect on the dominant modality. Settling the RNA encoder question first makes later tests of the image encoder and fusion type more meaningful. This run either finds a stronger RNA backbone or confirms PCA-2000 as the base to exploit with ViT-L and weighted fusion. Since all results so far are single runs, small differences should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200 within the previous best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat), making it a one-factor comparison against llm_summary_005 (0.6186 acc, 0.6103 F1). It reached 0.6315 validation accuracy, about 1.3 points higher and the new best by the primary metric, but its F1 was 0.6068, about 0.35 points lower, so the supporting evidence is mixed. The result is initial evidence that scVI-200 performs at least comparably to PCA-2000. Its strong showing, compared with scGPT's drop to 0.5121 acc, suggests scGPT's weakness is not a general property of learned or latent RNA embeddings, although that contrast may also reflect differences in how each encoder was used. Because both runs are single runs with unknown seed variance, a 1.3-point accuracy gain paired with a slight F1 loss may not exceed run-to-run noise, so PCA-2000 and scVI-200 are best treated as roughly tied candidate RNA backbones. Still untested are scVI in RNA-only or single-profile settings, other scVI latent sizes, ViT-L, weighted fusion, and the transformer aggregator with scVI.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The current best is config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.6315 accuracy and 0.6068 F1. PCA-2000 is roughly tied with it. RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation and adding images have each had a one-factor test. The image encoder has never been varied. ResNet50 was weak on its own (0.208 accuracy single-profile), yet adding it still helped fusion by about 3 points. So the image pathway may be the weakest link, and a stronger encoder could matter a lot. 2. What this tests: Swapping only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L in the current best setup, with everything else fixed, isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal under fusion. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: The image encoder is a major untested design axis, and this change could plausibly produce a larger gain than weighted fusion. If ViT-L clearly helps, later experiments can build on it. If it does not, the image encoder is unlikely to be a bottleneck, and the search can focus on the fusion type next. One caveat: these are single runs, so a small difference in either direction should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 swapped only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L in the previous best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, avgpool, concat), making it a one-factor comparison against llm_summary_007 (0.6315 acc, 0.6068 F1). It reached 0.7150 validation accuracy and 0.6872 F1, gains of about 8.4 and 8.0 points, making it the new best on both metrics; the effect is larger than the earlier ~2.8-point gain from adding ResNet50 images. This is initial evidence that the image representation was a meaningful bottleneck and that a stronger pretrained image encoder adds more complementary signal under fusion. Several points remain uncertain: this is a single run with unknown seed variance, though the gain is large relative to earlier small differences. The gain could partly reflect ViT-L's larger embedding size or capacity rather than representation quality alone. ViT-L has not been tested image-only, with PCA-2000, with other aggregators, or with weighted fusion, so it is unknown how much of the improvement comes from standalone image strength versus interaction with scVI and concat fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The current best is config_036 (scVI-200, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. Earlier one-factor comparisons point toward avgpool over the transformer aggregator, PCA/scVI over scGPT, and ViT-L over ResNet50. Fusion is the one design axis never tested: every multimodal run so far used concat, so whether weighted fusion helps is unknown. 2. What this tests: config_037 changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) within the best setup. It is a clean one-factor test of whether learned modality weighting adds anything beyond simple concatenation. That matters because the two modalities differ greatly in standalone strength (RNA is strong, image-only ResNet50 was weak), and weighted fusion could balance their contributions. 3. Why now: it explores an entirely untested design dimension while staying close to the strongest configuration, so it could also yield a new best. If weighted fusion matches or beats concat, fusion becomes a lever worth tuning. If it underperforms, we can fix concat and spend the remaining budget on other questions, such as PCA versus scVI with ViT-L, or image-only ViT-L to check complementarity. Since this is a single run, small differences should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted within the current best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool). This makes it a clean one-factor comparison against llm_summary_008 (0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1), and it is the first test of the fusion axis. It reached 0.7062 validation accuracy and 0.6671 F1, about 0.9 points lower in accuracy and 2.0 points lower in F1, so weighted fusion did not beat concat and the slightly larger F1 drop hints at somewhat worse class balance. Because both are single runs with unknown seed variance, the accuracy gap may be within run-to-run noise, so the safest reading is that weighted fusion is at best comparable to concat here. It remains untested whether weighted fusion would behave differently with other encoders (e.g., the weaker ResNet50 image pathway or PCA-2000), other aggregators, or other tuning of the weighting mechanism. Still open are PCA-2000 vs. scVI-200 with ViT-L and an image-only ViT-L run to gauge complementarity.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L gave the largest single gain so far (0.6315 to 0.7150 accuracy, with F1 up about 8 points) in the multimodal multiprofile setup with scVI, avgpool and concat. Weighted fusion did not beat concat. What remains unclear is where that gain comes from. ViT-L has never been run on its own, and the only image-only result is weak (ResNet50 single-profile, 0.208). So we cannot tell whether ViT-L images now carry most of the signal, or whether they are truly complementary to RNA. 2. What this tests: config_014 is image-only ViT-L with multiprofile input and avgpool. It removes only the RNA branch from the current best (config_036), so it is a one-factor ablation. If it scores near 0.715, RNA adds little on top of strong image features, and later budget should go to the image side and aggregation. If it falls well below, fusion is confirmed as useful. In that case, refining the RNA encoder (PCA vs scVI with ViT-L) becomes the next priority. 3. Why it is the best next run: This single run tells us how much each modality contributes to the best model. That decides where the remaining experiments should go. Tuning around the current best (PCA vs scVI with ViT-L, transformer aggregator) would likely give only small gains that are hard to separate from run-to-run noise.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 removed only the RNA branch from the current best (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, concat; 0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1), leaving an image-only multiprofile ViT-L model with avgpool. This one-factor ablation reached 0.3316 validation accuracy and 0.3150 F1, about 38 points lower in accuracy. That puts it well below RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 (0.5907) but above the ResNet50 image-only single-profile run (0.2079). The latter comparison is confounded by both encoder and profile setting. This is initial evidence that ViT-L image features are weak on their own and that the large ViT-L gain under fusion reflects complementarity with RNA rather than images carrying most of the signal, so fusion appears clearly useful and refining the RNA side (e.g., PCA-2000 vs. scVI-200 with ViT-L) is a reasonable next priority. Several points remain uncertain: this is a single run with unknown seed variance, chance-level performance is unknown, and no scVI-200 RNA-only multiprofile run exists, so RNA's standalone contribution in the best setup is not directly measured. It is also untested whether the image-only gap depends on avgpool, multiprofile input, or ViT-L's interaction with concat fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest, lowest-variance baseline. It sets a reference point that later experiments can change one factor at a time. Swapping the RNA encoder to scVI or scGPT isolates representation. Adding multiprofile with avgpool or transformer isolates profile setting and aggregation. Adding an image encoder isolates the value of multimodal fusion. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: With a limited budget, a clean and interpretable anchor makes every later comparison informative. It also avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will help. Starting with a complex configuration would mix several factors together, and its result would be hard to attribute to any one design choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.464. F1 sits close to accuracy, which loosely suggests performance is not dominated by a few classes, though per-class results were not examined. This is the first completed experiment, so the result is a reference point only, not evidence about any design choice. It remains unknown whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), or adding image features would improve on it. With a single run, the variance of this estimate across seeds or splits is also uncharacterized.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA) scored 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. It is a reference point with unknown variance, and it says nothing yet about any design choice. 2. Test: config_002 changes one factor. It moves from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, keeping the RNA-only PCA setup. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles helps, using the simplest aggregator so that architecture complexity does not confound the result. 3. Why now: profile setting affects every branch of the remaining space (RNA, image and multimodal). Knowing early whether multiprofile aggregation is worthwhile will guide many later choices, and a clean one-factor comparison against the existing baseline is the most informative use of the next run. An encoder swap (e.g., config_004) is an equally clean alternative and a reasonable follow-up.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 changed one factor from the llm_summary_001 baseline: it moved from single-profile to multiprofile input with simple avgpool aggregation, keeping the RNA-only pca_n2000 encoder and using no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591, and validation F1 rose in step from 0.464 to 0.573. Because only the profile setting differs, this is initial evidence that multiprofile aggregation helps in the RNA-only PCA setting. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, so the size and reliability of the roughly 0.11 gain are uncertain. It is also unknown whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), to image-only or multimodal settings, or whether a richer aggregator such as a transformer would add further gains.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool (config_001 to config_002) raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose with it. This is initial but fairly strong evidence that profile aggregation matters. It is still unknown whether the aggregation method itself matters, since simple averaging may discard profile-level structure that a learned aggregator could use. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from the current best config_002 (RNA-only, pca_n2000, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the aggregator. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It builds directly on the strongest signal so far while staying a clean one-factor comparison. Aggregation choice also recurs across many remaining configurations, including image-only and multimodal ones, so knowing whether a transformer is worth it will help prune or prioritize much of the search space. Encoder and modality comparisons are better run once the aggregation question is partly settled. Because each configuration has only one run, a small difference here should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 changed only the aggregator relative to the best prior configuration (llm_summary_002): it replaced avgpool with a transformer while keeping RNA-only input, the pca_n2000 encoder, multiprofile input, and no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480, leaving it only slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This is a clean one-factor comparison, so it is initial evidence that in this RNA-only PCA setting the transformer aggregator, as configured, did not beat simple averaging and may have hurt. The evidence is not conclusive: each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, and transformer training choices (capacity, regularization, optimization, number of profiles) were not explored. It is also unknown whether the result carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only settings, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All three runs so far are RNA-only PCA models. Multiprofile with avgpool is the best so far (0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1). Single-profile (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519) were both clearly worse, though each result is a single run. The image modality is completely untested, yet most of the remaining configurations (36 of 48) depend on image features. 2. What this tests: config_011 keeps the best-performing profile and aggregation setting (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps the RNA PCA input for ResNet50 image features. This gives a direct image-only comparison against config_002. It shows how much signal images carry alone, and it is an early check on whether the avgpool advantage holds in a second modality. 3. Why now: Knowing the strength of the image modality is the largest open question under the limited budget. It determines whether multimodal fusion experiments are worth pursuing and how to interpret their gains. An RNA-encoder swap (e.g., config_005) would be useful, but it would only refine a modality we already have a reference for.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 was the first image-only run. It used ResNet50 image features with multiprofile avgpool aggregation, matching the best prior configuration (llm_summary_002) except that image features replaced RNA pca_n2000 input. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 and F1 of 0.288, well below RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (0.591 / 0.573) and the RNA single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464), with a slightly wider accuracy–F1 gap than the RNA runs. This is initial evidence that ResNet50 image features, as used here, carry less class signal than RNA PCA features. However, modality and encoder change together, so the comparison cannot separate weak image signal from a poorly suited image encoder or feature pipeline, and no image-only single-profile or transformer run exists yet to test whether the avgpool advantage holds in this modality. With single runs and uncharacterized seed and split variance, it is also unknown whether image features add complementary value when fused with RNA, which is the key question for the many remaining image-dependent configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA multiprofile with avgpool (config_002: 0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1). Multiprofile avgpool beat both single-profile and the transformer aggregator. Image-only ResNet50 with avgpool was much weaker (0.328 / 0.288). It is still unknown whether image features add complementary signal when combined with RNA, and most remaining configurations (36 of 47) are multimodal. 2) Test: config_018 keeps everything from config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion. Because only one factor changes, the comparison isolates the effect of adding the image modality. 3) Why now: weak image-only performance does not rule out complementary value, and this result will decide whether the large multimodal branch deserves budget. If it beats config_002, the next steps are fusion type and image encoder. If it does not, the budget can shift toward RNA encoders such as scVI and scGPT.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best prior configuration (llm_summary_002: RNA pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and changed one factor, adding ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.610, making this the best result so far, with a narrower accuracy–F1 gap than any prior run. Because only the image modality was added, this is initial evidence that image features carry signal complementary to RNA PCA, even though image-only performance was weak (0.328 / 0.288), and it supports giving budget to the multimodal branch (fusion type, image encoder). However, the roughly 0.03 accuracy gain is small, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, and it is unknown whether the gain holds with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), other fusion methods, or other image encoders, or whether it partly reflects added input dimensionality rather than image-specific information.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant signal. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, image-only only 0.328, and adding ResNet50 features via concat gave a further 0.619 (F1 0.610). Within RNA, multiprofile avgpool beat both single-profile and the transformer aggregator. The RNA encoder is still the biggest untested axis, since every RNA and multimodal result so far uses pca_n2000, and about two-thirds of the remaining configurations depend on the scVI or scGPT choice. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder (pca_n2000 to scvi_n200) relative to config_002, keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. That gives a clean one-factor comparison of RNA representation quality, without image features or fusion as confounds. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: whether a learned 200-dimensional scVI latent beats 2000-component PCA directly decides which RNA encoder to carry into the multimodal branch. That makes it more informative than smaller multimodal tweaks such as weighted fusion or ViT-L image features, which act on a weaker modality. If scVI wins, configs 030 and 031 become logical exploitation steps. If it loses, budget can go to scGPT or to fusion and image-encoder refinements of config_018.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder relative to llm_summary_002, replacing pca_n2000 with a 200-dimensional scVI latent (scvi_n200) while keeping RNA-only input, multiprofile input, and avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.628. This makes it the best result so far, ahead of the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat run (0.619 / 0.610), even without image features. Because this is a clean one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that scVI is a stronger RNA representation than PCA in this setting and supports carrying scVI into the multimodal branch. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance; the accuracy–F1 gap (about 0.023) is slightly wider than in the multimodal PCA run; scGPT is untested; and it is unknown whether image features still add complementary value on top of scVI, or whether the avgpool-over-transformer advantage holds with this encoder.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI with RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (config_005: 0.650 / 0.628) is the best run so far. It beat PCA in a clean one-factor comparison. Adding ResNet50 through concat fusion helped the PCA model (0.591 to 0.619 accuracy, with a larger F1 gain from 0.573 to 0.610). It is unknown whether the image signal is still complementary once the stronger scVI RNA representation is used, or whether it was only making up for weak PCA features. 2) Test: config_030 keeps config_005 fixed (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes one factor, adding ResNet50 with concat fusion. This mirrors the config_002 to config_018 comparison. The result shows whether the multimodal gain holds on top of scVI. That decides whether the many image-dependent configurations are worth budget, or whether effort should go to RNA encoders such as scGPT. 3) Why now: this is a single-factor exploitation of the two strongest findings so far, and it is a likely candidate for a new best. Either outcome is informative. If it fails to beat 0.650, that is evidence that image features add little beyond a good RNA encoder. Fusion type and the ViT image encoder can then be tested from whichever baseline proves stronger.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best prior configuration (llm_summary_006: RNA-only scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, 0.650 / 0.628) fixed and changed one factor, adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion, which mirrors the PCA comparison from llm_summary_002 to llm_summary_005 where adding images raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.619. Here validation accuracy fell slightly from 0.650 to 0.632 and F1 from 0.628 to 0.607, so this did not produce a new best, and llm_summary_006 remains the strongest configuration. Because only the image modality changed, this is initial evidence that ResNet50 concat features add no measurable value on top of scVI, and that the earlier multimodal gain may have partly compensated for weaker PCA features; this favors directing budget toward RNA-side improvements such as scGPT over image-dependent configurations built on this fusion setup. The roughly 0.02 drop is small, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, and other fusion methods, the ViT image encoder, and possible concat-specific issues (for example, mismatch between the 200-dimensional scVI latent and the image feature scale or dimensionality, or training choices) are untested, so it remains open whether images could still be complementary to scVI under a different integration.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA representation has been the strongest single lever so far. Replacing PCA with scVI in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.628, giving the current best. Adding ResNet50 through concat fusion did not help on top of scVI (0.632 / 0.607). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_008 changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT relative to the best configuration (config_005), keeping RNA-only input, multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation fixed. This cleanly asks whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the most influential design axis found so far and has a realistic chance of a new best. It also tells us which RNA encoder should anchor the many remaining multimodal configurations, including tests of weighted fusion and ViT image features. Weighted fusion is the main alternative, but image-dependent experiments are better chosen once the strongest RNA backbone is known, so the reduction in uncertainty per run is highest here.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed only the RNA encoder relative to the best configuration (llm_summary_006: RNA-only scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, 0.650 / 0.628), replacing scVI with scGPT embeddings and adding no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.530 and F1 to 0.515, well below both scVI (0.650) and PCA (0.591) in the same setting and only modestly above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485 / 0.464). Because this is a clean one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that scGPT embeddings, as used here, are a weaker RNA representation than scVI or PCA, and it supports keeping scVI as the RNA backbone for the remaining multimodal configurations. However, each configuration has a single run with uncharacterized seed and split variance, and scGPT-specific choices were not explored (for example, pretrained versus fine-tuned embeddings, embedding extraction or gene-vocabulary overlap, and embedding dimensionality or scaling relative to avgpool), so it remains open whether scGPT is inherently less informative or poorly integrated in this pipeline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 through concat fusion helped the weaker PCA backbone (0.591 to 0.619) but slightly hurt scVI (0.650 to 0.632). The earlier summary raised a possible cause: concat may handle the mismatch between the 200-dimensional scVI latent and the image features poorly in scale or dimensionality.
